column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Paradox>a statement that although seemingly contradictory or absurd may actually be well-founded or true<; Metaphor>an analogy identifying one object with another and ascribing to the first object one or more of the qualities of the second<; Simile>a figure in which a similarity between two objects is directly expressed<; Litotes>a form of understatement in which a thing is affirmed by stating the negative of its opposite<; Consonance>the relation between words in which the final consonants in the stressed syllables agree but the vowels that precede them differ<; Metonymy>the substitution of the name of an object closely associated with a word for the word itself<; Synecdoche>a trope in which a part signifies the whole or the whole signifies the part<; Assonance>generally, patterning of vowel sounds without regard to consonants<; Apostrophe>a figure of speech in which someone (usually but not always absent), some abstract quality, or a nonexistent personage is directly addressed as though present<; Zeugma>a term used in several ways, all involving a sort of “yoking”; for example, as a synonym of syllepsis, when an object-taking word has two or more objects on different levels<; Allusion>a figure of speech that makes brief reference to a historical or literary figure, event, or object<; Dissonance>harsh and inharmonious sounds; a marked breaking of the music of poetry, which may be intentional, as it often is in Browning and Hardy<; Onomatopoeia>words that by their sound suggest their meaning: “hiss,” “buzz,” “whirr,” “sizzle.<; Sigmatism>The excessive or deliberate repetition of the s sound.<; Tautology>the use of repetitious words<; Anaphora>one of the devices of repetition, in which the same expression (word or words) is repeated at the beginning of two or more lines, clauses, or sentences<; Enjambment (Enjambement)>the continuation of the sense and grammatical construction of a line on to the next verse or couplet<; Oxymoron>a self-contradictory combination of words or smaller verbal units; usually noun-noun, adjective-adjective, adjective-noun, adverb-adverb, or adverb-verb<; Alliteration>the repetition of initial identical consonant sounds or any vowel sounds in successive or closely associated syllables<; Leonine Rhyme>the internal rhyming of the last stressed syllable before the caesura, with the last stressed syllable of the line<; Conceit>a type of poetic metaphor implying ingenuity; originally, the term—cognate and almost synonymous with “concept”—implied something conceived in the mind<; Chiasmus>a pattern in which the second part is balanced against the first but with the parts reversed<; Feminine Rhyme>a rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllables are followed by an undifferentiated identical unstressed syllable<; Iamb (or Iambus)>a foot consisting of an unaccented syllable and an accented<; Trochee>a foot consisting of an accented and an unaccented syllable<; Synesthesia>the concurrent response of two or more of the senses to the stimulation of one<; Polyptoton>the repetition in close proximity of words that have the same roots<; Ambiguity>the state of having more than one meaning, with resultant uncertainty as to the intended significance of the statement<; Compound Rhyme>rhyme between primary and secondary stressed syllables<; Resonance>The quality of a work or image to evoke associations, meanings, and feelings beyond its literal content.<; Imagery>the collection of images in a literary work; in another sense, synonymous with trope or figure of speech<; Epanalepsis>the repetition at the end of a clause of a word or phrase that occurred at its beginning<; Masculine Rhyme>rhyme that falls on the stressed concluding syllables of the rhyme words<; Euphemism>a device in which indirectness replaces directness of statement, usually in an effort to avoid offensiveness<; Irony>the recognition of a reality different from appearance<; Realistic Period in American Literature, 1865-1900>the period following the Civil War, marked by the triumphant emergence of industrialism and the rise of realism<; Spondee>a foot composed of two accented syllables<; Reification>the treatment of abstractions as concrete things<; Metathesis>the interchange of position between sounds in a word<; Jacobean Age>that portion of the Renaissance during the reign of James I (1603-1625)<; Personification>a figure that endows animals, ideas, abstractions, and inanimate objects with human form, personality, intelligence, and emotions<; Romantic Period in American Literature, 1830-1865>the period between the “second revolution” of the Jacksonian Era and the close of the Civil War, which saw the testing of a nation and its development by ordeal<; Spenserian Sonnet>a sonnet of the English type in that it has three quatrains and a couplet but features quatrains joined by the use of linking rhymes: abab bcbe cdcd ee<; Anapest>a metrical foot consisting of three syllables, with two unaccented syllables followed by an accented one<; Dactyl>a foot consisting of one accented syllable followed by two unaccented<; Muckrakers>a group of American writers who between 1902 and 1911 worked to expose the dishonest methods and unscrupulous motives in big business and in city, state, and national government<; Caroline>applied in general to the age of Charles I of England (1625-1642) and in particular to the spirit of the court<; Miltonic Sonnet>a variation made by Milton on the Italian sonnet, in which the rhyme scheme is kept but the “turn” between the octave and the sestet is eliminated<; Pleonasm>the use of superfluous syllables or words<; Harangue>a vehement speech designed to arouse strong emotions<; Pathetic Fallacy>a phrase coined by Ruskin to denote the tendency to credit nature with human emotions<; Edwardian Age>the period between the death of Victoria in 1901 and the beginning of World War I in 1914, so called after Edward VII, who ruled from 1901 to 1910<; Epiphany>literally, a manifestation or showing-forth, usually of some divine being; given currency as a critical term by James Joyce<; Asyndeton>a condensed form of expression in which elements customarily joined by conjunctions are presented in series without the conjunctions<; Boustrophedon>running alternately from left to right and from right to left; a term—literally, “ox plowing”—that describes the direction of writing in certain ancient inscriptions<; Italian Sonnet>a sonnet divided into an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet rhyming cdecde<; Satanic School>southey’s phrase (1821) for the literary group of Byron, Shelley, Hunt, and others, whose irregular lives and radical ideas suggested the term<; Soliloquy>a speech delivered while the speaker is alone (solus), calculated to inform the audience of what is passing in the character’s mind<; Kenning>a figurative phrase used in Old Germanic languages as a synonym for a simple noun<; Inversion>the placing of a sentence element out of its normal position<; Period of Confession and Postmodernism in American Literature, 1960—>the period beginning in the 1960s, a time of uncertainty, revolt, and cynicism in America and a strong turning inward of many American writers<; Rhyme>identity of terminal sound between accented syllables, usually occupying corresponding positions in two or more lines of verse<; Truncation>in metrics, the omission of a syllable or syllables at the beginning or end of a line<; Spasmodic School>a phrase applied by W. E. Aytoun in 1854 to a group of contemporary English poets<; Augustan>specifically refers to the age of the Emperor Augustus of Rome; by analogy, applied to other epochs when literary culture was high, such as the Augustan Age of English letters<; Aside>a dramatic convention by which an actor directly addresses the audience but is not supposed to be heard by the other actors on the stage<; Parnassians>a group of nineteenth-century French poets, so called from their journal Parnasse contemporain<; Agrarians>literally people living in an agricultural society or espousing its merits; in literary history, usually a group of Southern American writers who published The Fugitive (1922-1925)<; Pyrrhic>a foot of two unaccented syllables<; Terza rima>a three-line stanza, supposedly devised by Dante (for his Divine Comedy) with rhyme scheme aba bcb cdc ded and so forth<; Allonym>the name of an actual person other than the author that is signed by the author to a work<; Barbarism>a mistake in the form of a word or a word that results from such a mistake<; Lost Generation>a group of American writers, born around 1900, who served in the First World War and reacted against certain tendencies of older writers in the 1920s<; Pun>a play on words based on the similarity of sound between two words with different meanings<; Eye Rhyme>rhyme that appears correct from the spelling but is not so from the pronunciation<; Epistolary Novel>a novel in which the narrative is carried forward by letters written by one or more of the characters<; Polysyndeton>the use of more conjunctions than is normal<; Sonnet>a poem almost invariably of fourteen lines and following one of several set rhyme schemes<; Syllepsis>a grammatically correct construction in which one word is placed in the same grammatical relationship to two words but in quite different senses<; Dead Metaphor>a figure of speech used so long that it is taken in its denotative sense only, without any conscious comparison to a physical object it once conveyed<; Objective Correlative>t. S. Eliot’s term for a pattern of objects, actions, or events or a situation that can serve effectively to awaken in the reader an emotional response without being a direct statement of that subjective emotion<; Cockney School>a derogatory title applied by Blackwood’s Magazine to a group of nineteenth-century writers—including William Hazlitt, Leigh Hunt, and John Keats—because of their alleged poor taste in such matters as diction and rhyme<; Meliorism>the belief—widely held in the nineteenth century—that society has an innate tendency toward improvement and that that tendency can be furthered by conscious human effort<; In Medias Res>a term from Horace, literally “in or into the middle parts of things,” applied to the technique of opening a story in the middle of the action<; Pantoum>the pantoum may consist of any number of four-line stanzas, but in any case, the second and fourth lines of one stanza must reappear as the first and third lines of the following stanza<; Volta>the turn in thought—from question to answer; problem to solution—that occurs at the beginning of the sestet in the Italian sonnet<; Shakespearean Sonnet>the English sonnet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Eponym>A person from whose name the name of a thing, place, or term is derived.<; Aestheticism>a nineteenth-century literary movement that rested on the credo of “art for art’s sake.<; Colonial Period in American Literature, 1607-1765>the period from the founding of Jamestown to the Stamp Act in 1765, when the writing produced in America was generally utilitarian, polemical, or religious<; Hartford Wits>a group of Connecticut writers, active around the period of the American Revolution<; Haiku>a form of Japanese poetry that states—in three lines of five, seven, and five syllables—a clear picture designed to arouse a distinct emotion and suggest a specific spiritual insight<; Symploce>a figure of speech combining anaphora and epistrophe: the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses and of another at their end<; Antithesis>a figure of speech characterized by strongly contrasting words, clauses, sentences, or ideas<; Ballad>a form of verse to be sung or recited and characterized by its presentation of an exciting episode in narrative or dramatic form<; Caesura (or Cesura)>a pause or break in a line of verse<; Fugitives, The>a group associated with Vanderbilt University, which in the 1920s published the magazine The Fugitive<; Elision>the omission of part of a word<; Malapropism>an inappropriateness of speech resulting from the use of one word for another, which resembles it<; New York School>a group of American poets who flourished between 1950 and 1970, distinguished by urbanity, wit, learning, spontaneity, and exuberance<; Rondeau>a set French verse pattern; artificial but very popular with many English poets<; Spoonerism>an accidental interchange of sounds—usually the initial consonants—in two or more words<; Broken Rhyme>the breaking of a word at the end of a line for the sake of a rhyme<; Blank Verse>unrhymed but otherwise regular verse—usually iambic pentameter<; Lake Poets and Lake School>coleridge, Wordsworth, and Southey—three poets who at the beginning of the nineteenth century were living in the Lake District of northwest England (Cumbria and Lancashire)<; Knickerbocker Group>a New York group of writers during the first half of the nineteenth century, named after Washington Irving’s Knickerbocker’s History of New York<; Pastoral>a poetic treatment of shepherds and rustic life, after the Latin for “shepherd”: pastor<; Senryu>a form with the same structure as the haiku—seventeen syllables in lines of five, seven, and five—but relying on humor or satire rather than conventions related to the seasons<; Understatement>a common figure of speech in which the literal sense of what is said falls detectably short of (or “under”) the magnitude of what is being talked about<; Romantic Period in English Literature, 1798-1870>in the period between the publication of Lyrical Ballads (1798) and the death of Dickens, English literature was dominated by romanticism<; Carpe Diem>“Seize the day”; a phrase used by Horace and applied to literature, especially lyric poems, that exemplifies the spirit of “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.<; Ubi Sunt Formula>a convention much used in verse, rhetorically asking “where are those who were before us?” (ubi sunt qui ante nos fuerunt?<; Affective Fallacy>the judging of a work of art in terms of its results, especially its emotional effect<; English Sonnet>a sonnet consisting of three quatrains followed by a couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Free Verse>vers libre; verse that is relatively free, managing without rhyme, meter, or regular rhythm<; Heteromerous Rhyme>a fairly rare species of multiple rhyme (also called “mosaic”) in which typically one word is forced into a rhyme with two or more words<; Pre-Raphaelitism>the movement begun in 1848 by the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Holman-Hunt, John Everett Millais, and others as a protest against the conventional methods of painting<; Novel of Manners>a novel dominated by social customs, manners, conventions, and habits of a definite social class<; Tetrameter>a line consisting of four feet<; Transcendentalism>a reliance on the intuition and the conscience—a form of idealism; a philosophical romanticism reaching America a generation or two after it developed in Europe<; Surrealism>a movement in art emphasizing the expression of the imagination as realized in dreams and presented without conscious control<; Run-on Lines>the carrying over of grammatical structure from one line to the next<; Allegory>a form of extended metaphor in which objects, persons, places, and actions in a narrative are equated with meanings outside the narrative itself<; Elegy>a sustained formal poem setting forth meditations on death or another solemn theme<; Limerick>a form of light verse that follows a definite pattern: five anapestic lines of which the first, second, and fifth, consisting of three feet, rhyme; and the third and fourth lines, consisting of two feet, rhyme<; Hypallage>a figure of speech in which an epithet is moved from the proximate to the less proximate of a group of nouns<; Aubade>a lyric about dawn or a morning serenade—a song of lovers parting at dawn<; Caudate Sonnet>an Italian form, rarely adopted into English, in which a standard fourteen-line sonnet is augmented by the addition of other lines, including “tails.<; Martian School (or Martians)>a school of British poets born in the 1940s—so labeled by James Fenton after Craig Raine’s A Martian Sends a Postcard Home (1979)—who struggle to see the world afresh, as might a visitor from Mars<; Jeremiad>a work that foretells destruction because of the evil of a group<; Putative Author>the fictional author of a work, supposedly written by someone other than its actual author<; Peripety (or Peripeteia)>the reversal of fortune for a protagonist—possibly either a fall, as in a tragedy, or a success, as in a comedy<; Restoration Age>the literary period embracing the latter part of the seventeenth century, named for the restoration of the Stuarts in 1660<; Abridgment>a shortened version of a work but one that attempts to preserve essential elements<; Chrestomathy>a collection of choice passages to be used in the study of a language or a literature and, thus, a kind of anthology<; Climax>a rising order of importance in the ideas expressed<; Controlling Image>an image or metaphor that runs throughout and determines the form or nature of a literary work<; Harlem Renaissance>the first major, self-conscious literary movement of African-American writers, although there had been much black writing in America earlier<; Naturalistic and Symbolistic Period in American Literature>the period between 1900 and 1930 in America, divided by World War I into a part dominated by naturalism and a part marked by growing international awareness and symbolism<; Philistinism>the worship of material and mechanical prosperity and the disregard of culture, beauty, and spirit<; Revolutionary and Early National Period in American Literature, 1765-1830>the period of the establishment of the new nation, ending with the “second revolution” represented by the ascendancy of Jacksonian democracy<; Cacophony>the opposite of euphony; a harsh, unpleasant combination of sounds<; Catharsis>aristotle’s term, in the Poetics, for the “proper purgation” of pity and fear effected by tragedy<; Madrigal>a short lyric, usually dealing with love or a pastoral theme and designed for—or at least suitable for—a musical setting<; Mimesis>the Greek for imitation, often used specifically to indicate Aristotle’s theory of imitation<; Pentameter>a line of verse of five feet<; Renaissance>the period of transition from the medieval to the modern world in Western Europe; the word means “rebirth.<; Slant Rhyme>near rhyme; usually the substitution of assonance or consonance for true rhyme<; Burlesque>a form of comedy characterized by ridiculous exaggeration and distortion, marked by a discrepancy between subject matter and style<; Chiaroscuro>contrasting light and shade<; Gongorism>a highly affected style taking its name from the Spanish poet Luis de Góngora y Argote (1561-1627), whose writings exhibited stylistic extravagances<; Legend>a narrative or tradition handed down from the past; distinguished from a myth by having more of historical truth and perhaps less of the supernatural<; Syzygy>in classical prosody, a term for two coupled feet serving as a unit<; Aesthetic Distance>the effect produced when an emotion or an experience—whether autobiographical or not—is so objectified that it can be understood as being independent of the immediate experience of its maker<; Didacticism>instructiveness in a work, one purpose of which is to give guidance, particularly in moral, ethical, or religious matters<; Hedonism>a doctrine that pleasure is the chief good of human beings<; Heteroglossia>“Different tongues” or “different speech”; a term introduced by Mikhail Bakhtin to designate the presence of more than one voice in a given narrative or another work<; Internal Rhyme>rhyme that occurs at some place before the last syllables in a line<; Realistic Period in English Literature, 1870-1914>the period in which the reaction to romanticism reached its peak in full-fledged realism, in the latter portion of Victoria’s reign and the reign of Edward VII<; Pseudonym>a false name sometimes assumed by writers and others<; Rhopalic>a sequence that “thickens” as it moves toward its end, with each word a syllable longer than the preceding one<; Victorian>a term used (1) to designate broadly the literature written during the reign of Queen Victoria (1837-1901); and (2) to suggest a certain complacency, hypocrisy, or squeamishness assumed to characterize Victorian attitudes<; Transferred Epithet>an adjective used to limit a noun that it really does not logically modify<; Tanka>a type of Japanese poetry similar to the haiku<; Anadiplosis>a kind of repetition in which the last word or phrase of one sentence or line is repeated at the beginning of the next<; Beat Generation>a group of American poets and novelists of the 1950s and 1960s in rebellion against the prevailing culture<; Clerihew>a form of light verse invented by and named for Edmund Clerihew Bentley (1875-1956), who also wrote detective fiction<; Motif (or Motive)>a simple element that serves as a basis for expanded narrative; or, less strictly, a conventional situation, device, interest, or incident<; Metafiction>a work of fiction, a major concern of which is the nature of fiction itself<; Neoclassic Period>the period in English literature between the return of the Stuarts to the English throne in 1660 and the publication of Lyrical Ballads by Wordsworth and Coleridge in 1798<; Identical Rhyme>a phenomenon, also called redundant rhyme or rime riche, in which a syllable both begins and ends in the same way as a rhyming syllable, without being the same word<; Hiatus>a pause or break between two vowel sounds not separated by a consonant<; Vorticism>a movement in modern poetry, originating in 1914 with Wyndham Lewis, related to certain abstract developments in painting and sculpture<; Scriblerus Club>a club organized in London in 1714 by Jonathan Swift to satirize literary incompetence<; Verbum Infans Formula>a conventional paradoxical topos, meaning “the unspeaking word,” applied to the infant (infans, “not speaking”) Christ, who incarnates the Word (verbum)<; Memento Mori>A reminder of death, such as a skull, used to encourage reflection on mortality.<; Black Mountain School>certain writers—Charles Olson, Robert Creeley, and Robert Duncan among them—associated with Black Mountain College, an experimental school in North Carolina<; End-Stopped Lines>lines in which both the grammatical structure and the sense reach completion at the end<; “Graveyard School”>a group of eighteenth-century poets who wrote long poems on death and immortality<; Exposition>one of the four chief types of composition, with the others being argumentation, description, and narration; its purpose is to explain something<; Epigram>a pithy saying, often antithetical; also a short poem characterized by compression, balance, and polish<; Elizabethan Age>the segment of the Renaissance during the reign of Elizabeth I (1558-1603)<; Early Tudor Age, 1500-1557>the period in which the ideals of the Renaissance were rapidly replacing those of the Middle Ages, marked by the reformation of the English church and the revival of learning known as Humanism<; Equivoque>a kind of pun in which language is so used that it has two different but appropriate meanings<; Dramatic Monologue>a poem that reveals “a soul in action” through the speech of one character in a dramatic situation<; Humanism>broadly, any attitude that tends to exalt the human element, as opposed to the supernatural, divine elements—or as opposed to the grosser, animal elements<; Reduplication>(1) The rhetorical repetition of a word or phrase; (2) repetition of material in a syllable, common for diminutives or nicknames<; Ploce>a kind of repetition whereby different forms and senses of a word are “woven” through an utterance<; Reversal>the change in fortune for a protagonist<; Novel of Character>a novel that emphasizes character rather than exciting episode<; Early Victorian Age, 1832-1870>a time of the gradual tempering of the romantic impulse and the steady growth of realism<; Heteronym>a word spelled the same as another but pronounced and defined differently<; Villanelle>a fixed nineteen-line form, originally French, employing only two rhymes and repeating two of the lines according to a set pattern<; Satire>a work or manner that blends a censorious attitude with humor and wit for improving human institutions or humanity<; Exegesis>an explanation and interpretation of a text<; Merism>generally, a repetition of parts; specifically, the use of a pair of opposites to mean a whole<; Kabuki>a popular form of theater in Japan since the mid-seventeenth century<; Rhetorical Accent>the accent determined by the meaning or intention of the sentence; used in metrics in opposition to metrical accent, in which only the prosodic pattern of the line determines the placement of stress<; Solecism>a violation of prescriptive grammatical rules<

M. Manly saw three necessary elements in drama: a story told in action by actors who impersonate the characters<; Drame>a form of play between tragedy and comedy developed by the French in the eighteenth century and later introduced into England, where it is often called a “drama.<; Folk Drama>in the stricter and older sense, dramatic activities of the folk—the unsophisticated treatment of folk themes by the folk themselves, particularly activities connected with popular festivals and religious rites<; Daytime Drama>see Soap Opera<; Disguisings>in medieval times (and in some places into the twentieth century) a species of game or spectacle with a procession of masked figures<; Dramatic Poetry>a term that, logically, should be restricted to poetry employing dramatic form or some element of dramatic technique<; Droll>a short dramatic piece (also known as “drollery” or “droll humor”) cultivated on the Commonwealth Interregnum stage in England as a substitute for full-length or serious plays that were not permitted by the government<; Light Opera>a form of opera that lacks the passion, dignity, and seriousness of grand opera<; Jig>a nonliterary farcical dramatic performance, the words being sung to the accompaniment of dancing<; Lyrical Drama>a dramatic poem (see dramatic poetry) that uses drama to express lyric themes (such as the author’s own emotions or ideas of life) instead of relying on a story as the basis of the action<; Hornpipe>an obsolete wind instrument, a dance to its music (usually by one person), or the music for such a dance<; Legitimate Theater>the presentation of regular plays, depending entirely on acting, on a stage before an audience, using living actors<; Mummings>masked folk processions, dancing, and plays<; Musical Comedy>a combination of music with comic drama<; Pièce bien faite>see Well-Made Play, the English equivalent of the French term<; Revival>bringing back an old work for new performance; also such a work itself<; Passion Play>a drama that portrays a portion of the life of a god<; Play-Poem>the genre into which Virginia Woolf placed her novel The Waves (1931)<; Operetta>a comic opera, with music, songs, and spectacular effects but with the dialogue spoken<; Opera>musical drama in which the dialogue instead of being spoken is sung to the accompaniment of instrumental music<; Religious Drama>the drama of the Middle Ages, when its relation to the church and to religious subject matter was very great<; Play>a literary composition of any length, ordinarily written to be performed by actors who impersonate the characters, speak the dialogue, and enact the appropriate actions<; Opéra bouffe>a French term for a very light form of comic opera developed from vaudeville music and said to be the ancestor of the comic operas of Gilbert and Sullivan<; Thesis Play>a drama that presents a social problem and proposes a solution; sometimes known by the French “pièce à thèse.<; Saint’s Play>a medieval play based on the legend of a saint<; Telenovela>a novel for television, very popular in Latin America and elsewhere around the world, appealing to viewers of many sorts<; School Plays>plays written and performed at schools, one of the most important traditions contributing to the development of Elizabethan drama<; Virgin Play>a medieval nonscriptural play based on saints’ Lives, in which the Virgin Mary takes an active role in performing miracles<; Skit>a short dramatic sketch or a brief, self-contained comic or burlesque scene, usually presented as a part of a revue or on a television or radio program<; Soap Opera, Soap>daily daytime drama series broadcast on radio and television<; Scriptural Drama>plays based on the Old and New Testaments, produced first by churches and then by town guilds in the Middle Ages<; University Plays>plays produced by undergraduates at Oxford and Cambridge during the Elizabethan Age<; Vaudeville>an entertainment consisting of successive performances of unrelated songs, dances, sketches, acrobatic feats, juggling, pantomime, puppet shows, animal acts, and varied stunts<

column4: Pastoral>a poetic treatment of shepherds and rustic life, after the Latin for “shepherd”: pastor<; Idyll (or Idyl)>one or another of the poetic genres that are short and possess marked descriptive, narrative, and pastoral qualities<; Arcadian>suggesting simple happiness; applied to any person or place with idealized rural simplicity, after Arcadia, the Greek home of pastoral poetry<; Bucolic>pastoral writing that deals with rural life in a manner rather formal and fanciful<; Doric>simple; applied to a rustic of “broad” dialect or to simple idyllic pieces of literature, after the Doric dialect of ancient Greece, thought of as lacking in refinement<; Topographical Poetry>poetry in which, according to Samuel Johnson’s definition, “the fundamental subject is some particular landscape.<; Amoebean Verses>pastoral verses in matched strophes or stanzas spoken by two speakers alternately<; Georgic>a poem ostensibly about farming and the practical aspects of rustic life; so called from Virgil’s Georgics<; Pastoral Drama>a form of drama, occasionally cultivated by English dramatists, that reflects the pastoral conventions of the eclogue and the pastoral romance<; Pastourelle>a medieval dialogue poem in which a shepherdess is wooed by a man of higher social rank<; Country Song>a poem related to country life, customarily having to do with young love<; Eclogue>a formal pastoral poem following the traditional technique derived from the idylls of Theocritus; in Greek, eclogue meant “selection.<; Idyllium>archaic or affected equivalent of idyll<; Prose Idyll>an idyll in prose<; Pastoral Romance>a prose narrative—usually long and complicated in plot—in which the characters bear pastoral names and in which pastoral conventions dominate<; Pastoral Elegy>a poem employing conventional pastoral imagery, written in dignified, serious language, and taking as its theme the expression of grief at the loss of a friend or important person<

column4: Meliorism>the belief—widely held in the nineteenth century—that society has an innate tendency toward improvement and that that tendency can be furthered by conscious human effort<; Aestheticism>a nineteenth-century literary movement that rested on the credo of “art for art’s sake.<; Transcendentalism>a reliance on the intuition and the conscience—a form of idealism; a philosophical romanticism reaching America a generation or two after it developed in Europe<; Hedonism>a doctrine that pleasure is the chief good of human beings<; Humanism>broadly, any attitude that tends to exalt the human element, as opposed to the supernatural, divine elements—or as opposed to the grosser, animal elements<; Existentialism>a group of attitudes, current during and after World War II, that emphasizes existence rather than essence and sees the inadequacy of human reason to explain the enigma of the universe<; Dialectic>in the broadest sense, simply the art of argumentation or debate; in classical literature, the tradition of continuing debate or discussion of eternally unresolved issues<; Animism>The attribution of a living soul or spirit to inanimate objects, plants, and natural forces.<; Determinism>the belief that all ostensible acts of the will are actually the result of causes that determine them<; Objectivism>a term used by various philosophies to stress the reality or value of the objective world, the need for some sort of objectivity, or the importance of the status of an artwork as a physical object<; Stoicism>the philosophy of the Stoics, a group of Greek philosophers, founded by Zeno late in the fourth century B.C. Stoicism exalts endurance and self-sufficiency<; Pantheism>The belief that God is identical with the universe and nature.<; Primitivism>the doctrine that supposedly primitive peoples—because they had remained closer to nature and had been less subject to the influences of society—were nobler than civilized peoples<; Fatalism>The belief that all events are predetermined and inevitable.<; Hebraism>Matthew Arnold’s term for the moral, strict-conscience element of culture, contrasted with Hellenism.<; Classicism>a body of doctrine thought to be derived from or to reflect the qualities of ancient Greek and Roman culture, including restraint, restricted scope, and dominance of reason<; Ockham’s (or Occam’s) Razor>the principle of parsimony, attributed to William of Ockham: “Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity.<; Physiocrats>Eighteenth-century French economists who held that land and agriculture are the source of wealth.<; Rationalism>The view that reason, not experience or revelation, is the chief source of knowledge.<; Scholasticism>The medieval system of philosophy and theology that used Aristotelian logic to reconcile reason and Christian faith.<; Enlightenment>a philosophical movement of the eighteenth century, particularly in France but effectively over much of Europe and America<; Hellenism>The culture and ideals of ancient Greece; Matthew Arnold’s term for the free play of intellect, contrasted with Hebraism.<; Perspectivism>The view that knowledge and truth are always relative to a particular perspective.<; Noble Savage>the idea that primitive human beings are naturally good and that whatever evil they develop is the product of the corrupting action of civilization<; Subjectivity>the quality of originating and existing in the mind of a perceiving subject and not necessarily corresponding to any object outside that mind<; Logical Positivism>a philosophical movement that primarily emphasizes empirical sensory observation as the means of evaluating claims about matters of fact<; Pragmatism>a term first used by C. S. Peirce in 1878 that describes a doctrine that determines value through the test of consequences or utility<; Positivism>a philosophy that denies validity to speculation or metaphysical questions, maintaining that the proper goal of knowledge is the description and not the explanation of phenomena<; Objectivity>a quality in an artwork of impersonality and freedom from the expression of personal sentiments, attitudes, or emotions by the author<; Deism>Belief in a creator God known through reason and nature rather than revelation.<; Aesthetics>the study or philosophy of the beautiful in nature and art<; Chronological Primitivism>the belief that, on the whole, the lives and actions of human beings were more admirable and desirable at an earlier stage of history than at present<; Cultural Primitivism>the belief that nature (what exists undisturbed by human artifice) is preferable and fundamentally better than any aspect of human culture<; Epicureanism>a philosophy similar to that of the Greek Epicurus, who saw philosophy as the art of making life happy, with pleasure the highest goal and pain and emotional disturbance the greatest evils<; Nominalism>a philosophical doctrine, advanced by Roscellinus and revived by William of Ockham, holding that abstract concepts, general terms, and universals have no objective referents but exist only as names<; Relativism>the denial of the validity of principles that are everlasting, ubiquitous, changeless, and absolute<; Essentialism>The belief that things, or categories of people, have a fixed set of inherent, defining properties.<; Pantisocracy>A utopian scheme for an equal, communal society, planned by Coleridge and Southey in 1794.<; Alexandrianism>the spirit prevailing in the literary and scientific work of Hellenistic writers flourishing in Alexandria for about three centuries after 325 B.C<; Pluralism>a philosophical position that recognizes the possibility of multiple ultimate principles, contrasted with monism<; Idealism>The philosophical view that reality is fundamentally mental; also, the pursuit of ideals over practical considerations.<; Nihilism>The rejection of all religious and moral principles, often with the belief that life is meaningless.<; Pessimism>The belief that evil outweighs good, or that the world tends toward the worst.<; Optimism>The belief that good ultimately prevails, or that this is the best of all possible worlds.<; Utilitarianism>The ethical theory that right actions are those that produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number.<; Alterity>the general idea of otherness, expressed most influentially in the philosophy of G. W. F. Hegel, who argued that much Western thought defined itself by reference to opposition to something alien or other<; American Dream, The>a grand ideal of the sort of success made possible by the charters and habits of the United States of America; the dream includes freedom, success, wealth, and fulfillment<; “Art for Art’s Sake”>the doctrine—corresponding to the French “l’art pour l’art”—that art is its own excuse for being and that its values are aesthetic and not moral, political, or social<; Courtly Love>a philosophy of love and a code of lovemaking that flourished in chivalric times—first in France and later in other countries, especially in England<; Dualism>a doctrine (opposed to monism) that recognizes the possibility of the co-existence of antithetical or complementary principles<; Doctrinaire>an adjective applied to one whose attitude is controlled by preconception and who disregards other points of view as well as practical considerations<; Neoplatonism>a philosophical system that originated in Alexandria in the third century, with elements of platonism mixed with Oriental beliefs and with some aspects of Christianity<; Phonocentrism>an old attitude that regards speech as superior to writing, which amounts to a feeble and secondary attempt to record speech<; Altruism>Selfless concern for the welfare of others.<; Egoism>The view that self-interest is the proper motive or basis of conduct; excessive concern with oneself.<; Empiricism>The view that knowledge comes chiefly from sense experience.<; Individualism>The view that emphasizes the moral worth, independence, and self-reliance of the individual.<; Hegelianism>The philosophy of G. W. F. Hegel, especially his dialectic of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.<; Platonism>The philosophy of Plato, especially his theory that ideal Forms are more real than the physical world.<; Absolute>anything totally independent of conditions, limitations, controls, or modifiers<; Anti-Intellectualism>a philosophic doctrine that, assigning reason or intellect to a subordinate place, questions or denies the ability of the intellect to comprehend the true nature of things<; Apollonian (or, earlier, Apollinian)>a term used, along with Dionysian, in Friedrich Nietzsche’s The Birth of Tragedy for contrasting elements in Greek tragedy<; Augustinianism>the doctrines of Saint Augustine of Hippo (354-430), author of Confessions—the first extended, honest self-analysis—and of the monumental De Civitate Dei (The City of God) as well as a vast amount of other writing<; Nature>a term with many meanings—A. O. Lovejoy found as many as sixty in its normative functions—that both neoclassicists and romanticists claimed to “follow.<; Mysticism>the theory that a knowledge of God or immediate reality is attainable by a human faculty that transcends intellect and logic<; Humanism, The New.>a movement called The New Humanism took place in America between 1910 and 1930, inspired somewhat by the humanist position of Matthew Arnold<; Monism>a system that reduces phenomena to the effects of one single cause or principle<; Naive and Sentimental>a distinction by Schiller (1795) arguing that poets are either naive (original, pure, authentic, directly in touch with nature) or sentimental (derivative, civilized, removed from nature)<; New Humanism, The>an American critical school in the first third of the twentieth century that emphasized the moral qualities of literature<

column4: In Medias Res>a term from Horace, literally “in or into the middle parts of things,” applied to the technique of opening a story in the middle of the action<; Prolepsis>A flash-forward; the anticipation of a future event as if it had already happened.<; Theme>a central idea; in nonfiction, the general topic of discussion; in poetry, fiction, and drama, the abstract concept made concrete through representation<; Foreshadowing>the presentation of material in a work in such a way that later events are prepared for<; Flashback>a device by which a work presents material that occurred prior to the opening scene of the work<; Mythos>The plot or story of a work; also, a body of myths belonging to a culture.<; Point of View>the vantage point from which an author presents a story<; Omniscient Point of View>the point of view in a work of fiction in which the narrator is capable of knowing, seeing, and telling all<; Narrator>anyone who recounts a narrative<; Milieu>The social and cultural environment or setting in which something occurs.<; Narratology>the sophisticated analysis of the relations among a story—conceived in simple terms—and all the other elements involved in the telling thereof<; Panoramic Method>that point of view in which an author presents material by exposition rather than in scenes, giving actions and conversations in summary rather than in detail<; Tone (or Tone Color)>the attitudes toward the subject and toward the audience implied in a literary work; also a musical quality in language<; Flashforward>the opposite of flashback; the action moves to something in the future, possibly an actual occurrence to come or an imagined or foreseen future outcome of present action<; Showing versus Telling>an empirical concept, unsophisticated but still useful, that emphasizes the superiority of dramatization, demonstration, enactment, and embodiment over mere telling<; Analepsis>A flashback; a narrative return to events that occurred before the present moment of the story.<; Free Indirect Discourse>a way of indicating inner states of mind or feeling without direct or indirect discourse in the ordinary senses<; Locale>the physical setting of some action<; Stream of Consciousness>the total range of awareness and emotive-mental response of an individual, from the lowest pre-speech level to the highest fully articulated level of rational thought<; Setting>the background against which action takes place<; Suspense>anticipation as to the outcome of events, particularly as they affect a character for whom one has sympathy<; Exoticism>a spirit of adherence to foreign or exotic elements, especially in setting<; Interior Monologue>one of the techniques for presenting the stream of consciousness of a character, recording the character’s internal emotional experience<; Chronotope>Bakhtin’s term for the connectedness of time and space as represented in a literary work.<; Action>the series of events that constitute a plot—what the characters say, do, think, or in some cases fail to do<; Cliffhanger>a work issued in installments that end at a point of great suspense<; Episode>an incident presented as one continuous action<; MacGuffin>a term—originated by Angus MacPhail but most often associated with Alfred Hitchcock—for any pretext in itself not very important or relevant but necessary to get a plot moving<; Mood>in a literary work, the mood is the emotional-intellectual attitude of the author toward the subject<; Stock Situation>a situation recurring frequently in a literary form, whether a general plot situation—such as boy-meets-girl—or a recurrent detail, such as mixed identity<; Atmosphere>the prevailing tone or mood of a literary work, particularly—but not exclusively—when that mood is established in part by setting or landscape<; Background>a term loosely used to specify either the setting of a piece of writing or the tradition and point of view from which authors present their ideas<; Camera Eye Narration>a kind of storytelling, resembling the “Camera Eye” sections of John Dos Passos’s U.S.A. (1936), in which the writing gives the appearance or impression of being thoroughly objective, realistic, and anatomical<; Characterization>the creation of imaginary persons so that they seem lifelike<; Coincidence>the coinciding of events so that the movement of a plot is determined or significantly altered without a sense of necessity or causal relationship among the events<; Conflict>the struggle that grows out of the interplay of two opposing forces<; Counterplot>a secondary plot that contrasts with the principal plot of the work; a subplot<; Diegesis>a statement, description, or narration without explanation, conclusion, or judgment; an obsolescent theological term recently resurrected by critical theorists<; Donnée>literally, “a given”; Henry James’s term for the data given, out of which one works out the meaning or solution of a work<; Incident>a single event or occurrence; the smallest unit of action<; Narrative Theory>see Narratology<; Narrative Hook>any device at the opening of a work to capture the interest of readers and make them continue reading<; Minor Plot>a subordinate action of complication running through a work of fiction or drama<; Plot>the arrangement of incidents in a work of fiction or drama; Aristotle called it “the first principle, and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy.<; Spoiler>information that spoils suspense<; Subplot>a subordinate or minor story in a piece of fiction<; Stream-of-Consciousness Novel>the type of novel taking as its subject matter the flow of the stream of consciousness of one or more of its characters<; Situation>(1) A given group of circumstances in which characters find themselves or (2) the given conditions under which a story opens before the plot proper actually begins<; Surprise Ending>an ending that the audience may not have expected or foreseen<

column4: Burlesque>a form of comedy characterized by ridiculous exaggeration and distortion, marked by a discrepancy between subject matter and style<; Satire>a work or manner that blends a censorious attitude with humor and wit for improving human institutions or humanity<; Parody>a composition imitating another—usually serious—piece<; Travesty>writing that by its incongruity of treatment ridicules a subject inherently noble or dignified<; Goliardic Verse>lilting Latin verse, usually satiric, composed by university students and wandering scholars in Germany, France, and England in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries<; Lampoon>writing that ridicules and satirizes a person in a bitter, scurrilous manner in verse or prose<; Menippean Satire>a form of satire originally developed by the Greek cynic Menippus and transmitted by his disciples Lucian and Varro<; Pastiche>a French word for a parody or literary imitation<; Horatian Satire>satire in which the voice is indulgent, tolerant, amused, and witty<; Juvenalian Satire>formal satire in which the speaker attacks vice and error with contempt and indignation<; Mock Epic (or Mock Heroic)>terms for a literary form that burlesques the epic by treating a trivial subject in the “grand style” or uses the epic formulas to make a trivial subject ridiculous by ludicrously overstating it<; Varronian Satire>a form of indirect satire, named for the Roman writer Varro<; Caricature>writing that exaggerates certain qualities of a person and produces a burlesque, ridiculous effect<; Pasquinade>a satire or lampoon hung up in a public place<; Squib>a short satirical piece; a lampoon<; Adversarius>the “straight” character in a formal satire who is addressed by the persona and who functions to elicit and shape that speaker’s remarks<; City Comedy>a type of drama flourishing around 1558-1642, mostly satire set in the London of the playwright’s day with low-life characters engaged in various crimes, follies, and misdeeds<; Comedy of Morals>comedy that uses ridicule to correct abuses—hence, a form of dramatic satire aimed at the moral state of a people or a special class of people<; Formal Satire>one of the two major categories of satire, in which the persona speaks in the first person either directly to the reader or to the adversarius; the other is indirect satire<; Indirect Satire>satire in narrative or dramatic form, in which the characters who speak and act are themselves the objects of the satire<

an account of an imaginary world, usually in the future, in which present tendencies are carried out to their intensely unpleasant culminations<; Utopia>a fiction describing an imaginary ideal world<; Fantasy>a conscious breaking free from reality; sometimes used as an equivalent of fancy and even of imagination<; Adventure Story (or Film)>a story in which action—often exterior, usually physical, and frequently violent—is the predominant material, stressed above characterization, motivation, or theme<; Cock-and-Bull Story>a long, rambling, somewhat vague and unlikely story; a meandering tall tale<; Uchronia>A work of fiction set in an alternate history.<; Action-Adventure>a style of entertainment popular in film and television productions after about 1950<; Dream Allegory (or Vision)>a conventional narrative frame, widely used in the Middle Ages, in which the narrator falls asleep and dreams a dream that is the actual story<; Fiction>narrative writing drawn from the imagination rather than from history or fact<; Narrative>an account of events; anything that is narrated<; Science Fiction>a form of fantasy in which scientific facts, assumptions, or hypotheses form the basis—by logical extrapolation—of adventures in the future, on other planets, or in other dimensions in time or space<; Alternative History>a species of fiction in which much depends on some major reversal of known geography or history<; Detective Story>a story in which a crime—usually a murder, with the identity of the perpetrator unknown—is solved by a detective through a logical assembling and interpretation of palpable evidence, known as clues<; Ghost Story>a story that involves a ghost or similar spirit<; Eutopia>an ideally good place; the word was devised as a play on Utopia, which means “no-place.<; Mystery Story (or Novel)>a work in which mystery or terror plays a controlling part<; Medical Thriller>popular melodramatic fiction concentrating on plots and characters drawn from the world of illness, research, medicine, and threats such as epidemics and criminal malpractice<; Historical Fiction>fiction whose setting is in some time other than that in which it is written<; Oriental Tale (also Oriental Novel, Eastern Tale, Eastern Novel)>a work set in some Eastern place that takes advantage of exotic possibilities for melodrama, romance, and adventure; a fashion traceable to the first English translation of The Arabian Nights<; Short-Short Story>a brief short story, usually no more than two thousand words, sometimes with a surprise ending<; Thriller>a fast-paced work involving crime, pursuit, suspense, and surprise<; Story>any account of actions in a time sequence; any narrative of events in a sequential arrangement<; Tale>a relatively simple narrative<; Short Story>a brief prose narrative; storytelling of this kind reaches back to the Egyptian papyri<

column4: Alienation Effect>bertolt Brecht’s term (translating the German Verfremdungseffekt) for a quality of theater by which the audience is kept at such a distance that unthinking emotional and personal involvement is inhibited<; Fused Rhyme>a curious phenomenon, scarcely found anywhere in English outside a few poems by Gerard Manley Hopkins, in which a rhyme sound is begun at the end of a line but not completed until the beginning of the next<; Apocope>the omission of one or more sounds from a word<; Epic>a long narrative poem in elevated style presenting characters of high position in adventures, forming an organic whole through their relation to a central heroic figure<; Frontier Literature>writing about the American frontier and frontier life<; Melodrama>a work—usually a play—based on a romantic plot and developed sensationally, with little regard for motivation and with an excessive appeal to the emotions of the audience<; Middle English Period>the period in English literature between the replacement of French by Middle English as the language of court and the early appearances of definitely Modern English writings, roughly between 1350 and 1500<; Muses, The>nine goddesses represented as presiding over the various departments of art and science<; Quibble>earlier, a pun; nowadays, a verbal device for evading the point at issue<; Polyhyphenation>the use of more than a usual number of hyphens<; Nonsense Verse>a variety of light verse entertaining because of its strong rhythmic quality and lack of logic, often with coined nonsense words<; Nonce Word>a word invented by an author for a particular usage or special meaning; in earlier forms of a language, a word with a single recorded occurrence<; Old English Period>the period between the invasion of England by the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, beginning around 428, and the establishment of Norman rule around 1100<; Palindrome>writing that reads the same from left to right and from right to left<; Novel of the Soil>a special kind of regionalism in the novel, in which the lives of people struggling for existence in remote rural sections are starkly portrayed<; Projective Verse>a kind of free verse that regards meter and form as artificial and in which the poet “projects” a voice primarily through the content and the propulsive quality of breathing, which alone determines the line<; Threnody>a song of death; a dirge<; Sentimentalism>(1) An overindulgence in emotion, especially the conscious effort to induce emotion in order to enjoy it; (2) an optimistic overemphasis of the goodness of humanity<; Sestina>one of the most difficult and complex of verse forms, consisting of six six-lined stanzas and a three-lined envoy<; Aphorism>a concise statement of a principle or precept given in pointed words<; Blood and Thunder>a class of work specializing in bloodshed and violence<; Dynamic Character>a character who develops or changes as a result of the actions of the plot<; Dolce Stil Nuovo>the “sweet new style” (called so in Dante’s Purgatory) that flourished among lyric poets in certain Romance languages during the thirteenth century, with a premium on lucidity and complex musicality<; Ellipsis (or Ellipse)>the omission of one or more words that, while essential to a grammatic structure, are easily supplied<; Dramatic Irony>a situation in which the words or acts of a character carry a meaning unperceived by the character but understood by the audience<; Expressionism>a movement affecting painting and literature, which followed and went beyond impressionism in its efforts to “objectify inner experience.<; Ethos>the character of the speaker or writer as reflected in speech or writing; the quality or set of emotions that a speaker or writer enacts in order to affect an audience<; Hamartia>the error, frailty, mistaken judgment, or misstep through which the fortunes of the hero of a tragedy are reversed<; Epithet>strictly, an adjective used to point out a characteristic of a person or thing<; Folklore>the study of the survivals of archaic beliefs, customs, and traditions in modern ages; a term first used by W. J. Thoms as a substitute for “popular antiquities.<; Nekuia>a work having to do with the land of the dead, especially a visit by a living person<; Psychological Novel>prose fiction that places unusual emphasis on interior characterization and on the motives, circumstances, and internal action that spring from and develop external action<; Pathos>the quality in art and literature that stimulates pity, tenderness, or sorrow; from the Greek root for feeling<; Nom de plume (or pen name)>a name adopted by a writer for professional use or to disguise his or her true identity<; Regionalism>fidelity to a particular geographical area; the representation of its habits, speech, manners, history, folklore, or beliefs<; Saturday Club>a club of literary and scientific people in and around Cambridge and Boston in the mid-nineteenth century who came together at irregular intervals chiefly for social intercourse and good conversation<; Sfumato>an Italian word meaning “smoked” that refers to a quality of smokily obscuring details in a painting; later applied to film and television productions with a similar quality: vapory, foggy, soft-focus, dark, or dim<; Tritagonist>the actor taking the part third in importance in a Greek drama<; Virelay>a French verse form (related to lai) of which the number of stanzas and the number of lines to the stanza are unlimited<; Verisimilitude>the semblance of truth; the degree to which a work creates the appearance of the truth<; Telestich>an acrostic in which the final letters form a word<; Triple Rhyme>rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllable is followed by two unstressed, undifferentiated syllables<; Symbol>something that is itself and also stands for something else<; Gigantism>Exaggeration of size or scale, especially for comic or grotesque effect.<; Bard>in modern use, any poet; historically, poets who recited verses glorifying the deeds of heroes and leaders, especially the early poets of the Celts<; Bob and Wheel>a stanza in the revived alliterative verse of the later Middle English period in which unrhymed alliterative lines are followed by a very short line, the bob, and a short-lined rhymed quatrain, the wheel<; Cinquain>any five-line stanza; more precisely, the five-line stanza used by Adelaide Crapsey, of unrhymed lines of two, four, six, eight, and two syllables<; Concordance>an alphabetical index of most or all of the words in a text or in the works of an author<; Emblem>a graphic device of some sort that stands for a special meaning<; Epistolary Literature>literature—usually prose fiction—entirely or partly written as letters<; Flashback>a device by which a work presents material that occurred prior to the opening scene of the work<; Fourteeners>a verse form consisting of fourteen syllables arranged in iambs<; Discordia Concors>a term used by Samuel Johnson for “a combination of dissimilar images or discovery of occult resemblances in things apparently unlike” in metaphysical poetry<; Dénouement>literally, “unknotting”; the final unraveling of a plot; the solution of a mystery; an explanation or outcome<; Dialects>varieties of the same “language” spoken by two groups or persons whose speech exhibits very marked differences<; Movement, The>a focus of British literary activity in the mid-1950s, mostly in poetry and prose fiction, with emphases on normality, regularity, practicality, stoicism, traditionalism, and solid middle-class values<; Jewish-American Literature>a field of study that has emerged since about 1935 and concentrated on the work of Jewish writers living in America<; Myth>an anonymous story that presents supernatural episodes as a means of interpreting natural events<; Kitsch>shallow, flashy art designed to have popular appeal and commercial success; from the German for “gaudy trash.<; Imagists>a group of poets active in England and America between 1909 and 1918<; Philippic>any bitter speech or harangue<; Prosopopoeia>another name for personification<; Travesty>writing that by its incongruity of treatment ridicules a subject inherently noble or dignified<; Yellow Journalism>newspapers and magazines specializing in scandal and sensation<; Transliteration>a character-by-character transfer of a word from one alphabet or writing system to another<; Unities>the principles of dramatic structure involving the unities of action, time, and place<; Accentualism>paul Fussell’s term for “the theory of the line which considers the number of stresses to be its fundamental prosodic skeleton.<; African-American Literature>frequently called Afro-American or Black literature; the writing of African Americans, which began in the eighteenth century with the poetry of Jupiter Hammon and Phillis Wheatley<; Altar Poem>another term for a carmen figuratum, a poem in which the lines are so arranged that they form a design on the page, taking the shape of the subject—frequently, an altar or a cross<; Chain Rhyme>a device in which the sound of the last syllable of one line recurs as the sound of the first syllable of the next but with a change of meaning<; Colloquialism>an expression used in informal conversation but not accepted universally in formal speech or writing<; Epic Simile>an elaborated comparison, more involved and ornate than an ordinary simile, in a conscious imitation of the Homeric manner<; Framework-Story>a story inside a framework; a story inside a story<; Grundy, Mrs.>a character from Thomas Morton’s play Speed the Plough, who does not actually appear but of whose judgments everyone in the play is very much afraid<; Fabliau (plural, Fabliaux)>a humorous tale popular in medieval France<; Episodic Structure>writing that consists of little more than a series of incidents, with the episodes succeeding each other and with no particularly logical arrangement or complication<; Dystopia>literally, “bad place”; an account of an imaginary world, usually in the future, in which present tendencies are carried out to their intensely unpleasant culminations<; Humours (or Humors)>in an old theory of physiology, the four chief liquids of the human body—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were called humours<; Lament>a poem expressing grief—usually more intense and more personal than in a complaint<; Locus Classicus>that place or passage invariably cited as the “classic example” of a principle or type<; Palimpsest>a writing surface, whether of vellum, papyrus, or other material, that has been used more than once for manuscript purposes<; Protagonist>the chief character in a work<; Saga>in a strict sense, Icelandic and Norse stories of the medieval period that give accounts of heroic adventure<; Suspension of Disbelief>the willingness to withhold questions about truth, accuracy, or probability in a work<; Tercet>a stanza of three lines—a triplet—in which each line ends with the same rhyme<; Roman à Thèse>french: a thesis novel—one intended to establish and illustrate a social doctrine<; Thesis>an attitude or position on a problem taken by a writer or speaker with the purpose of proving or supporting it<; Utopia>a fiction describing an imaginary ideal world<; Theater of the Absurd>see Absurd, Theater of the<; School of Night>a group of Elizabethan dramatists, poets, and scholars, led by Sir Walter Ralegh, who studied the natural sciences, philosophy, and religion and were suspected of being atheists<; Scop>an Anglo-Saxon court poet<; Stock Characters>conventional character types<; Vade Mecum>an article that one keeps constantly on hand<; Mythos>The plot or story of a work; also, a body of myths belonging to a culture.<; Lipogram>A composition in which one or more letters of the alphabet are deliberately omitted.<; Modulation>A change in tone, pitch, or rhythm in verse or speech.<; Logos>Persuasion by appeal to reason and logic; also, the divine Word or rational principle of the universe.<; Cavalier Lyricists>followers of Charles I (1625-1649)—such as Thomas Carew, Richard Lovelace, and Sir John Suckling—who composed lighthearted poems<; Couplet>two consecutive lines of verse with end rhymes<; Dumb Show>a pantomimic performance used in a play<

column4: Barbarism>a mistake in the form of a word or a word that results from such a mistake<; Heteroglossia>“Different tongues” or “different speech”; a term introduced by Mikhail Bakhtin to designate the presence of more than one voice in a given narrative or another work<; Solecism>a violation of prescriptive grammatical rules<; Neologism (or Neology)>a new word introduced into a language, especially for enhancing style<; Archaism>obsolete phrasing, idiom, syntax, or spelling<; Xenoglossia (also Xenoglossia, Xenolalia)>the intelligible use of a foreign language that one does not know<; Denotation>the basic meaning of a word, independent of its emotional coloration or associations<; Cliché>any expression so often used that its freshness and clarity have worn off; from the French word for a stereotype plate<; Connotation>the emotional implications and associations that words may carry, as distinguished from their denotative meanings<; Macaronic>(1) Pejoratively, “a blockhead” or “a dandy.” (2) Writing that combines two or more languages<; Nonce Word>a word invented by an author for a particular usage or special meaning; in earlier forms of a language, a word with a single recorded occurrence<; Dialects>varieties of the same “language” spoken by two groups or persons whose speech exhibits very marked differences<; Provincialism>a word, phrase, or manner of expression peculiar to a special region and not commonly used outside that region—therefore, not fashionable or sophisticated<; Koine>the language spoken throughout the ancient Greek world; colloquial Attic with numerous supplements from other dialects and other languages<; Philology>in its general sense, philology means the scientific study of both language and literature<; Orphism>defined by Gerald L. Bruns as “the idea of poetic speech as the ground of all signification.<; Structuralism>an intellectual movement utilizing the methods of structural linguistics and structural anthropology<; Deconstruction>a widespread philosophical and critical movement that owes its name and energy to the precepts and examples of Jacques Derrida<; Jargon>The specialized vocabulary of a profession or group; also, unintelligible or pretentious language.<; Grimm’s Law>a principle formulated by Jakob Grimm in 1822 that describes a complex of relations among consonants in Indo-European languages<; Idiotism>a departure from linguistic norms, peculiar to a single speaker, dialect, or period<; Grammatology>Derrida’s term for the study of writing as a system, prior to and distinct from speech.<; Bombast>originally, any sort of ornamental but unnecessary padding; now mostly limited to ranting, insincere and extravagant language, and outlandish grandiloquence<; Semiotics>the study of the rules that enable social phenomena—considered as signs—to have meaning<; Slang>vernacular speech not accepted as suitable for highly formal usage, although it is much used in conversation<; Hermeticism>defined by Gerald L. Bruns as “the idea of the ‘pure expressiveness’ of literary speech,” in which a writer’s use of language deviates from ordinary discourse enough to arrest the function of signification<; Gossip>a staple of human culture from the beginning, gossip is the unofficial exchange of information and opinions having to do with the private conduct of others<; Macaronic Verse>a type of verse that mingles two or more languages<; Literal>accurate to the letter; without embellishment<; Patter Song>most often, a comic solo of rapidly spoken words with only sketchy musical accompaniment<; Patter>the special language of low-life types in general; the spiel delivered by a street-seller or carnival barker; rapid speech associated with comedians, magicians, or other such performers<; Billingsgate>Coarse, foul, or abusive language.<; Glossolalia>Speaking in tongues; fluent but unintelligible speech.<; Idiolect>one person’s particular language—including vocabulary, syntax, pronunciation—slightly different from everybody else’s<; Synonyms>words with the same or similar meanings<; Semantics>the study of meaning; sometimes limited to linguistic meaning (see linguistics); and sometimes used to discriminate between surface and substance<; Coprology>Obscene or scatological writing or language.<; Anglo-Saxon>a Teutonic tribal group resident in England in post-Roman times<; Anglo-Norman (Language)>the term Anglo-Norman (also Anglo-French) is applied to the French language as it was used in England in the period following the Norman Conquest (c. 1100-1350) and also to the literature written in Anglo-Norman<; Deictic>a word—usually a pronoun, adjective, or adverb—that refers to another part of the discourse and not outward to a world or context<; Dithyramb>literary expression characterized by wild, excited, passionate language<; Meaning>that which is communicated; I. A. Richards distinguished four aspects of meaning: sense, feeling, tone, and intention<; Logocentrism>a key term in deconstruction; it argues that there is a persistent but morbid centering of Logos (meaning thought, truth, law, reason, logic, word, and the Word) in Western thought since Plato<; Lyric Present>a term suggested by George T. Wright to designate the use of the simple present tense (“I walk”) in a place where a normal speaker would use the progressive (“I am walking”)<; Morpheme>a minimal meaningful linguistic unit<; Linguistics>the scientific study of language<; Old English (Language)>that Germanic dialect spoken in the British Isles between the Anglo-Saxon invasions in the fifth century and the Norman Conquest in the eleventh<; Phoneme>in linguistics, the smallest potentially significant unit of articulated sound in a language<; Signifier and Signified>in Saussurean linguistics, the two elements of a piece of language—the signifier being the relatively concrete and the signified the relatively abstract<; Wardour-Street English>a style strongly marked by archaisms; an insincere, artificial expression<; Great Vowel Shift>A major change in the pronunciation of English long vowels between about 1400 and 1700.<; American Language>certain idioms, pronunciations, and forms peculiar to the English language in America<; Anglo-French>the French language as used in England between 1100 and 1350<; Binary Opposition>a principle originating in linguistics around 1915 that elements of a system do not exist as absolute substances but only as entities-defined in structural opposition to something else<; Cognate>descended from a common ancestor; applied to languages (as Greek, Latin, and English qualify as cognate languages in the Indo-European family) as well as to words (as odous, dens, and tooth in the same languages)<; Différance>a virtually untranslatable French neologism introduced by Jacques Derrida to combine various denotations and connotations of difference, differing, deferring, and deferral<; Franco-Norman>material written in England shortly after the Conquest by Normans or persons of Norman descent using the Norman dialect of French<; Dissemination>in Jacques Derrida’s application, a term exploiting its root in Latin semen (“seed”) and a fancied relation to Greek sēma (“sign”) to suggest that meaning in language is variously scattered<; English Language>the language that developed from the West Germanic dialects spoken by the Angles, Saxons, and other Teutonic invaders who occupied England in the fifth and sixth centuries<; Dialogism>according to Mikhail Bakhtin, a feature of certain literature that permits the polyphonic interplay of many different voices rather than allowing a single monologic voice to dominate<; Deixis>the use of deictics<; Linguistics and Literary Criticism>the connection between the study of language and of literature, which reached a high point after World War II when the techniques of structural linguistics were extended to individual texts and to literature as a whole<; Morphology>a word coined by Goethe for the study of forms at any level<; Inkhorn>a term almost five hundred years old for needlessly learned, pedantic, and affected language, especially the use of foreign words<; Locution>a word or a group of words that constitutes a meaning group<; Lento Form>opposite of allegro form<; Linguistic Atlas>a reference work that records in tables and maps geographical differences in vocabulary, syntax, inflection, pronunciation, and any such feature of language that changes from place to place<; Monoglot>using only one language<; Loan Word>a word that passes in its native form from one language to another without being translated<; Middle English>english as spoken and written between the Norman Conquest and the Modern English period beginning at the Renaissance<; Monolingual>same as monoglot<; Phonetics>the study of the production of speech sounds; the study of sounds as physical objects or events<; Paradigmaticity>the quality of a choice made from a paradigm of possibilities; in ordinary discourse, a speaker chooses one item from a paradigm and joins it to items drawn from other paradigms<; Saussurean Linguistics>an influential theory derived from the work of the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure (1857-1913)<; Sign>in Saussurean linguistics, a unit made up of a signifier (such as a sound-image) and a signified (such as a mental concept), the relation between them being arbitrary<

column4: Verbum Infans Formula>a conventional paradoxical topos, meaning “the unspeaking word,” applied to the infant (infans, “not speaking”) Christ, who incarnates the Word (verbum)<; Exegesis>an explanation and interpretation of a text<; Typology>the study of allegorical symbols, especially with the Bible, in which much of the Old Testament is read as a type of the revelation to come in the New Testament<; Vulgate>from Latin vulgus, “crowd,” meaning “common”; chiefly, the Latin version of the Bible made by Saint Jerome in the fourth century<; Septuagint>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, made in the third and second centuries B.C.<; Apocrypha>books of the Bible not regarded as inspired and hence excluded from the sacred canon; the word originally meant “hidden or secret things.<; Bible>from a Greek term meaning “the books”; the collection of writings known as the Holy Scriptures, the sacred writings of the Christian religion<; Testament>the term may refer to a literary “last will and testament” or to a piece of literature that “bears witness to” or “makes a covenant with” in the biblical sense<; Torah>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible; more broadly, the whole of Jewish teaching and law.<; Tetrapla>An edition of a text in four parallel versions, especially Origen’s four-column Old Testament.<; Bible, English Translations of>the translations and paraphrases of the Bible into English, from the Old and Middle English versions (all based on the Latin Vulgate) of Caedmon to Wycliffe and later<; Dead Sea Scrolls>about 800 documents written between the first century B.C. and about A.D. 70, discovered in 1947 (and later) in caves near the Dead Sea<; Apocryphon>rare singular of Apocrypha, meaning a single apocryphal work<; Bible as Literature>the study of the Bible for its literary qualities, which are accounted for partly by the themes, partly by the character of the Hebrew language, and partly by the literary skill of biblical writers and translators<; Bible, Influence on Literature>the subtly pervasive influence of the Bible on English literature, much of it indirect—through its effect on language and on the mental and moral interests of the English and American people<; Higher Criticism>certain aspects of the study of biblical texts in the nineteenth century, seeking to determine the authorship, date, place of origin, and historical credibility of the books of the Bible<; Hexapla (also Hexaple)>a sixfold text arranged in parallel columns to permit detailed comparison of versions<; Masorah>the body of critical commentary on the texts of Hebrew Scriptures, compiled at least a thousand years ago by Jewish scholars known as Masoretes<; Midrash>rabbinical notes and commentaries on the Scriptures; Hebrew for “explanation.<
