column4: Leonine Rhyme>the internal rhyming of the last stressed syllable before the caesura, with the last stressed syllable of the line<; Feminine Rhyme>a rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllables are followed by an undifferentiated identical unstressed syllable<; Compound Rhyme>rhyme between primary and secondary stressed syllables<; Masculine Rhyme>rhyme that falls on the stressed concluding syllables of the rhyme words<; Rhyme>identity of terminal sound between accented syllables, usually occupying corresponding positions in two or more lines of verse<; Eye Rhyme>rhyme that appears correct from the spelling but is not so from the pronunciation<; Broken Rhyme>the breaking of a word at the end of a line for the sake of a rhyme<; Heteromerous Rhyme>a fairly rare species of multiple rhyme (also called “mosaic”) in which typically one word is forced into a rhyme with two or more words<; Slant Rhyme>near rhyme; usually the substitution of assonance or consonance for true rhyme<; Internal Rhyme>rhyme that occurs at some place before the last syllables in a line<; Identical Rhyme>a phenomenon, also called redundant rhyme or rime riche, in which a syllable both begins and ends in the same way as a rhyming syllable, without being the same word<; Homeoteleuton>sameness or similarity of endings of consecutive words or words near each other—often considered unsettling or graceless but sometimes unavoidable<; Perfect Rhyme (or True Rhyme)>Rhyme in which the stressed vowels and all following sounds are identical, while the preceding consonants differ.<; Mosaic>another name for heteromerous rhyme<; Rime Riche>words with identical sounds but different meanings<; Assonance Rhyme>assonance is a common substitution for end rhyme in the popular ballad<; Fused Rhyme>a curious phenomenon, scarcely found anywhere in English outside a few poems by Gerard Manley Hopkins, in which a rhyme sound is begun at the end of a line but not completed until the beginning of the next<; Triple Rhyme>rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllable is followed by two unstressed, undifferentiated syllables<; Chain Rhyme>a device in which the sound of the last syllable of one line recurs as the sound of the first syllable of the next but with a change of meaning<; Beginning Rhyme>rhyme that occurs in the first syllable or syllables of lines<; Near Rhyme>the repetition in accented syllables of the final consonant sound without the correspondence of the preceding vowel sound<; Half Rhyme>imperfect rhyme, usually the result of consonance<; Pararhyme>an acoustic effect—systematically practiced by Wilfred Owen, W. H. Auden, Keith Douglas, and others—whereby the place of ordinary rhyme is taken by a combination of alliteration and consonance rhyme<; Amphisbaenic Rhyme>backward rhyme—that is, two rhyme words or syllables, the second of which inverts the order of the first; named for the monster in Greek fable that has a head at each end<; Cento>a literary patchwork—usually in verse—made up of scraps from one or many authors<; Feminine Ending>an extrametrical unstressed syllable added to the end of a line in iambic or anapestic rhythm<; Homeoarchy>the occurrence of the same or similar unstressed syllables preceding rhyming stressed syllables<; Oblique Rhyme>approximate but not true rhyme; oblique rhyme is another term for near rhyme, half rhyme, and slant rhyme<; Successive Patterning>an arrangement by succession, as in a rhyme scheme of aabb and so forth; distinguished from alternation (abab) and chiasmus (abba)<; Rhyme Royal (or Rime Royal)>a seven-lined iambic pentameter stanza rhyming ababbcc, sometimes with an alexandrine (hexameter) seventh line<; Analyzed Rhyme>a complex form of rhyme that involves breaking down or analyzing components<; Enclosed Rhyme>the rhyme pattern of the In Memoriam stanza: abba<; Double Rhyme>feminine rhyme; that is, rhyme in which the similarly stressed syllables are followed by identically unstressed syllables<; Recessed Rhyme>a complex device whereby rhyme occurs between stressed syllables that are recessed one or two syllables from the end of a word, without qualifying as feminine rhyme<; Rime Couée>a tail-rhyme stanza, in which two lines—usually in tetrameter—are followed by a short line—usually in trimeter—as in aabccb<; Anisobaric>a meteorological term having to do with unequal weight or atmospheric pressure; also used in prosody for rhyming syllables that bear significantly different levels of accent<; Monorhyme>a poem that uses only one rhyme<; Interlaced Rhyme>see Crossed Rhyme<; Crossed Rhyme>couplets—usually hexameter or longer—in which the words preceding the caesura rhyme<; End Rhyme>rhyme at the ends of lines in a poem<; Masculine Ending>a line of verse that ends on a stressed syllable, as does any regular iambic line<; Rime retournée>the relation between such syllables as “pal” and “lap”; also called amphisbaenic or boustrophedon rhyme<; Apocopated Rhyme>rhyme in which the final stressed syllable of a word is rhymed with the stressed syllable of a word ending in a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable (see masculine rhyme and feminine rhyme)<; Cross-Compound Rhyme>rhyme between the first syllable of one word and the second syllable of another—and vice versa<; Interlocking Rhyme>a rhyme pattern in which one line in a rhyming unit carries forward the rhyme for the next unit<; Linked Rhyme>another name for fused rhyme<; Light Ending>a feminine ending<; Rhyme Scheme>the pattern in which rhyme sounds occur in a stanza<; Terminal Rhyme>see End Rhyme<

column4: Pun>a play on words based on the similarity of sound between two words with different meanings<; Epigram>a pithy saying, often antithetical; also a short poem characterized by compression, balance, and polish<; Equivoque>a kind of pun in which language is so used that it has two different but appropriate meanings<; Stichomythia>a form of repartee developed in classical drama and often employed by Elizabethan writers, especially those imitating the Senecan tragedies<; Quibble>earlier, a pun; nowadays, a verbal device for evading the point at issue<; Aphorism>a concise statement of a principle or precept given in pointed words<; Repartee>a “comeback”; a quick, ingenious response or rejoinder; a retort aptly twisted; conversation made up of brilliant witticisms; loosely, any clever reply; also, anyone’s facility and aptness in such ready wit<; Quip>a retort or sarcastic jest; hence, any witty saying<; Jeu d’esprit>a witty playing with words; a clever sally<; Paronomasia>pun<; Adage>a proverb or saying made familiar by long use<; Malaphorism>an aphorism or otherwise familiar saying given enough of a twist to become humorous or satirical<; Maxim>a concise statement, usually drawn from experience and inculcating some practical advice; an adage<; Proverb>a saying that briefly and memorably expresses some recognized truth about life, originally preserved by oral tradition<; Axiom>a maxim or aphorism whose truth is held to be self-evident<; Agnomination (also adnomination, annomination)>a term used between 1600 and 1800 to mean, variously, any play on words, especially such as involved names of persons<; Apothegm>an unusually terse, pithy, witty saying, even more concise and pointed than an aphorism<; Bon Mot>a witty repartee or statement<; Breviora>a collection of brief writings or sayings<; Mot>french for “word”; sometimes bon mot, “good word.” A brief, apt saying<; Punchline>the line in a joke—normally the last—containing the point of it all<; Sentence>a rhetorical term formerly in use in the sense of maxim (Latin sententia), usually applied to quoted “wise sayings.<

column4: Allegory>a form of extended metaphor in which objects, persons, places, and actions in a narrative are equated with meanings outside the narrative itself<; Legend>a narrative or tradition handed down from the past; distinguished from a myth by having more of historical truth and perhaps less of the supernatural<; Parable>an illustrative story teaching a lesson<; Folklore>the study of the survivals of archaic beliefs, customs, and traditions in modern ages; a term first used by W. J. Thoms as a substitute for “popular antiquities.<; Myth>an anonymous story that presents supernatural episodes as a means of interpreting natural events<; Fabliau (plural, Fabliaux)>a humorous tale popular in medieval France<; Fable>a brief tale told to point a moral<; Märchen>german fairy tales, either simple folktales or short allegories laid in a fantastic realm<; Apologue>a moral fable, such as that in C. Day Lewis’s “A Country Comet.<; Fantasy>a conscious breaking free from reality; sometimes used as an equivalent of fancy and even of imagination<; Folktale>a short narrative handed down through oral tradition, with various tellers and groups modifying it, so it acquires cumulative authorship<; Fairy Tale>a story relating mysterious pranks and adventures of spirits who manifest themselves in the form of diminutive human beings<; Riddle>a puzzling question or description to be solved, with a dignified ancestor in the riddles of ancient and medieval literature<; Folk Song>a song of unknown authorship preserved and transmitted orally<; Beast Fable>a short tale in which the principal actors are animals<; Graustark>a fictional country that seems to be a small and minor Central European monarchy that has held on to some feudal ways<; Tall Tale>a kind of humorous tale, common on the American frontier, that uses realistic detail, a literal manner, and common speech to recount extravagantly impossible happenings<; Nursery Rhyme>brief verses—often anonymous and traditional—with percussive rhythm and frequent, heavy rhyme, written for young children<; Pegasus>the winged horse of Grecian fable said to have sprung from Medusa’s body at her death<; Moral>The lesson or principle taught by a story, fable, or other work.<; Animal Epic>see Beast Epic<; Beast Epic>a medieval literary form consisting of a series of linked stories grouped around animal characters and often presenting satirical comment on the church or court by means of human qualities attributed to beast characters<; Counting-Out Rhyme or Song>a formulaic chant used to determine who is to be excluded from or included in an activity; largely but not exclusively a children’s concern<; Exemplum (plural Exempla)>a moralized tale; a tale, anecdote, or incident used by medieval preachers to point morals or illustrate doctrines<; Ghost Story>a story that involves a ghost or similar spirit<; Fantastic>sometimes a synonym for fantasy; sometimes distinguished from fantasy and science fiction by its reliance on the imagination for the realization of inward states of mind<; Mabinogion>a collection of old Welsh tales translated by Lady Charlotte Guest from the Red Book of Hergest, a manuscript from the thirteenth or fourteenth century that contains tales composed centuries earlier<; Oriental Tale (also Oriental Novel, Eastern Tale, Eastern Novel)>a work set in some Eastern place that takes advantage of exotic possibilities for melodrama, romance, and adventure; a fashion traceable to the first English translation of The Arabian Nights<; Oral Transmission>the transmission of material by word of mouth and memory<

column4: Abridgment>a shortened version of a work but one that attempts to preserve essential elements<; Rebus>a text in which ordinary verbal symbols are supplemented by pictures and other devices to suggest a total meaning<; Transliteration>a character-by-character transfer of a word from one alphabet or writing system to another<; Synopsis>a summary of the main points of a composition so made as to show the relation of parts to the whole; an abstract<; Uncial>descriptive of large, rounded letters such as those used in some Latin and Greek manuscripts from the Middle Ages through the eighteenth century<; Compendium>a brief condensation of a longer work or of a whole field of knowledge<; Analecta (Analects)>literary gleanings, fragments, or passages from the writings of an author or authors; also, the title for a collection of choice extracts—for example, Analects of Confucius<; Epitome>a summary or abridgment; a “miniature representation” of a subject<; Recension>a text that incorporates the best readings taken by critical editing from several sources<; Translation>the rendering of a work from one language to another<; Adaptation>the rewriting of a work from its original form to fit it for another medium; also, the new form of such a rewritten work<; Abstract (noun)>an abridgment that summarizes the principal ideas in a longer work<; Brief>a condensed statement, a résumé, of the main arguments or ideas presented in a speech or piece of writing<; Condensation>a shortened form of a longer work but one that attempts to retain its salient characteristics, including style<; Conspectus>a survey, summary, or outline<; Cybertext>texts of sorts other than conventional linear narratives, such as hypertext fiction, computer games, and collaborative interactive texts on the Internet<; Digest>a systematic arrangement of condensed materials on some specific subject, so that it summarizes the information on that subject<; Hypertext>defined by T. H. Nelson, the coiner of the term, as “a body of written or pictorial material interconnected in such a complex way that it could not conveniently be presented or represented on paper.<; Précis>an abstract or epitome of the essential facts or statements of a work, retaining the order of the original<; Textuality>the condition of being a text as such and not another kind of work or document<; Version>a particular form or variant<; Vulgaria>(1) Up through the early seventeenth century, a set of vernacular selections to be translated into Latin as an exercise. column4: Romance>a kind of fiction, originally the Old French tales translated from Latin and named after the Romance languages derived from Latin<; Chivalry in English Literature>the system of manners and morals known as chivalry—a product of medieval feudalism—presented in idealized form in medieval romance and furnishing colorful subject matter for much later literature<; Chanson d’aventure>a poem recounting a romantic adventure, often involving a journey on horseback or a sea voyage<; Alliterative Romance>a metrical romance written in alliterative verse, especially produced during the revival of interest in alliterative poetry in the fourteenth century<; Arthurian Legend>the vast body of romantic story about Arthur and the knights of the Round Table, which probably grew out of the deeds of some historical person—presumably a Welsh or Roman military leader of the fifth century<; Breton Romance>a medieval French metrical romance that emphasizes love as the central force in the plot<; Breton Lay>a relatively brief form of the medieval French romance, professed to have been sung by Breton minstrels on Celtic themes; also, English medieval poems written in imitation of such works<; Chivalric Romance>medieval romance reflecting the customs and ideals of chivalry<; Courts of Love>tribunals for settling questions involved in the system of courtly love<; Greek Romance>a work of prose fiction such as those produced between A.D. 100 and A.D. 300 by the Erotici Graeci<; Metrical Romance>a romantic tale in verse<; Medieval Romance>a tale of adventure in which knights, kings, or distressed ladies—motivated by love, religious faith, or the mere desire for adventure—are the chief figures<; Pastoral Romance>a prose narrative—usually long and complicated in plot—in which the characters bear pastoral names and in which pastoral conventions dominate<; Tail-Rhyme Romance>metrical romances employing the tail-rhyme stanza, especially a group employing a twelve-line stanza of four parts, each with a short “tail” line<; Romantic Epic>a type of long narrative poem developed by Italian Renaissance poets (late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries) by combining the medieval romance with the classical epic<

column4: Paean>a song of praise or joy; originally, an ode sung by a Greek chorus in honor of Apollo<; Ode>a single, unified strain of exalted lyrical verse, directed to a single purpose, and dealing with one theme<; Alcaics>verses written according to the manner of the odes of Alcaeus—usually a four-stanza poem, with each stanza composed of four lines<; Antistrophe>one of the three stanzaic forms of the Greek choral ode, identical in meter with the strophe, which precedes it<; Odelet>a little ode<; Homostrophic>consisting of structurally identical strophes; hence, made up of stanzas of the same pattern<; Palinode>a piece of writing recanting or retracting a previous writing—particularly such a recanting in verse of an earlier ode<; Strophe>a stanza; in the Pindaric ode, the first stanza and every subsequent third stanza<; Alloeostropha (also spelled alloeostrophe)>milton’s term for the variable division of the choric odes in Samson Agonistes into what he called irregular “stanzas or pauses.<; Apolelymenon>milton’s term for the monostrophic design of such choruses as those in his Samson Agonistes<; Cowleyan Ode>a form of the irregular ode used by Abraham Cowley in the seventeenth century<; Epode>one of the three stanza forms in the Pindaric ode; the others are strophe and antistrophe<; Irregular Ode>an ode that does not follow either the pattern of strophe, antistrophe, and epode of the Pindaric ode or the repetition of stanzas of the Horatian ode but freely alters its stanzaic forms both in number and in length<; Horatian Ode>horace applied the term ode to informal poems written in a single stanzaic form, in contrast to the strophe, antistrophe, and epode of the Pindaric ode<; Monostrophic>a term used by Milton for the form of the choruses in Samson Agonistes<; Pindaric Ode>the regular ode, characterized by a division into units containing three parts: the strophe and antistrophe, alike in form, and the epode, different from the other two<

column4: In Medias Res>a term from Horace, literally “in or into the middle parts of things,” applied to the technique of opening a story in the middle of the action<; Ubi Sunt Formula>a convention much used in verse, rhetorically asking “where are those who were before us?” (ubi sunt qui ante nos fuerunt?<; Verbum Infans Formula>a conventional paradoxical topos, meaning “the unspeaking word,” applied to the infant (infans, “not speaking”) Christ, who incarnates the Word (verbum)<; Mythopoeia>myth-making, construed as either an individual function of a single artist or a collective spirit<; Verisimilitude>the semblance of truth; the degree to which a work creates the appearance of the truth<; Unities>the principles of dramatic structure involving the unities of action, time, and place<; Episodic Structure>writing that consists of little more than a series of incidents, with the episodes succeeding each other and with no particularly logical arrangement or complication<; Gazebo>notably boring material that takes up time and space without advancing a plot, explaining a character, or even affording entertainment<; Formulaic>work that relies excessively on set patterns of plot, character, sentiment, and language—as though written to a formula<; Genre>used to designate the types or categories into which literary works are grouped according to form, technique, or, sometimes, subject matter<; Stereotype>the metal duplication of a printing surface, cast from a mold made of the surface, usually by wet paper pulp<; Coda>a conclusion that usually restates or summarizes or integrates the preceding themes or movements<; Type>a group having certain characteristics in common that distinguish them as being members of a definite class<; Archetype>in the psychology of Carl Jung, a “primordial image” from the “collective unconscious” of the human race, shaped by the experience of our ancestors and expressed in myths, religion, dreams, fantasies, and literature<; Open-Endedness>the possibility that a work need not be tied up tidily at the end but can stop without concluding or closing<; Stream of Consciousness>the total range of awareness and emotive-mental response of an individual, from the lowest pre-speech level to the highest fully articulated level of rational thought<; Topos>a rhetorical commonplace or frequently used literary situation or subject; etymologically, a place<; Theatrum Mundi>The idea that the world is a stage and people are actors on it.<; Formula>a hackneyed sequence of events characteristic of some popular forms of writing<; Mode>broad categories of treatment of material, such as romance, comedy, tragedy, or satire; broader than genre<; Scenario>an outline giving the sequence of actions making up the plot and the appearances of the principal characters<; Stock Situation>a situation recurring frequently in a literary form, whether a general plot situation—such as boy-meets-girl—or a recurrent detail, such as mixed identity<; Moral>The lesson or principle taught by a story, fable, or other work.<; Convention>a literary convention is any device or style or subject matter which has become—in its time and by reason of its habitual usage—a recognized means of literary expression; an accepted element in technique<; Contrapuntal>the adjective of counterpoint, a musical term; applied by analogy to literary works in which elements are played against each other<; Decorum>a term loosely describing what is proper to a character, subject, or setting<; Form>the organization of the elementary parts of a work of art in relation to its total effect<; Kind>a term used in the Neoclassic Period for genre or literary type<; Mise en Abyme>any occasion when a small text is imprinted on or contained in a bigger text that it replicates; from the heraldic term for a small shield on a big shield<; Organic Form>a notion of the structure of a literary work as growing from its conception in the thought, feeling, and personality of the writer rather than being shaped arbitrarily and mechanically in a preconceived mold<; Prototype>a first form or original instance of a thing or model or pattern for later form or examples<; Nostos (plural Nostoi)>a work describing a return, especially a homecoming<; Propriety>in the general sense, conformity to accepted standards of taste or conduct<; Spatial Form>joseph Frank’s term for forms of modern writing that suspend or abolish the customary temporal structure of literature and substitute virtual space for time<; Unity>the concept that a work shall have in it some organizing principle to which all its parts are related so the work is an organic whole<; Structure>the planned framework of a piece of literature<

column4: Zeugma>a term used in several ways, all involving a sort of “yoking”; for example, as a synonym of syllepsis, when an object-taking word has two or more objects on different levels<; Asyndeton>a condensed form of expression in which elements customarily joined by conjunctions are presented in series without the conjunctions<; Inversion>the placing of a sentence element out of its normal position<; Barbarism>a mistake in the form of a word or a word that results from such a mistake<; Polysyndeton>the use of more conjunctions than is normal<; Syllepsis>a grammatically correct construction in which one word is placed in the same grammatical relationship to two words but in quite different senses<; Antithesis>a figure of speech characterized by strongly contrasting words, clauses, sentences, or ideas<; Transferred Epithet>an adjective used to limit a noun that it really does not logically modify<; Solecism>a violation of prescriptive grammatical rules<; Parenthesis>an explanatory remark inside a statement and frequently separated from it by parentheses ( )<; Parallelism>such an arrangement that one element of equal importance with another is similarly developed and phrased<; Parataxis>an arrangement of sentences, clauses, phrases, or words in coordinate rather than subordinate constructions, often without connectives<; Archaism>obsolete phrasing, idiom, syntax, or spelling<; Rhetorical Question>a question propounded for its rhetorical effect and not requiring a reply or intended to induce a reply<; Polyhyphenation>the use of more than a usual number of hyphens<; Ellipsis (or Ellipse)>the omission of one or more words that, while essential to a grammatic structure, are easily supplied<; Epithet>strictly, an adjective used to point out a characteristic of a person or thing<; Hendiadys>a figure of speech in which an idea is expressed by giving two components as though they were independent and connecting them with a coordinating conjunction rather than subordinating one part to the other<; Apposition>the placing in immediately succeeding order of two or more coordinate elements, one of which is an explanation, qualification, or modification of the first<; Anastrophe>inversion of the usual, normal, or logical order of the parts of a sentence<; Balance>balance characterizes a structure in which parts of the whole—as words, phrases, or clauses in a sentence—are set off against each other so as to emphasize a contrast<; Expletive>an interjection to lend emphasis to a sentence or, in verse especially, the use of a superfluous word (some form of the verb “to do” for example) to make for rhythm<; Hypotaxis>arrangement of clauses, phrases, or words in dependent or subordinate relationships<; Homeric Epithet>an adjectival phrase so often repeated in connection with a person or thing that it almost becomes a part of the name<; Syntax>the rule-governed arrangement of words in sentences; with vocabulary, one of the two components of diction<; Poetic License>the privilege—sometimes claimed by poets—of departing from normal order, diction, rhyme, or pronunciation<; Enallage>the substitution of one grammatical form for another, as past for present tense, singular for plural, noun for verb<; Hypozeuxis>the paralleling of a number of clauses, each with a subject and predicate<; Tmesis>a verbal figure whereby a word is cut into two parts between which other verbal matter is inserted; literally, a “cutting.<; Syndeton>The use of conjunctions between the words, phrases, or clauses in a series.<; Anacoluthon>the failure—accidental or deliberate—to complete a sentence according to the structural plan on which it was started<; Antimeria (also Anthimeria, Anthemeria)>a species of enallage, using one part of speech for another<; Aposiopesis>the intentional failure to complete a sentence<; Hysteron Proteron>“Latter before”; a figure of speech in which what should logically come last comes first<; Heterosis>a lexical figure in which one form of a word (noun, pronoun, adjective, verb) is replaced by another<; Loose Sentence>a sentence grammatically complete before the end; the opposite of periodic sentence<; Hypozeugma>the combination of a single subject with several predicates<; Periodic Sentence>a sentence not grammatically complete before its end; the opposite of a loose sentence<; Period>a complete sentence, especially when containing more than one clause<; Priamel>a style of verse in which a series of parallel statements act as a preamble to a climactic conclusion—usually a statement of praise<; Question>the grammatical form of asking; interrogation<; Sleight of “and”>a general term that indicates those tropes—such as hendiadys, syllepsis, and zeugma—that involve “and” or another coordinating conjunction<; Synchysis (also, erroneously, Synchisis and Synchesis)>confusion, as of words poured out on a page<

column4: Haiku>a form of Japanese poetry that states—in three lines of five, seven, and five syllables—a clear picture designed to arouse a distinct emotion and suggest a specific spiritual insight<; Senryu>a form with the same structure as the haiku—seventeen syllables in lines of five, seven, and five—but relying on humor or satire rather than conventions related to the seasons<; Tanka>a type of Japanese poetry similar to the haiku<; Dramatic Monologue>a poem that reveals “a soul in action” through the speech of one character in a dramatic situation<; Doggerel>rude verse; any poorly executed attempt at poetry<; Lai>a song or short narrative poem<; Metaphysical Poetry>poetry of the seventeenth-century writers called the “Metaphysical Poets”; sometimes used in the broad sense of philosophical poetry<; Katauta>A Japanese poetic form of three lines in a 5-7-7 syllable pattern.<; Almanac>in medieval times, a permanent table showing the movements of the heavenly bodies; later, a calendar for a single year that came to include useful information, especially for farmers<; Gnomic>aphoristic, moralistic, sententious—from gnome, a Greek poem that expressed a general truth<; Confessional Poetry>the work of a group of modern poets whose work features a public and sometimes painful display of private, personal matters<; Didactic Poetry>poetry that is primarily intended to teach a lesson<; Topographical Poetry>poetry in which, according to Samuel Johnson’s definition, “the fundamental subject is some particular landscape.<; Companion Poems>poems designed to complement each other<; Narrative Poem>a poem that tells a story<; Boasting Poem>a poem in which characters boast of their exploits; frequently found in oral literatures and in works such as ballads and epics<; Conversation Piece (or Conversation Poem)>a relaxed and informal poem of “discourse” or “conversation” with an addressee, after Horace’s sermones<; Meditative Poetry>certain kinds of metaphysical poetry of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries that yoke religious meditation with Renaissance poetic techniques<; Almanac Poem>a poem suitable for inclusion in an old-fashioned almanac, with advice for farmers and astrological information<; Country House Poem>a type of poem—flourishing in the seventeenth century—that used an actual country house—usually the seat of an important family—as the center of a meditation on life and society<; Cubist Poetry>poetry that attempts to do in verse what cubist painters do on canvas—that is, take the elements of an experience, fragment them, and then rearrange them in a meaningful new synthesis<; Definition Poem>an Elizabethan mode defined by Louis Martz as “a rapid sequence of analogies.<; Lay (or Lai)>a song or short narrative poem<; Night-Piece>a literary work with a night setting and subject; originally, a painting of a night scene<; Priamel>a style of verse in which a series of parallel statements act as a preamble to a climactic conclusion—usually a statement of praise<; Prose Poem>a poem printed as prose, with both margins justified<

Forster’s term for a character constructed around a single idea or quality<; Persona>literally, a mask; a “second self” created by an author and through whom the narrative is told<; Round Character>a term used by E. M. Forster for a character sufficiently complex to be able to surprise the reader without losing credibility<; Braggadocio>a noisy braggart who is actually a coward<; Static Character>a character who changes little if at all<; Redende Name>german, “speaking name”; a name that is significant<; Dynamic Character>a character who develops or changes as a result of the actions of the plot<; Ethos>the character of the speaker or writer as reflected in speech or writing; the quality or set of emotions that a speaker or writer enacts in order to affect an audience<; Tritagonist>the actor taking the part third in importance in a Greek drama<; Grundy, Mrs.>a character from Thomas Morton’s play Speed the Plough, who does not actually appear but of whose judgments everyone in the play is very much afraid<; Protagonist>the chief character in a work<; Stock Characters>conventional character types<; Eiron>a basic comic character in Greek drama—typically a swindler, trickster, hypocrite, or picaresque rogue—who feigns ignorance in order to trick others<; Nemesis>the Greek goddess of retributive justice or vengeance<; Alazon>the braggart or impostor in Greek comedy<; Doppelganger>german, “double goer”; a mysterious double, a common figure in literature<; Naive Narrator (or Hero)>an ingenuous character who is the ostensible author (often the oral narrator) of a narrative, the implications of which are plainer to the reader than they are to the narrator<; Antagonist>the character directly opposed to the protagonist<; Byronism>the qualities associated with Lord Byron (1788-1824), whose unique electricity provoked the coining of such terms as “Byronic,” “Byroniad,” and “Byronism.<; Foil>any person who through contrast underscores the distinctive characteristics of another; literally, a “leaf” of bright metal placed under a jewel to increase its brilliance<; Agroikos>a character added by Northrop Frye to the traditional three stock characters of Greek old comedy<; Deuteragonist>the role second in importance to the protagonist in Greek drama<; La Femme Inspiratrice>a type of real person or literary character: the woman who inspires an artist<; Femme Fatale>a stock character type; the dangerously attractive woman<; Ingénue>an innocent, artless, often virginal young girl, common in many literary forms as well as television<; Dramatis Personae>the characters in a drama, a novel, or a poem<; Antihero>a protagonist of a modern play or novel who has the converse of most of the traditional attributes of the hero<; Miles Gloriosus>the braggart soldier; a stock character in comedy<; Hero or Heroine>the central character (masculine or feminine) in a work<; Pegasus>the winged horse of Grecian fable said to have sprung from Medusa’s body at her death<; Character>the moral constitution of the human personality, or the presence in art of creatures that seem to be human beings; also, a brief descriptive sketch of a personage who typifies some definite quality<; Manic Pixie Dream Girl>A stock character: a quirky, free-spirited young woman who exists mainly to bring joy and growth to a brooding male hero.<; Adversarius>the “straight” character in a formal satire who is addressed by the persona and who functions to elicit and shape that speaker’s remarks<; Buffoon>a comic character—akin to the clown, fool, and jester—given to raillery, boasting, and indecency<; Characterization>the creation of imaginary persons so that they seem lifelike<; Choral Character>a character in a play or a novel who stands aside from the action and comments on it or speaks about it as a communal voice<; Clown>a comic character originally with a marked rustic quality, much like the hick, bumpkin, or yokel<; Confidant (feminine, Confidante)>a character who takes little part in the action but is close to the protagonist and receives the confidences and intimate thoughts of the protagonist<; Counterplayers>characters who plot against the hero or heroine<; Ficelle>henry James’s term for a confidante, a means by which a self-effacing author conveys necessary information; literally, one of the strings by which marionettes are controlled<; Lord of Misrule (also Abbot, King, Monk, or Master of Misrule)>around the beginning of the sixteenth century, an official appointed to preside over Christmas revels at court and in some academic communities<; Raissoneur>a character who is the levelheaded personification of reason<; Old Man, Old Woman>stock characters in the theater and also the performers who customarily take such roles<; Villain>an evil character, potentially or actually guilty of serious crimes; he or she acts in opposition to the hero<; Surrogate>a person or a thing substituted for or speaking for another<; Straight Man>in a minstrel show or other comic performance, the character who asks the seemingly serious questions or makes the grave comment that triggers the comic or satiric retort<; Vice>a stock character in the morality play; a tempter both sinister and comic<

column4: Invocation>an address to a deity for aid<; Epic>a long narrative poem in elevated style presenting characters of high position in adventures, forming an organic whole through their relation to a central heroic figure<; Roman de Geste>same as chanson de geste<; Chanson de geste>a “song of great deeds”; a term applied to the early French epic<; Art Epic>a term employed to distinguish such an epic as Milton’s Paradise Lost or Virgil’s Aeneid from so-called folk epics<; Folk Epic>an epic of unknown authorship, assumed to be the product of communal composition<; Rhapsody>a selection from epic poetry sung by a rhapsodist—that is, a wandering minstrel or court poet of ancient Greece<; Epopee>epic poetry in general or (more rarely) a particular epic<; Epic Question>the request or question addressed to the Muse at the beginning of an epic; the answer constitutes the narrative of the work<; Epic Formula>the conventions of structure employed by most epic poets<; Homeric>indicative of or resembling the work of the Greek epic poet Homer (ca. eighth century B.C.), author of the Iliad and the Odyssey; hence, possessing grandeur and imposing magnitude, having heroic dimensions<; Mock Epic (or Mock Heroic)>terms for a literary form that burlesques the epic by treating a trivial subject in the “grand style” or uses the epic formulas to make a trivial subject ridiculous by ludicrously overstating it<; Comitatus>The bond of loyalty between a Germanic chieftain and his warriors.<; Animal Epic>see Beast Epic<; Beast Epic>a medieval literary form consisting of a series of linked stories grouped around animal characters and often presenting satirical comment on the church or court by means of human qualities attributed to beast characters<; Epyllion>a narrative poem usually presenting an episode from the heroic past and resembling an epic but much briefer and more limited<; Literary Epic>a long narrative poem by a poet self-consciously employing the epic formula<; Romantic Epic>a type of long narrative poem developed by Italian Renaissance poets (late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries) by combining the medieval romance with the classical epic<

column4: Muckrakers>a group of American writers who between 1902 and 1911 worked to expose the dishonest methods and unscrupulous motives in big business and in city, state, and national government<; Satanic School>southey’s phrase (1821) for the literary group of Byron, Shelley, Hunt, and others, whose irregular lives and radical ideas suggested the term<; Spasmodic School>a phrase applied by W. E. Aytoun in 1854 to a group of contemporary English poets<; Parnassians>a group of nineteenth-century French poets, so called from their journal Parnasse contemporain<; Agrarians>literally people living in an agricultural society or espousing its merits; in literary history, usually a group of Southern American writers who published The Fugitive (1922-1925)<; Lost Generation>a group of American writers, born around 1900, who served in the First World War and reacted against certain tendencies of older writers in the 1920s<; Cockney School>a derogatory title applied by Blackwood’s Magazine to a group of nineteenth-century writers—including William Hazlitt, Leigh Hunt, and John Keats—because of their alleged poor taste in such matters as diction and rhyme<; Hartford Wits>a group of Connecticut writers, active around the period of the American Revolution<; Fugitives, The>a group associated with Vanderbilt University, which in the 1920s published the magazine The Fugitive<; New York School>a group of American poets who flourished between 1950 and 1970, distinguished by urbanity, wit, learning, spontaneity, and exuberance<; Lake Poets and Lake School>coleridge, Wordsworth, and Southey—three poets who at the beginning of the nineteenth century were living in the Lake District of northwest England (Cumbria and Lancashire)<; Knickerbocker Group>a New York group of writers during the first half of the nineteenth century, named after Washington Irving’s Knickerbocker’s History of New York<; Pre-Raphaelitism>the movement begun in 1848 by the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Holman-Hunt, John Everett Millais, and others as a protest against the conventional methods of painting<; Martian School (or Martians)>a school of British poets born in the 1940s—so labeled by James Fenton after Craig Raine’s A Martian Sends a Postcard Home (1979)—who struggle to see the world afresh, as might a visitor from Mars<; Beat Generation>a group of American poets and novelists of the 1950s and 1960s in rebellion against the prevailing culture<; Scriblerus Club>a club organized in London in 1714 by Jonathan Swift to satirize literary incompetence<; Black Mountain School>certain writers—Charles Olson, Robert Creeley, and Robert Duncan among them—associated with Black Mountain College, an experimental school in North Carolina<; “Graveyard School”>a group of eighteenth-century poets who wrote long poems on death and immortality<; Angry Young Men>a group of British writers in the 1950s and 1960s who demonstrated a particular bitterness in their attacks on outmoded, bourgeois values<; Bloomsbury Group>a group of writers and thinkers, many of whom lived in Bloomsbury, a residential district near central London<; Geneva School>a group of critics, including Georges Poulet, Marcel Raymond, Albert Béguin, and the early J. Hillis Miller, who see a literary work as a series of existential expressions of the author’s individual consciousness<; Fleshly School of Poetry, The>a critical essay by Robert W. Buchanan (as “Thomas Maitland”) in the Contemporary Review, October 1871, attacking Swinburne, Morris, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti<; Transcendental Club>An informal group of New England Transcendentalists who met from 1836 to about 1840.<; Kailyard School>a group of Scottish writers whose work dealt idealistically with village life in Scotland<; Bluestockings>women of pronounced intellectual interests<; Fireside Poets>a group of poets devoted to providing intellectual and moral education for the new generation of literates produced by free public education in the nineteenth century<; Literary Club, The (also Doctor Johnson’s Circle)>a club formed in London in 1764 at the suggestion of Sir Joshua Reynolds, the painter, and with the cooperation of Samuel Johnson<; Lollards>the followers of John Wycliffe, who inspired a popular religious reform movement in England late in the fourteenth century<; Saturday Club>a club of literary and scientific people in and around Cambridge and Boston in the mid-nineteenth century who came together at irregular intervals chiefly for social intercourse and good conversation<; Imagists>a group of poets active in England and America between 1909 and 1918<; School of Night>a group of Elizabethan dramatists, poets, and scholars, led by Sir Walter Ralegh, who studied the natural sciences, philosophy, and religion and were suspected of being atheists<; Cavalier Lyricists>followers of Charles I (1625-1649)—such as Thomas Carew, Richard Lovelace, and Sir John Suckling—who composed lighthearted poems<; Inkhornists>a group in the Renaissance who favored the introduction of heavy Latin and Greek words into the standard English vocabulary<; “Tribe of Ben”>a contemporary nickname for young poets and dramatists of the seventeenth century who acknowledged “rare Ben Jonson” as their master<; Silver-Fork School>a name applied in derision to a group of nineteenth-century English novelists who emphasized gentility and etiquette<; Frankfurt School>A group of Marxist social theorists associated with the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt.<; Decadents>a group of late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century writers who held that art was superior to nature and that the finest beauty was that of dying or decaying things<; Grub Street>the “tribe” of poor writers or hacks, or the qualities that characterized them, after the London street where some of them lived<; Physiocrats>Eighteenth-century French economists who held that land and agriculture are the source of wealth.<; Ciceronians>a group of Latin stylists in the Renaissance who would not use any word that could not be found in Cicero’s writings<; New Criticism>the body of criticism that concentrates on the work of art as an object in itself; strictly, the criticism of Ransom, Tate, Blackmur, Warren, and Brooks, named from Ransom’s The New Criticism (1941)<; Stationers’ Company and Stationers’ Register>the company of stationers (publishers and booksellers) granted a royal charter in 1557, and the register in which members entered the names of forthcoming books<; University Wits>certain young university people who came to London in the late 1580s and undertook careers as professional writers<; Apocalyptics>a movement in English poetry flourishing between 1935 and 1950, led by Henry Treece and J. R. Hendry; resembling surrealism, it favored extreme imagery<; School of Donne>another name for the Metaphysical poets<; Roundheads>The Parliamentarian supporters in the English Civil War, opposed to the Royalist Cavaliers.<; Acmeism>a movement in Russian poetry, begun around 1912 by members of the Poets’ Guild, to promote precise treatment of realistic subjects<; Della Cruscans>a late-eighteenth-century group of poets, including Robert Merry, Hannah Cowley, and Hester Thrale<; Johnson’s Circle (also Doctor Johnson’s Circle)>a literary group whose leader was Samuel Johnson, but which was better known as the literary Club<; Pléiade>a group of critics and poets that flourished in France in the second half of the sixteenth century, led by Ronsard and Du Bellay; originally, an ancient group of seven authors<; School of Spenser>a name given to a group of seventeenth-century poets who showed the influence of Edmund Spenser<; Brook Farm>A utopian community founded in Massachusetts in 1841 by members of the Transcendentalist movement.<; Phosphorists>A group of Swedish Romantic poets of the early nineteenth century, named after their journal Phosphoros.<; Kit-Cat Club>An eighteenth-century London club of Whig politicians and writers.<; Luddites>english workmen of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries who sabotaged textile machinery that was taking away their jobs<; Language Poets, The>a group of American poets, so named around 1980, whose work shows radical suspicion, skepticism, or cynicism about the efficacy of written language to express anything much beyond its own apparatus<; Inns of Court>The four London legal societies that train and admit barristers, historically centers of literary life.<; Connecticut Wits>see Hartford Wits<; Center for Scholarly Editions>A committee of the Modern Language Association that reviews and approves scholarly editions of texts.<; “Condition of England” Works>works by serious writers in England from about the middle of the nineteenth century that addressed grave problems of society, culture, class, and education<; “Courtly Makers”>court poets of the reign of Henry VIII who introduced the “new poetry” from Italy and France into England; “maker” meant “poet.<; Dogme 95>a filmmaking collective established in Denmark in 1995 led by Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg and devoted to radical principles that subvert the dominance of fiction, illusion, and gimmickry<; Trouvère>poets who flourished in northern France in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries<; “Sons of Ben”>poets of the reign of Charles I who were admirers and imitators of the lyric poetry of Ben Jonson; more commonly called the “tribe of Ben.<; Academies>associations devoted to the advancement of special fields of interest<; American Academy of Arts and Letters>an organization created in 1904 to recognize accomplishment in literature, art, or music<; Chicago Critics>a group associated with the University of Chicago who in 1952 published Critics and Criticism; also used to mean the followers of the group<; Field Day>the Field Day Theater Company, founded in Northern Ireland in 1980 by Brian Friel and Stephen Rea<; Jesuits>members of the Society of Jesus, a Catholic religious order founded by Saint Ignatius Loyola in 1534<; Imagism>see Imagists<; Purist>one who habitually stresses correctness in language, particularly in minor points of grammar, pronunciation, and style<; Oxford Reformers>a group of humanist scholars whose association began at Oxford in the early Renaissance, particularly John Colet, Sir Thomas More, and the Dutch scholar Erasmus<; Oulipo (also OuLiPo)>the Ouvroir de Littérature Potentielle (Workshop of Potential Literature), a group of writers and mathematicians interested in subverting ordinary literary production in favor of chance or arbitrary limitations<; Schoolroom Poets>see Fireside Poets<; Scottish Chaucerians>poets of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Scotland who wrote in imitation of Chaucer<

column4: Spoken Word Movement>A movement in poetry written to be performed aloud, emphasizing sound, rhythm, and audience.<; Poem>a cultural artifact of some sort; commonly, a literary composition typically characterized by imagination, emotion, significant meaning, sense impressions, and concrete language<; Canto>a section or division of a long poem<; Poetry>the many forms in which human beings have given rhythmic expression to their most intense perceptions of the world, themselves, and the relation of the two<; Poetics>a system or body of theory about poetry; the principles and rules of poetic composition<; Dramatic Poetry>a term that, logically, should be restricted to poetry employing dramatic form or some element of dramatic technique<; Naive and Sentimental>a distinction by Schiller (1795) arguing that poets are either naive (original, pure, authentic, directly in touch with nature) or sentimental (derivative, civilized, removed from nature)<; Pure Poetry>poetry supposedly free from conceptualized statement or moral preachment or those portions of a poem remaining after such materials as can be paraphrased adequately in prose are removed<; Prose Poem>a poem printed as prose, with both margins justified<; Poesie or Poesy>a variant and synonym of poetry, current until about 1650 but thereafter picking up connotations of archaism, preciousness, affectation, and folly<

column4: Iamb (or Iambus)>a foot consisting of an unaccented syllable and an accented<; Trochee>a foot consisting of an accented and an unaccented syllable<; Spondee>a foot composed of two accented syllables<; Anapest>a metrical foot consisting of three syllables, with two unaccented syllables followed by an accented one<; Dactyl>a foot consisting of one accented syllable followed by two unaccented<; Pyrrhic>a foot of two unaccented syllables<; Tetrameter>a line consisting of four feet<; Pentameter>a line of verse of five feet<; Hexameter>a line of six feet; in Latin or Greek, the conventional medium for epic and didactic poetry<; Trimeter>a line of three feet<; Antibacchius>a metrical foot of three syllables, of which the first two are stressed and the third unstressed (accentual) or the first two are long and the third short (quantitative)<; Octameter>a line of eight feet<; Tribrach>a foot of three short or unstressed syllables<; Choree>obsolete equivalent of trochee; now preserved only in choriambus (choree + iambus)<; Foot>the unit of rhythm in verse, whether quantitative or accentual-syllabic<; Triple Meter>the use of feet of three syllables—that is, of anapests, dactyls, amphibrachs, or amphimacers<; Heptameter>a line consisting of seven feet<; Dimeter>a line of verse consisting of two feet<; Bacchius (or Bacchic)>a three-syllable foot usually defined quantitatively as a short followed by two longs or qualitatively as a weak followed by two strongs<; Paeon>a foot consisting of one long or stressed syllable and three short or unstressed syllables<; Tetrabrach>A metrical foot of four short (or unstressed) syllables.<; Septenary>A line of seven metrical feet; a group of seven.<; Dipody (or Dipodic Verse)>in classical prosody, a measure consisting of two metrical feet, usually slightly different from each other<; Galliambic>a line in the galliambic measure, consisting quantitatively of four four-syllable feet; named for the Galli, eunuch priests of Cybele<; Monometer>a line of verse consisting of one foot<; Ionic>a classical foot with two long and two short syllables<; Adonic Verse>in Greek and Latin prosody, the measure that consists of a dactyl and a spondee or a dactyl and a trochee—probably so called after the Adonia, the festival of Adonis<; Amphibrach>a metrical foot consisting of three syllables—the first and last unaccented; the second accented<; Amphimacer>a metrical foot consisting of three syllables—the first and last accented; the second unaccented<; Antispast>in prosody, a foot consisting of four syllables, with the accents falling on the two middle syllables, or a verse pattern in which an iambic foot is followed by a trochaic foot<; Aristophanic>an ancient Greek measure, usually consisting of three quantitative feet: dactyl, trochee, trochee (or spondee)<; Asclepiad>an ancient Greek measure, normally the following quantitative series: spondee, two or three choriambs, and an iamb; mentioned in Sidney’s Arcadia<; Choriambus>a foot in which two accented syllables flank two unaccented syllables<; Choliambus>the most important variety of scazon because it has to do with the iambic rhythm that is the most important in English<; Age of Reason>the Enlightenment in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, a period that emphasized self-knowledge, self-control, rationalism, discipline, and the rule of law, order, and decorum<; Age of Sensibility>a name frequently applied by literary historians to the last half of the eighteenth century in England, the time earlier called the Age of Johnson<; Revolutionary Age in American Literature, 1765-1790>the period between the Stamp Act in 1765 and the formation of the federal government in 1789, when American writers were mostly engaged in nonbelletristic pursuits<; Diminishing Age in English Literature, 1940-1965>the period of English literature following the coming of World War II in 1939, which profoundly changed British life<; Tudor>the royal house that ruled England from 1485 to 1603: Henry VII (1485-1509), Henry VIII (1509-1547), Edward VI (1547-1553), Mary (1553-1558), and Elizabeth I (1558-1603)<; American Literature, Periods of>the division of American literary history into periods—the early ones based on political and social history and the later ones on the dominance of literary types or movements<; English Literature, Periods of>the division of English literary history into periods, which offers a limited but convenient approach; there are almost as many arrangements as there are books on the subject<; “Long”>applied to a lengthy period of which the significant boundaries exceed a hundred years, especially the Long Eighteenth Century (about 1660-1840) and the Long Nineteenth Century (about 1789-1914)<; Periods of English and American Literary History>see English Literature, American Literature, and Outline of Literary History<; Norman Conquest>the conquest of England by the Normans following the victory of William I in 1066 at the Battle of Senlac (Hastings)<

column4: Antithesis>a figure of speech characterized by strongly contrasting words, clauses, sentences, or ideas<; Fugitives, The>a group associated with Vanderbilt University, which in the 1920s published the magazine The Fugitive<; New York School>a group of American poets who flourished between 1950 and 1970, distinguished by urbanity, wit, learning, spontaneity, and exuberance<; Broken Rhyme>the breaking of a word at the end of a line for the sake of a rhyme<; Blank Verse>unrhymed but otherwise regular verse—usually iambic pentameter<; Lake Poets and Lake School>coleridge, Wordsworth, and Southey—three poets who at the beginning of the nineteenth century were living in the Lake District of northwest England (Cumbria and Lancashire)<; Knickerbocker Group>a New York group of writers during the first half of the nineteenth century, named after Washington Irving’s Knickerbocker’s History of New York<; Pastoral>a poetic treatment of shepherds and rustic life, after the Latin for “shepherd”: pastor<; Senryu>a form with the same structure as the haiku—seventeen syllables in lines of five, seven, and five—but relying on humor or satire rather than conventions related to the seasons<; Understatement>a common figure of speech in which the literal sense of what is said falls detectably short of (or “under”) the magnitude of what is being talked about<; Romantic Period in English Literature, 1798-1870>in the period between the publication of Lyrical Ballads (1798) and the death of Dickens, English literature was dominated by romanticism<; Carpe Diem>“Seize the day”; a phrase used by Horace and applied to literature, especially lyric poems, that exemplifies the spirit of “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.<; Ubi Sunt Formula>a convention much used in verse, rhetorically asking “where are those who were before us?” (ubi sunt qui ante nos fuerunt?<; Affective Fallacy>the judging of a work of art in terms of its results, especially its emotional effect<; English Sonnet>a sonnet consisting of three quatrains followed by a couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Free Verse>vers libre; verse that is relatively free, managing without rhyme, meter, or regular rhythm<; Heteromerous Rhyme>a fairly rare species of multiple rhyme (also called “mosaic”) in which typically one word is forced into a rhyme with two or more words<; Pre-Raphaelitism>the movement begun in 1848 by the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Holman-Hunt, John Everett Millais, and others as a protest against the conventional methods of painting<; Novel of Manners>a novel dominated by social customs, manners, conventions, and habits of a definite social class<; Tetrameter>a line consisting of four feet<; Transcendentalism>a reliance on the intuition and the conscience—a form of idealism; a philosophical romanticism reaching America a generation or two after it developed in Europe<; Surrealism>a movement in art emphasizing the expression of the imagination as realized in dreams and presented without conscious control<; Run-on Lines>the carrying over of grammatical structure from one line to the next<; Allegory>a form of extended metaphor in which objects, persons, places, and actions in a narrative are equated with meanings outside the narrative itself<; Elegy>a sustained formal poem setting forth meditations on death or another solemn theme<; Limerick>a form of light verse that follows a definite pattern: five anapestic lines of which the first, second, and fifth, consisting of three feet, rhyme; and the third and fourth lines, consisting of two feet, rhyme<; Hypallage>a figure of speech in which an epithet is moved from the proximate to the less proximate of a group of nouns<; Aubade>a lyric about dawn or a morning serenade—a song of lovers parting at dawn<; Caudate Sonnet>an Italian form, rarely adopted into English, in which a standard fourteen-line sonnet is augmented by the addition of other lines, including “tails.<; Martian School (or Martians)>a school of British poets born in the 1940s—so labeled by James Fenton after Craig Raine’s A Martian Sends a Postcard Home (1979)—who struggle to see the world afresh, as might a visitor from Mars<; Jeremiad>a work that foretells destruction because of the evil of a group<; Putative Author>the fictional author of a work, supposedly written by someone other than its actual author<; Peripety (or Peripeteia)>the reversal of fortune for a protagonist—possibly either a fall, as in a tragedy, or a success, as in a comedy<; Restoration Age>the literary period embracing the latter part of the seventeenth century, named for the restoration of the Stuarts in 1660<; Abridgment>a shortened version of a work but one that attempts to preserve essential elements<; Chrestomathy>a collection of choice passages to be used in the study of a language or a literature and, thus, a kind of anthology<; Climax>a rising order of importance in the ideas expressed<; Controlling Image>an image or metaphor that runs throughout and determines the form or nature of a literary work<; Harlem Renaissance>the first major, self-conscious literary movement of African-American writers, although there had been much black writing in America earlier<; Naturalistic and Symbolistic Period in American Literature>the period between 1900 and 1930 in America, divided by World War I into a part dominated by naturalism and a part marked by growing international awareness and symbolism<; Philistinism>the worship of material and mechanical prosperity and the disregard of culture, beauty, and spirit<; Revolutionary and Early National Period in American Literature, 1765-1830>the period of the establishment of the new nation, ending with the “second revolution” represented by the ascendancy of Jacksonian democracy<; Cacophony>the opposite of euphony; a harsh, unpleasant combination of sounds<; Catharsis>aristotle’s term, in the Poetics, for the “proper purgation” of pity and fear effected by tragedy<; Madrigal>a short lyric, usually dealing with love or a pastoral theme and designed for—or at least suitable for—a musical setting<; Mimesis>the Greek for imitation, often used specifically to indicate Aristotle’s theory of imitation<; Pentameter>a line of verse of five feet<; Renaissance>the period of transition from the medieval to the modern world in Western Europe; the word means “rebirth.<; Slant Rhyme>near rhyme; usually the substitution of assonance or consonance for true rhyme<; Burlesque>a form of comedy characterized by ridiculous exaggeration and distortion, marked by a discrepancy between subject matter and style<; Chiaroscuro>contrasting light and shade<; Gongorism>a highly affected style taking its name from the Spanish poet Luis de Góngora y Argote (1561-1627), whose writings exhibited stylistic extravagances<; Legend>a narrative or tradition handed down from the past; distinguished from a myth by having more of historical truth and perhaps less of the supernatural<; Syzygy>in classical prosody, a term for two coupled feet serving as a unit<; Aesthetic Distance>the effect produced when an emotion or an experience—whether autobiographical or not—is so objectified that it can be understood as being independent of the immediate experience of its maker<; Didacticism>instructiveness in a work, one purpose of which is to give guidance, particularly in moral, ethical, or religious matters<; Hedonism>a doctrine that pleasure is the chief good of human beings<; Heteroglossia>“Different tongues” or “different speech”; a term introduced by Mikhail Bakhtin to designate the presence of more than one voice in a given narrative or another work<; Internal Rhyme>rhyme that occurs at some place before the last syllables in a line<; Realistic Period in English Literature, 1870-1914>the period in which the reaction to romanticism reached its peak in full-fledged realism, in the latter portion of Victoria’s reign and the reign of Edward VII<; Pseudonym>a false name sometimes assumed by writers and others<; Rhopalic>a sequence that “thickens” as it moves toward its end, with each word a syllable longer than the preceding one<; Victorian>a term used (1) to designate broadly the literature written during the reign of Queen Victoria (1837-1901); and (2) to suggest a certain complacency, hypocrisy, or squeamishness assumed to characterize Victorian attitudes<; Transferred Epithet>an adjective used to limit a noun that it really does not logically modify<; Tanka>a type of Japanese poetry similar to the haiku<; Anadiplosis>a kind of repetition in which the last word or phrase of one sentence or line is repeated at the beginning of the next<; Beat Generation>a group of American poets and novelists of the 1950s and 1960s in rebellion against the prevailing culture<; Clerihew>a form of light verse invented by and named for Edmund Clerihew Bentley (1875-1956), who also wrote detective fiction<; Motif (or Motive)>a simple element that serves as a basis for expanded narrative; or, less strictly, a conventional situation, device, interest, or incident<; Metafiction>a work of fiction, a major concern of which is the nature of fiction itself<; Neoclassic Period>the period in English literature between the return of the Stuarts to the English throne in 1660 and the publication of Lyrical Ballads by Wordsworth and Coleridge in 1798<; Identical Rhyme>a phenomenon, also called redundant rhyme or rime riche, in which a syllable both begins and ends in the same way as a rhyming syllable, without being the same word<; Hiatus>a pause or break between two vowel sounds not separated by a consonant<; Vorticism>a movement in modern poetry, originating in 1914 with Wyndham Lewis, related to certain abstract developments in painting and sculpture<; Scriblerus Club>a club organized in London in 1714 by Jonathan Swift to satirize literary incompetence<; Verbum Infans Formula>a conventional paradoxical topos, meaning “the unspeaking word,” applied to the infant (infans, “not speaking”) Christ, who incarnates the Word (verbum)<; Memento Mori>A reminder of death, such as a skull, used to encourage reflection on mortality.<; Black Mountain School>certain writers—Charles Olson, Robert Creeley, and Robert Duncan among them—associated with Black Mountain College, an experimental school in North Carolina<; End-Stopped Lines>lines in which both the grammatical structure and the sense reach completion at the end<; “Graveyard School”>a group of eighteenth-century poets who wrote long poems on death and immortality<; Exposition>one of the four chief types of composition, with the others being argumentation, description, and narration; its purpose is to explain something<; Epigram>a pithy saying, often antithetical; also a short poem characterized by compression, balance, and polish<; Elizabethan Age>the segment of the Renaissance during the reign of Elizabeth I (1558-1603)<; Early Tudor Age, 1500-1557>the period in which the ideals of the Renaissance were rapidly replacing those of the Middle Ages, marked by the reformation of the English church and the revival of learning known as Humanism<; Equivoque>a kind of pun in which language is so used that it has two different but appropriate meanings<; Dramatic Monologue>a poem that reveals “a soul in action” through the speech of one character in a dramatic situation<; Humanism>broadly, any attitude that tends to exalt the human element, as opposed to the supernatural, divine elements—or as opposed to the grosser, animal elements<; Reduplication>(1) The rhetorical repetition of a word or phrase; (2) repetition of material in a syllable, common for diminutives or nicknames<; Ploce>a kind of repetition whereby different forms and senses of a word are “woven” through an utterance<; Reversal>the change in fortune for a protagonist<; Novel of Character>a novel that emphasizes character rather than exciting episode<; Early Victorian Age, 1832-1870>a time of the gradual tempering of the romantic impulse and the steady growth of realism<; Heteronym>a word spelled the same as another but pronounced and defined differently<; Villanelle>a fixed nineteen-line form, originally French, employing only two rhymes and repeating two of the lines according to a set pattern<; Satire>a work or manner that blends a censorious attitude with humor and wit for improving human institutions or humanity<; Exegesis>an explanation and interpretation of a text<; Merism>generally, a repetition of parts; specifically, the use of a pair of opposites to mean a whole<; Kabuki>a popular form of theater in Japan since the mid-seventeenth century<; Rhetorical Accent>the accent determined by the meaning or intention of the sentence; used in metrics in opposition to metrical accent, in which only the prosodic pattern of the line determines the placement of stress<; Solecism>a violation of prescriptive grammatical rules<

column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Paradox>a statement that although seemingly contradictory or absurd may actually be well-founded or true<; Metaphor>an analogy identifying one object with another and ascribing to the first object one or more of the qualities of the second<;
