Assonance Rhyme>assonance is a common substitution for end rhyme in the popular ballad<; Connotation>the emotional implications and associations that words may carry, as distinguished from their denotative meanings<; Dirge>a wailing song sung at a funeral or in commemoration of death; a short lyric of lamentation<; Fused Rhyme>a curious phenomenon, scarcely found anywhere in English outside a few poems by Gerard Manley Hopkins, in which a rhyme sound is begun at the end of a line but not completed until the beginning of the next<; Freytag’s Pyramid>a diagram of the structure of a five-act tragedy, given by Gustav Freytag in Technik des Dramas (1863)<; Foreshadowing>the presentation of material in a work in such a way that later events are prepared for<; Great Chain of Being>the belief that everything partakes of a hierarchical system, extending upward from inanimate matter to living things, to the rational human being, to angels, and finally to God<; Echo Verse>poetry in which the closing syllables of one line are repeated, as by an echo, in the following line with a different meaning, forming a reply or a comment<; Invocation>an address to a deity for aid<; Lollards>the followers of John Wycliffe, who inspired a popular religious reform movement in England late in the fourteenth century<; Hexameter>a line of six feet; in Latin or Greek, the conventional medium for epic and didactic poetry<; Macaronic>(1) Pejoratively, “a blockhead” or “a dandy.” (2) Writing that combines two or more languages<; Parable>an illustrative story teaching a lesson<; Rhetorical Question>a question propounded for its rhetorical effect and not requiring a reply or intended to induce a reply<; Redende Name>german, “speaking name”; a name that is significant<; Wellerism>a type of expression, named for Dickens’s Sam and Tony Weller, with three parts: an utterance, a speaker, and a situation<; Apocope>the omission of one or more sounds from a word<; Epic>a long narrative poem in elevated style presenting characters of high position in adventures, forming an organic whole through their relation to a central heroic figure<; Frontier Literature>writing about the American frontier and frontier life<; Melodrama>a work—usually a play—based on a romantic plot and developed sensationally, with little regard for motivation and with an excessive appeal to the emotions of the audience<; Middle English Period>the period in English literature between the replacement of French by Middle English as the language of court and the early appearances of definitely Modern English writings, roughly between 1350 and 1500<; Muses, The>nine goddesses represented as presiding over the various departments of art and science<; Quibble>earlier, a pun; nowadays, a verbal device for evading the point at issue<; Polyhyphenation>the use of more than a usual number of hyphens<; Nonsense Verse>a variety of light verse entertaining because of its strong rhythmic quality and lack of logic, often with coined nonsense words<; Nonce Word>a word invented by an author for a particular usage or special meaning; in earlier forms of a language, a word with a single recorded occurrence<; Old English Period>the period between the invasion of England by the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, beginning around 428, and the establishment of Norman rule around 1100<; Palindrome>writing that reads the same from left to right and from right to left<; Novel of the Soil>a special kind of regionalism in the novel, in which the lives of people struggling for existence in remote rural sections are starkly portrayed<; Projective Verse>a kind of free verse that regards meter and form as artificial and in which the poet “projects” a voice primarily through the content and the propulsive quality of breathing, which alone determines the line<; Threnody>a song of death; a dirge<; Sentimentalism>(1) An overindulgence in emotion, especially the conscious effort to induce emotion in order to enjoy it; (2) an optimistic overemphasis of the goodness of humanity<; Sestina>one of the most difficult and complex of verse forms, consisting of six six-lined stanzas and a three-lined envoy<; Aphorism>a concise statement of a principle or precept given in pointed words<; Blood and Thunder>a class of work specializing in bloodshed and violence<; Dynamic Character>a character who develops or changes as a result of the actions of the plot<; Dolce Stil Nuovo>the “sweet new style” (called so in Dante’s Purgatory) that flourished among lyric poets in certain Romance languages during the thirteenth century, with a premium on lucidity and complex musicality<; Ellipsis (or Ellipse)>the omission of one or more words that, while essential to a grammatic structure, are easily supplied<; Dramatic Irony>a situation in which the words or acts of a character carry a meaning unperceived by the character but understood by the audience<; Expressionism>a movement affecting painting and literature, which followed and went beyond impressionism in its efforts to “objectify inner experience.<; Ethos>the character of the speaker or writer as reflected in speech or writing; the quality or set of emotions that a speaker or writer enacts in order to affect an audience<; Hamartia>the error, frailty, mistaken judgment, or misstep through which the fortunes of the hero of a tragedy are reversed<; Epithet>strictly, an adjective used to point out a characteristic of a person or thing<; Folklore>the study of the survivals of archaic beliefs, customs, and traditions in modern ages; a term first used by W. J. Thoms as a substitute for “popular antiquities.<; Nekuia>a work having to do with the land of the dead, especially a visit by a living person<; Psychological Novel>prose fiction that places unusual emphasis on interior characterization and on the motives, circumstances, and internal action that spring from and develop external action<; Pathos>the quality in art and literature that stimulates pity, tenderness, or sorrow; from the Greek root for feeling<; Nom de plume (or pen name)>a name adopted by a writer for professional use or to disguise his or her true identity<; Regionalism>fidelity to a particular geographical area; the representation of its habits, speech, manners, history, folklore, or beliefs<; Saturday Club>a club of literary and scientific people in and around Cambridge and Boston in the mid-nineteenth century who came together at irregular intervals chiefly for social intercourse and good conversation<; Sfumato>an Italian word meaning “smoked” that refers to a quality of smokily obscuring details in a painting; later applied to film and television productions with a similar quality: vapory, foggy, soft-focus, dark, or dim<; Tritagonist>the actor taking the part third in importance in a Greek drama<; Virelay>a French verse form (related to lai) of which the number of stanzas and the number of lines to the stanza are unlimited<; Verisimilitude>the semblance of truth; the degree to which a work creates the appearance of the truth<; Telestich>an acrostic in which the final letters form a word<; Triple Rhyme>rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllable is followed by two unstressed, undifferentiated syllables<; Symbol>something that is itself and also stands for something else<; Gigantism>Exaggeration of size or scale, especially for comic or grotesque effect.<; Bard>in modern use, any poet; historically, poets who recited verses glorifying the deeds of heroes and leaders, especially the early poets of the Celts<; Bob and Wheel>a stanza in the revived alliterative verse of the later Middle English period in which unrhymed alliterative lines are followed by a very short line, the bob, and a short-lined rhymed quatrain, the wheel<; Cinquain>any five-line stanza; more precisely, the five-line stanza used by Adelaide Crapsey, of unrhymed lines of two, four, six, eight, and two syllables<; Concordance>an alphabetical index of most or all of the words in a text or in the works of an author<; Emblem>a graphic device of some sort that stands for a special meaning<; Epistolary Literature>literature—usually prose fiction—entirely or partly written as letters<; Flashback>a device by which a work presents material that occurred prior to the opening scene of the work<; Fourteeners>a verse form consisting of fourteen syllables arranged in iambs<; Discordia Concors>a term used by Samuel Johnson for “a combination of dissimilar images or discovery of occult resemblances in things apparently unlike” in metaphysical poetry<; Dénouement>literally, “unknotting”; the final unraveling of a plot; the solution of a mystery; an explanation or outcome<; Dialects>varieties of the same “language” spoken by two groups or persons whose speech exhibits very marked differences<; Movement, The>a focus of British literary activity in the mid-1950s, mostly in poetry and prose fiction, with emphases on normality, regularity, practicality, stoicism, traditionalism, and solid middle-class values<; Jewish-American Literature>a field of study that has emerged since about 1935 and concentrated on the work of Jewish writers living in America<; Myth>an anonymous story that presents supernatural episodes as a means of interpreting natural events<; Kitsch>shallow, flashy art designed to have popular appeal and commercial success; from the German for “gaudy trash.<; Imagists>a group of poets active in England and America between 1909 and 1918<; Philippic>any bitter speech or harangue<; Prosopopoeia>another name for personification<; Travesty>writing that by its incongruity of treatment ridicules a subject inherently noble or dignified<; Yellow Journalism>newspapers and magazines specializing in scandal and sensation<; Transliteration>a character-by-character transfer of a word from one alphabet or writing system to another<; Unities>the principles of dramatic structure involving the unities of action, time, and place<; Accentualism>paul Fussell’s term for “the theory of the line which considers the number of stresses to be its fundamental prosodic skeleton.<; African-American Literature>frequently called Afro-American or Black literature; the writing of African Americans, which began in the eighteenth century with the poetry of Jupiter Hammon and Phillis Wheatley<; Altar Poem>another term for a carmen figuratum, a poem in which the lines are so arranged that they form a design on the page, taking the shape of the subject—frequently, an altar or a cross<; Chain Rhyme>a device in which the sound of the last syllable of one line recurs as the sound of the first syllable of the next but with a change of meaning<; Colloquialism>an expression used in informal conversation but not accepted universally in formal speech or writing<; Epic Simile>an elaborated comparison, more involved and ornate than an ordinary simile, in a conscious imitation of the Homeric manner<; Framework-Story>a story inside a framework; a story inside a story<; Grundy, Mrs.>a character from Thomas Morton’s play Speed the Plough, who does not actually appear but of whose judgments everyone in the play is very much afraid<; Fabliau (plural, Fabliaux)>a humorous tale popular in medieval France<; Episodic Structure>writing that consists of little more than a series of incidents, with the episodes succeeding each other and with no particularly logical arrangement or complication<; Dystopia>literally, “bad place”; an account of an imaginary world, usually in the future, in which present tendencies are carried out to their intensely unpleasant culminations<; Humours (or Humors)>in an old theory of physiology, the four chief liquids of the human body—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were called humours<; Lament>a poem expressing grief—usually more intense and more personal than in a complaint<; Locus Classicus>that place or passage invariably cited as the “classic example” of a principle or type<; Palimpsest>a writing surface, whether of vellum, papyrus, or other material, that has been used more than once for manuscript purposes<; Protagonist>the chief character in a work<; Saga>in a strict sense, Icelandic and Norse stories of the medieval period that give accounts of heroic adventure<; Suspension of Disbelief>the willingness to withhold questions about truth, accuracy, or probability in a work<; Tercet>a stanza of three lines—a triplet—in which each line ends with the same rhyme<; Roman à Thèse>french: a thesis novel—one intended to establish and illustrate a social doctrine<; Thesis>an attitude or position on a problem taken by a writer or speaker with the purpose of proving or supporting it<; Utopia>a fiction describing an imaginary ideal world<; Theater of the Absurd>see Absurd, Theater of the<; School of Night>a group of Elizabethan dramatists, poets, and scholars, led by Sir Walter Ralegh, who studied the natural sciences, philosophy, and religion and were suspected of being atheists<; Scop>an Anglo-Saxon court poet<; Stock Characters>conventional character types<; Vade Mecum>an article that one keeps constantly on hand<; Mythos>The plot or story of a work; also, a body of myths belonging to a culture.<; Lipogram>A composition in which one or more letters of the alphabet are deliberately omitted.<; Modulation>A change in tone, pitch, or rhythm in verse or speech.<; Logos>Persuasion by appeal to reason and logic; also, the divine Word or rational principle of the universe.<; Abecedarian, Abecedarius, Abecedary>an Acrostic so arranged that the initial letters of successive lines (or other units) form an alphabet<; Analogy>a comparison of two things, alike in certain aspects; particularly, a method used in exposition and description by which something unfamiliar is explained by being compared to something more familiar<; Beginning Rhyme>rhyme that occurs in the first syllable or syllables of lines<; Catastrophe>the conclusion of a play, particularly of a tragedy; the last of the four parts into which the ancients divided a play<; Catalexis>incompleteness of the last foot of a line; truncation by omission of one or two final syllables; the opposite of anacrusis<; Cavalier Lyricists>followers of Charles I (1625-1649)—such as Thomas Carew, Richard Lovelace, and Sir John Suckling—who composed lighthearted poems<; Comedy>originally, works marked by a happy ending and a less exalted style than tragedy; a lighter form than tragedy that aims primarily to amuse<; Couplet>two consecutive lines of verse with end rhymes<; Doggerel>rude verse; any poorly executed attempt at poetry<; Georgian Age in English Literature, 1914-1940>the period of English literature beginning with World War I, named for George V<; Hendiadys>a figure of speech in which an idea is expressed by giving two components as though they were independent and connecting them with a coordinating conjunction rather than subordinating one part to the other<; Diction>strictly, the use of words in oral or written discourse, including vocabulary and syntax<; Farce>any short humorous play; from Late Latin farsus, “to stuff,” originally an extemporaneous addition, such as jokes or gags, in a play<; Dumb Show>a pantomimic performance used in a play<; Goliardic Verse>lilting Latin verse, usually satiric, composed by university students and wandering scholars in Germany, France, and England in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries<; Eiron>a basic comic character in Greek drama—typically a swindler, trickster, hypocrite, or picaresque rogue—who feigns ignorance in order to trick others<; Determinism>the belief that all ostensible acts of the will are actually the result of causes that determine them<; Nemesis>the Greek goddess of retributive justice or vengeance<; Local Color Writing>writing that exploits the speech, dress, mannerisms, habits of thought, and topography peculiar to a certain region, primarily for the portrayal of the life of a geographical setting<; Mixed Figures>the incongruous mingling of one figure of speech with another immediately following<; Interpolation>in editing, the supplying of an item in a series or a damaged text by some process of deduction or induction<; Native American Literature>literature by Native Americans—older than any other on the continent—that includes such anonymous tribal records as the Walam Olum of the Leni-Lenape<; Lampoon>writing that ridicules and satirizes a person in a bitter, scurrilous manner in verse or prose<; Luminism>a movement in painting, especially since about 1875, in which the art concentrates on the effect of light<; Impressionism>a highly personal manner of writing in which the author presents materials as they appear to an individual temperament at a precise moment rather than as they are presumed to be in actuality<; Heroic Verse>poetry composed in heroic couplets<; Jumping the Shark>a desperate recourse that attempts to reverse a downward trend in ratings for a series, usually on television<; Melopoeia>a Greek term renovated by Ezra Pound, who used it for the whole articulatory-acoustic-auditory range of poetry<; Provincialism>a word, phrase, or manner of expression peculiar to a special region and not commonly used outside that region—therefore, not fashionable or sophisticated<; Popular Literature>writing in one of the commercially viable modes, especially prose fiction<; Revenge Tragedy>a form of tragedy made popular on the Elizabethan stage by Thomas Kyd, whose Spanish Tragedy is an early example of the type<; Novel of Sensibility>a novel in which the characters have a heightened emotional response to events, producing in the reader a similar response<; Tragedy of Blood>an intensified form of the revenge tragedy popular on the Elizabethan stage<; Trimeter>a line of three feet<; Sapphic>a stanzaic pattern named for the Greek poet Sappho, with three lines of eleven or twelve syllables each and a fourth of five syllables<; Scansion>a system for describing conventional rhythms by dividing lines into feet, indicating the locations of binomial accents, and counting the syllables<; Vignette>a sketch or brief narrative characterized by precision and delicacy<; Dizain>A poem or stanza of ten lines, usually with eight or ten syllables per line.<; Anonym>An anonymous person or work; also, a pseudonym used to conceal identity.<; Alazon>the braggart or impostor in Greek comedy<; Allelograph>a variant form of a word used in the vicinity of the basic form itself<; Anglo-Norman Period>the period in English literature between 1100 and 1350, so called because of the dominance of Norman-French culture<; Chant Royal>one of the most complex French verse forms, consisting of sixty lines arranged in five stanzas of eleven lines each and an envoy of five lines<; Complication>that part of a plot in which the entanglement caused by the conflict of opposing forces is developed<; Coup de Théâtre>a surprising and usually unmotivated stroke in a drama that produces a sensational effect; by extension, anything designed solely for effect<; Epitaph>an inscription used to mark burial places<; Darwinism>thought affected by the research and theories of Charles Darwin (1809-1882), especially The Origin of Species (1859)<; Doppelganger>german, “double goer”; a mysterious double, a common figure in literature<; Envoy (also envoi)>a conventionalized stanza appearing at the close of certain kinds of poems; particularly associated with the French ballade<; Epithalamium (or Epithalamion)>a poem written to celebrate a wedding<; Gothic>originally the Goths, a single Germanic tribe, but broadened to mean Teutonic or Germanic and, later, “medieval” in general<; Koine>the language spoken throughout the ancient Greek world; colloquial Attic with numerous supplements from other dialects and other languages<; Metaphysical Conceit>an ingenious kind of conceit widely used by the Metaphysical poets, who explored all areas of knowledge to find—in the startlingly esoteric or the shockingly commonplace—telling and unusual analogies for their ideas<; Incunabulum>any book printed in the last part of the fifteenth century (before 1501)<; Inkhornists>a group in the Renaissance who favored the introduction of heavy Latin and Greek words into the standard English vocabulary<; Montage>french for “mounting” or “editing”; in film, the juxtaposing of contrasting shots to create a meaning different from that recorded in any of the shots<; Irish Literature>the literature of Ireland, the early part of which is greater in bulk, earlier in date, and more striking in character than any other preserved vernacular Western European literature<; sometimes used broadly to include the mystery play<; Naive Narrator (or Hero)>an ingenuous character who is the ostensible author (often the oral narrator) of a narrative, the implications of which are plainer to the reader than they are to the narrator<; Oxford Movement>a reform movement in the English Church begun at Oxford in 1833 and led by John Henry Newman; also known as the “Tractarian Movement” and the “Anglo-Catholic Revival.<; Philology>in its general sense, philology means the scientific study of both language and literature<; Redaction>a revision or editing of a manuscript<; Theater of Cruelty>see Cruelty, Theater of<; Tragedy>a term with many meanings; in drama, a particular kind of play defined by Aristotle’s Poetics; in medieval narrative, a work recounting the fall of persons of high degree<; Troubadour>a name given to the lyric poets and composers of Provence (southern France) in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries<; “Tribe of Ben”>a contemporary nickname for young poets and dramatists of the seventeenth century who acknowledged “rare Ben Jonson” as their master<; Marinism>An ornate, extravagant poetic style of conceits and wordplay, after the Italian poet Giambattista Marino.<; Amphibology (Amphibologia or Amphiboly)>statements capable of two different meanings—a kind of ambiguity<; Anagram>a word or phrase made by transposing the letters of another<; Antagonist>the character directly opposed to the protagonist<; Antibacchius>a metrical foot of three syllables, of which the first two are stressed and the third unstressed (accentual) or the first two are long and the third short (quantitative)<; Byronism>the qualities associated with Lord Byron (1788-1824), whose unique electricity provoked the coining of such terms as “Byronic,” “Byroniad,” and “Byronism.<; Figure Poem>a poem written so that its printed shape suggests its subject matter<; Graces, The>in Greek myth, the three sister goddesses who confer grace, beauty, charm, and joy on human beings and nature<; Half Rhyme>imperfect rhyme, usually the result of consonance<; Foil>any person who through contrast underscores the distinctive characteristics of another; literally, a “leaf” of bright metal placed under a jewel to increase its brilliance<; Hieronymy>the idea of sacred names and naming, more recently applied to any special name (or proper noun) for persons, places, gods, days, months, and so forth<; Incantation>a formulaic use of language—usually spoken or chanted—either to create intense emotional effects or to produce magical results<; Lai>a song or short narrative poem<; Menippean Satire>a form of satire originally developed by the Greek cynic Menippus and transmitted by his disciples Lucian and Varro<; Hymn>a poem expressing religious emotion and generally intended to be sung by a chorus<; Hobson-Jobson>the process of transforming something foreign into a more familiar native article<; Point of View>the vantage point from which an author presents a story<; Orphism>defined by Gerald L. Bruns as “the idea of poetic speech as the ground of all signification.<; Reggae>a style of music, song, and performance that became popular in the 1970s, beginning in Jamaica and spreading through the Caribbean<; Pararhyme>an acoustic effect—systematically practiced by Wilfred Owen, W. H. Auden, Keith Douglas, and others—whereby the place of ordinary rhyme is taken by a combination of alliteration and consonance rhyme<; Omnibus (Latin dative plural, “for all”)>a volume of selected works, usually by one author but sometimes by several on one subject<; Pictorialism>pictorial style, extended from painting to the other arts insofar as they are capable of representing or depicting; usually patronizing or pejorative<; Quarto>a book size designating a book whose signatures result from sheets folded to four leaves (eight pages)<; Poulter’s Measure>a couplet—now rarely used—with a first line in iambic hexameter and a second line in iambic heptameter<; Scat>a vocal style developed during the 1920s, with a singer improvising patterns of repetitive nonsense syllables that suggest the sound of a musical instrument<; Stoicism>the philosophy of the Stoics, a group of Greek philosophers, founded by Zeno late in the fourth century B.C. Stoicism exalts endurance and self-sufficiency<; Silver-Fork School>a name applied in derision to a group of nineteenth-century English novelists who emphasized gentility and etiquette<; Romance>a kind of fiction, originally the Old French tales translated from Latin and named after the Romance languages derived from Latin<; Structuralism>an intellectual movement utilizing the methods of structural linguistics and structural anthropology<; Scottish Literature>the literature of Scotland, much of it a part of English literary history, often taken to begin with John Barbour’s Bruce (1375)<; Frankfurt School>A group of Marxist social theorists associated with the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt.<; Pantheism>The belief that God is identical with the universe and nature.<

column4: Syncopation>a musical term used for the effect produced by a temporary displacing or shifting of the regular beat<; Modulation>A change in tone, pitch, or rhythm in verse or speech.<; Cadence>in one sense, the sound pattern that precedes a marked pause or the end of a sentence, making it interrogatory, hortatory, pleading, and so forth<; Sprung Rhythm>a term coined by Gerard Manley Hopkins for rhythm based on the number of stressed syllables in a line without regard to the number of unstressed syllables<; Counterpoint Rhythm>a term used by Gerard Manley Hopkins to describe the superimposing of a different rhythm on one already established<; Falling Rhythm>a foot in which the first syllable is accented<; Homodyne>a word borrowed from electronics for the situation in a passage of verse when lexical and rhythmic units coincide<; Rhythm>the passage of regular or approximately equivalent time intervals between definite events or the recurrence of specific sounds or kinds of sound<; Heterodyne>a term borrowed from electronics to describe a piece of verse in which the lexical units and rhythmic units do not coincide<; Rest>a pause or silence that, as in music, is counted as a prosodic element<; Rising Rhythm>a foot in which the last syllable is accented; thus, in English, the iamb and the anapest<; Prose Rhythm>the recurrence of stress and emphasis at irregular intervals, affording a pleasurable rise and fall<; Rocking Rhythm>a foot in which a stressed syllable falls between two unstressed syllables; an amphibrach<; Running>generally applied to smoothly running verse<

column4: Ballad>a form of verse to be sung or recited and characterized by its presentation of an exciting episode in narrative or dramatic form<; Ballad Stanza>the stanza of the popular or folk ballad—usually consisting of four lines rhyming abcb, with the first and third lines carrying four accents and the second and fourth carrying three<; Folk Ballad>an anonymous ballad transmitted orally and usually existing in many variants<; Ballade>one of the most popular of the artificial French verse forms, usually three stanzas and an envoy, with a refrain recurring at the end of each stanza and of the envoy<; Folk Song>a song of unknown authorship preserved and transmitted orally<; Tradition>a body of beliefs handed down from generation to generation<; Broadside Ballad>a ballad prepared for circulation on folio sheets printed on one side only, soon after the development of printing in England<; Art Ballad>a term used to distinguish the literary ballad of known authorship from the early ballads of unknown authorship<; Ballad-Opera>a sort of burlesque opera that flourished on the English stage for several years following the appearance of John Gay’s The Beggar's Opera (1728), still the best-known example<; Come-All-Ye>a type of song, usually anonymous, with “come all ye” at the beginning or in a refrain or moralizing conclusion<; Literary Ballad>a ballad composed by an author, as opposed to the anonymous folk ballad<; Popular Ballad>a traditional ballad of unknown authorship, transmitted orally<; Oral Transmission>the transmission of material by word of mouth and memory<; Traditional Ballad>the folk ballad<; Street Ballad>a form of folk ballad that flourished during much of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries<

column4: Dialectic>in the broadest sense, simply the art of argumentation or debate; in classical literature, the tradition of continuing debate or discussion of eternally unresolved issues<; Ratiocination>a process of reasoning from data to conclusions<; Trivium>the three studies leading to the bachelor’s degree in the medieval universities: grammar, logic, and rhetoric<; Ockham’s (or Occam’s) Razor>the principle of parsimony, attributed to William of Ockham: “Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity.<; Reductio ad absurdum>a “reducing to absurdity” to show the falsity of an argument or position<; Syllogism>a formula for presenting an argument logically<; Axiom>a maxim or aphorism whose truth is held to be self-evident<; Deduction>the process of deductive reasoning, which moves from general principles to individual cases<; Induction>an old word for introduction<; Procatalepsis>A figure in which a speaker anticipates and answers an objection before it is raised.<; Antipophora>a strategy whereby a question or objection is answered with another question or objection<; Argumentation>one of the four chief “forms of discourse,” the others being exposition, narration, and description<; Apodictic (or Apodeictic)>the sort of argument that is clearly subject to demonstration and proof<; A Priori>a Latin phrase (“from what comes before”) for deductive reasoning, which proceeds from the general to the specific<; A Posteriori>a Latin phrase (“from what comes later”) for inductive reasoning, which proceeds from the specific to the general<; Argument>a statement summarizing the plot or stating the meaning of a long poem or occasionally of a play<; Begging the Question>a fallacious form of argument in which a conclusion is presented although a premise has not been proved<; Enthymeme>a syllogism informally stated and omitting either the major or the minor premise<; Paralogism>a piece of faulty reasoning<; Socratic>the “Socratic method” in argument or explanation is the use of the question-and-answer formula employed by Socrates in Plato’s Dialogues<

column4: Harangue>a vehement speech designed to arouse strong emotions<; Malapropism>an inappropriateness of speech resulting from the use of one word for another, which resembles it<; Hiatus>a pause or break between two vowel sounds not separated by a consonant<; Exposition>one of the four chief types of composition, with the others being argumentation, description, and narration; its purpose is to explain something<; Eulogy>a dignified, formal speech or form of writing that praises a person or a thing<; Flyting>an extended and vigorous verbal exchange<; Gasconade>bravado or boastful talk, because Gascons were considered inveterate boasters<; Rhetorical Question>a question propounded for its rhetorical effect and not requiring a reply or intended to induce a reply<; Quibble>earlier, a pun; nowadays, a verbal device for evading the point at issue<; Philippic>any bitter speech or harangue<; Colloquialism>an expression used in informal conversation but not accepted universally in formal speech or writing<; Logos>Persuasion by appeal to reason and logic; also, the divine Word or rational principle of the universe.<; Rodomontade>bragging or blustering; so called after the braggart Moorish king Rodomont<; Paraleipsis, Paralepsis, or Paralipsis>pretending to say nothing about something one goes on to say quite a bit about<; Polemic>a vigorously argumentative work, setting forth its author’s attitudes on a highly controversial subject<; Exordium>the first of the seven parts of a classical oration<; Turpiloquence, Turpiloquium>base, shameful speech<; Slang>vernacular speech not accepted as suitable for highly formal usage, although it is much used in conversation<; Diatribe>writing or discourse characterized by bitter invective or abusive argument; a harangue<; Cacozelia>An affected and tasteless use of foreign or learned words in an effort to sound elegant.<; Billingsgate>Coarse, foul, or abusive language.<; Phonology>the general study of phonemics—the nature and history of the sound system of a language<; Peroration>the conclusion of an oration in which the discussion is summed up; a recapitulation of the major points of any speech<; Preterition>in rhetoric, explicitly passing over something—either to call attention to it or to slight it<; Treatise>formerly used of any writing or story; now restricted to a formal treatment of a serious subject<; Equivocation>The deliberate use of ambiguous language to mislead or avoid commitment.<; Attemperation>a rhetorical term revived by Frank Kermode that designates a restriction or softening of something said earlier<; Auxesis>rhetorical augmentation, either a piling on of detail in no particular order or a climactic arrangement advancing from small to great<; Contrast>a rhetorical device by which one element (idea or object) is thrown into opposition to another for the sake of emphasis or clarity<; Locutionary Act>the usual act of saying something, with a verb that represents, describes, or narrates phenomena beyond itself<; Rhetoric>the art of persuasion; the presentation of ideas in clear, persuasive language<; Synchoresis>the rhetorical gesture of agreeing or seeming to agree with an opponent<; Invective>Harsh, abusive, or denunciatory language.<; Addubitatio>latin counterpart of diaporesis, in which a speaker expresses doubt (genuine or feigned)<; Ambages>a form of circumlocution in which the truth is spoken in a way that tends to deceive or mislead<; Anacoenesis (also Anachinosis)>asking a question as though to seek the opinion of one’s hearer, reader, opponent, or judge<; Anachinosis>see Anacoenesis<; Antanagoge>a rhetorical figure, variously defined, sometimes as answering a charge with a countercharge (“You’re another!”); sometimes as compensatory balancing of positive against negative<; Aparithmesis>rhetorical enumeration<; Apophasis>a rhetorical figure in which one makes an assertion while seeming or pretending to suppress or deny it<; Circumlocution>roundabout or evasive speech or writing, in which many words are used where a few would have served<; Defense>an argument defending something from charges or attacks<; Discourse>mode or category of expression; also used more specifically to mean “discussion.<; Dictamen>a formal pronouncement or dictate<; Description>one of the four chief types of composition (with argumentation, exposition, and narration) that has as its purpose the picturing of a scene or setting<; Diasyrm, Diasyrmus>a rhetorical disparaging—of another or of oneself—as in Richard III’s lengthy descanting on his own deformities<; Metanoia>a rhetorical figure whereby a speaker retracts or corrects something said<; Illocutionary Act>a speech act that is discharged in the act of speaking<; Narration>one of the four types of composition (with argumentation, description, and exposition); its purpose is to recount events<; Occupatio>device somewhat like occultatio, especially when one says “Not to mention...” or “To say nothing of...” and then goes ahead and mentions the topic<; Occultatio>emphasizing something by appearing to pass over it or by insinuation<; Perlocutionary Act>a speech act in which the utterance is defined by its effect<; Oration>a formal speech delivered in an impassioned manner<; Speech Act Theory>a development in the philosophy of language that divides utterances into the “constative” (describing some state of affairs) and the “performative” (performing what they utter)<

column4: Affective Fallacy>the judging of a work of art in terms of its results, especially its emotional effect<; Mimesis>the Greek for imitation, often used specifically to indicate Aristotle’s theory of imitation<; Typology>the study of allegorical symbols, especially with the Bible, in which much of the Old Testament is read as a type of the revelation to come in the New Testament<; Intentional Fallacy>the judging of the meaning or success of a work of art by the author’s expressed or ostensible intention in producing it<; Liminality>the state of being on a threshold in space or time<; Great Chain of Being>the belief that everything partakes of a hierarchical system, extending upward from inanimate matter to living things, to the rational human being, to angels, and finally to God<; Verisimilitude>the semblance of truth; the degree to which a work creates the appearance of the truth<; Suspension of Disbelief>the willingness to withhold questions about truth, accuracy, or probability in a work<; Determinism>the belief that all ostensible acts of the will are actually the result of causes that determine them<; Darwinism>thought affected by the research and theories of Charles Darwin (1809-1882), especially The Origin of Species (1859)<; Structuralism>an intellectual movement utilizing the methods of structural linguistics and structural anthropology<; Deconstruction>a widespread philosophical and critical movement that owes its name and energy to the precepts and examples of Jacques Derrida<; Decadence>a term denoting the decline that commonly marks the end of a great period; decadent qualities include self-consciousness, restless curiosity, oversubtilizing refinement, confusion of genres, eccentricity, and often moral perversity<; Foregrounding>the effect in any art of giving emphatic but unaccustomed prominence to something<; Baring the Device>a concept introduced by Viktor Šklovskij, the opposite of verisimilitude, in which art bares its devices and admits that it is not transparent but opaque<; Empathy>the act of identifying ourselves with an object and participating in its physical and emotional sensations; an “involuntary projection of ourselves” into something or someone else<; Reception Theory>the historical application of reader-response criticism<; Grammatology>Derrida’s term for the study of writing as a system, prior to and distinct from speech.<; Intertextuality>a term created by Julia Kristeva, who said, “Every text builds itself as a mosaic of quotations, every text is absorption and transformation of another text.<; Baconian Theory>The theory that Francis Bacon wrote the plays attributed to Shakespeare.<; Comparative Literature>the study of literatures of different languages, nations, and periods<; Semiotics>the study of the rules that enable social phenomena—considered as signs—to have meaning<; Autotelic>a nondidactic work—that is, one whose end lies within itself and does not depend on the achievement of objectives outside the work<; Showing versus Telling>an empirical concept, unsophisticated but still useful, that emphasizes the superiority of dramatization, demonstration, enactment, and embodiment over mere telling<; Archetype>in the psychology of Carl Jung, a “primordial image” from the “collective unconscious” of the human race, shaped by the experience of our ancestors and expressed in myths, religion, dreams, fantasies, and literature<; Paleography>the study of old forms of handwriting, important in textual studies for establishing texts and deciding authorship<; Concrete Universal>A literary representation in which a particular, concrete thing embodies a general or universal truth.<; Antiquarianism>the study of the past through relics, usually literary or artistic<; Emphasis>a principle dictating that important elements be given important positions and adequate development<; Distance>the degree of dispassionateness with which reader or audience can view the people, places, and events in a literary work; the degree of disinterest that the author displays toward his or her characters and actions<; Queer Theory>criticism that, succeeding gay and lesbian criticism around 1988, “assumes that sexual identities are a function of representations.<; Absurd>in contemporary literature and criticism, a term applied to the sense that human beings—cut off from their roots—live in meaningless isolation in an alien universe<; Gestalt>a configuration such that the whole possesses properties not derivable from its parts or their simple sum<; Indeterminacy>the concept that the meaning or reference of a text is ultimately undecidable<; Sublime>characterized by nobility and grandeur, impressive, exalted, raised above ordinary human qualities—these were asserted to be the essential qualities of great art in the treatise On the Sublime by Longinus (A.D. 50)<; Binary Opposition>a principle originating in linguistics around 1915 that elements of a system do not exist as absolute substances but only as entities-defined in structural opposition to something else<; Code>generally, an assigned or established meaning for some arbitrary symbol<; Culture>the body of institutions—practices, habits, customs, beliefs, traditions—that grows out of humankind’s struggle with the environment<; Defamiliarization>english rendering of Russian ostranenie, used by Russian Formalists for the property of great art of making the familiar suddenly seem strange<; Fancy>in Coleridge’s opposition of imagination and fancy, the mechanic, logical, “aggregative and associative power”; until the nineteenth century, fancy and imagination were synonyms<; Electra Complex>in psychoanalysis, an obsessive attachment of a daughter to her father and, thus, the approximate female counterpart of the Oedipus complex<; Disinterestedness>an ideal quality of objectivity and impartiality unpolluted by illegitimate self-interest or by conflict of interest<; Imitation>the concept of art as imitation, which has its origin with classical critics; Aristotle said that all arts are modes of imitation<; Mimetic Theory of Art>a theory emphasizing the actuality imitated in the artwork<; Homosocial>a word coined by Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick for the range of same-sex bonds among men, whether heterosexual or homosexual<; Imagination>the creative faculty of the mind, which the theories of Wordsworth, Coleridge, and others sought to distinguish from fancy<; Invention>original creative power of an independent sort; in Latin rhetoric, inventio meant the “finding” of material<; Popular Culture>the phenomenon of what people really but unofficially do and say; also the academic study thereof<; Poststructuralism>an array of critical and intellectual movements, including deconstruction and radical forms of psychoanalytic, feminist, and revisionist Marxist thinking, which are deemed to lie “beyond” structuralism<; Organic Form>a notion of the structure of a literary work as growing from its conception in the thought, feeling, and personality of the writer rather than being shaped arbitrarily and mechanically in a preconceived mold<; Oedipus Complex>in psychoanalysis, a libidinal feeling that develops in a child—especially a male child between the ages of three and six—for the parent of the opposite sex<; Pragmatic Theory of Art>a theory of art, according to M. H. Abrams, in which the major interest is in the effect that the art object produces in its audience<; Objective Theory of Art>m. H. Abrams’s term for the view that holds the literary work to be most significant as an object in itself, independent of its composition, the actuality it imitates, its author’s intention, or its effect<; Theory>since about 1980, a complex of literary, aesthetic, and cultural theory that operates at a high level of abstraction and tends to theorize about the problematic nature of language, meaning, art, culture, and history<; Speech Act Theory>a development in the philosophy of language that divides utterances into the “constative” (describing some state of affairs) and the “performative” (performing what they utter)<

column4: Truncation>in metrics, the omission of a syllable or syllables at the beginning or end of a line<; Caesura (or Cesura)>a pause or break in a line of verse<; Elision>the omission of part of a word<; Syzygy>in classical prosody, a term for two coupled feet serving as a unit<; Catalexis>incompleteness of the last foot of a line; truncation by omission of one or two final syllables; the opposite of anacrusis<; Scansion>a system for describing conventional rhythms by dividing lines into feet, indicating the locations of binomial accents, and counting the syllables<; Acatalectic>metrically complete; applied to lines that carry out the basic metrical and rhythmic pattern of a poem<; Brachycatalectic>a verse that lacks two syllables, normally unstressed<; Hypercatalectic (or Hypermetrical)>a line with an extra syllable at the end<; Sesquipedalian>used for a style unduly and pretentiously polysyllabic; literally, “a foot and a half.<; Anceps (Latin, “two-headed”)>in classical quantitative prosody, a syllable that can be counted as long or short<; Choliambus>the most important variety of scazon because it has to do with the iambic rhythm that is the most important in English<; Compensation>a means of making up for omissions in a line; a form of substitution<; Equivalence>in metrics, a kind of substitution, in which a foot equal to the one expected but different from it is used<; Substitution>the use of one kind of foot in place of that normally demanded by the pattern of a verse, as a trochee for an iamb or a dactyl or anapest for a trochee or iamb<; Scazon>another name for the choliamb; sometimes, choliamb is limited to the deliberate reversal of an iamb<

column4: Realistic Period in American Literature, 1865-1900>the period following the Civil War, marked by the triumphant emergence of industrialism and the rise of realism<; Jacobean Age>that portion of the Renaissance during the reign of James I (1603-1625)<; Romantic Period in American Literature, 1830-1865>the period between the “second revolution” of the Jacksonian Era and the close of the Civil War, which saw the testing of a nation and its development by ordeal<; Caroline>applied in general to the age of Charles I of England (1625-1642) and in particular to the spirit of the court<; Edwardian Age>the period between the death of Victoria in 1901 and the beginning of World War I in 1914, so called after Edward VII, who ruled from 1901 to 1910<; Period of Confession and Postmodernism in American Literature, 1960—>the period beginning in the 1960s, a time of uncertainty, revolt, and cynicism in America and a strong turning inward of many American writers<; Augustan>specifically refers to the age of the Emperor Augustus of Rome; by analogy, applied to other epochs when literary culture was high, such as the Augustan Age of English letters<; Colonial Period in American Literature, 1607-1765>the period from the founding of Jamestown to the Stamp Act in 1765, when the writing produced in America was generally utilitarian, polemical, or religious<; Romantic Period in English Literature, 1798-1870>in the period between the publication of Lyrical Ballads (1798) and the death of Dickens, English literature was dominated by romanticism<; Restoration Age>the literary period embracing the latter part of the seventeenth century, named for the restoration of the Stuarts in 1660<; Naturalistic and Symbolistic Period in American Literature>the period between 1900 and 1930 in America, divided by World War I into a part dominated by naturalism and a part marked by growing international awareness and symbolism<; Revolutionary and Early National Period in American Literature, 1765-1830>the period of the establishment of the new nation, ending with the “second revolution” represented by the ascendancy of Jacksonian democracy<; Renaissance>the period of transition from the medieval to the modern world in Western Europe; the word means “rebirth.<; Realistic Period in English Literature, 1870-1914>the period in which the reaction to romanticism reached its peak in full-fledged realism, in the latter portion of Victoria’s reign and the reign of Edward VII<; Victorian>a term used (1) to designate broadly the literature written during the reign of Queen Victoria (1837-1901); and (2) to suggest a certain complacency, hypocrisy, or squeamishness assumed to characterize Victorian attitudes<; Neoclassic Period>the period in English literature between the return of the Stuarts to the English throne in 1660 and the publication of Lyrical Ballads by Wordsworth and Coleridge in 1798<; Elizabethan Age>the segment of the Renaissance during the reign of Elizabeth I (1558-1603)<; Early Tudor Age, 1500-1557>the period in which the ideals of the Renaissance were rapidly replacing those of the Middle Ages, marked by the reformation of the English church and the revival of learning known as Humanism<; Early Victorian Age, 1832-1870>a time of the gradual tempering of the romantic impulse and the steady growth of realism<; Late Victorian Age, 1870-1901>the period between 1870 and the death of Queen Victoria, which saw the full flowering of the movement toward realism<; Commonwealth (or Puritan) Interregnum>the period between the execution of Charles I in 1649 and the restoration of the monarchy in 1660, during which England was ruled by Parliament under the control of Oliver Cromwell<; Modernist Period in English Literature>the period in England beginning with World War I in 1914, marked by the flowering of talent and experiment in the twenties, and ending around 1965<; Federalist Age in American Literature>the period between the formation of the national government and the “Second Revolution” of Jacksonian Democracy<; Postmodernist Period in English Literature, 1965—>the period of English literature beginning around 1965, in which the characteristics of the 1950s continued and were accentuated<; Middle English Period>the period in English literature between the replacement of French by Middle English as the language of court and the early appearances of definitely Modern English writings, roughly between 1350 and 1500<; Old English Period>the period between the invasion of England by the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, beginning around 428, and the establishment of Norman rule around 1100<; Georgian Age in English Literature, 1914-1940>the period of English literature beginning with World War I, named for George V<; Anglo-Norman Period>the period in English literature between 1100 and 1350, so called because of the dominance of Norman-French culture<; Age of Johnson>the interval between 1750 and 1798 marked a transition in English literature<; Age of the Romantic Movement in England, 1798-1832>the period of more than three decades, beginning with the publication of Lyrical Ballads in 1798 and often said to have ended in 1832 with the death of Scott, in which romanticism triumphed in British letters<; Age of Reason>the Enlightenment in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, a period that emphasized self-knowledge, self-control, rationalism, discipline, and the rule of law, order, and decorum<; Age of Sensibility>a name frequently applied by literary historians to the last half of the eighteenth century in England, the time earlier called the Age of Johnson<; Revolutionary Age in American Literature, 1765-1790>the period between the Stamp Act in 1765 and the formation of the federal government in 1789, when American writers were mostly engaged in nonbelletristic pursuits<; Georgian>used for two distinct periods in English literary history: the reigns of the first four Georges (1714-1830), and the period of the anthologies Georgian Poetry (1912-1922)<; Period of Modernism and Consolidation in American Literature, 1930-1960>the period in American literary history from 1930, a turning point marked by the Depression, until 1960<; Diminishing Age in English Literature, 1940-1965>the period of English literature following the coming of World War II in 1939, which profoundly changed British life<; Tudor>the royal house that ruled England from 1485 to 1603: Henry VII (1485-1509), Henry VIII (1509-1547), Edward VI (1547-1553), Mary (1553-1558), and Elizabeth I (1558-1603)<; American Literature, Periods of>the division of American literary history into periods—the early ones based on political and social history and the later ones on the dominance of literary types or movements<; English Literature, Periods of>the division of English literary history into periods, which offers a limited but convenient approach; there are almost as many arrangements as there are books on the subject<; “Long”>applied to a lengthy period of which the significant boundaries exceed a hundred years, especially the Long Eighteenth Century (about 1660-1840) and the Long Nineteenth Century (about 1789-1914)<; Periods of English and American Literary History>see English Literature, American Literature, and Outline of Literary History<; Norman Conquest>the conquest of England by the Normans following the victory of William I in 1066 at the Battle of Senlac (Hastings)<

column4: Arthurian Legend>the vast body of romantic story about Arthur and the knights of the Round Table, which probably grew out of the deeds of some historical person—presumably a Welsh or Roman military leader of the fifth century<; Breton Lay>a relatively brief form of the medieval French romance, professed to have been sung by Breton minstrels on Celtic themes; also, English medieval poems written in imitation of such works<; Chivalric Romance>medieval romance reflecting the customs and ideals of chivalry<; Courts of Love>tribunals for settling questions involved in the system of courtly love<; Mabinogion>a collection of old Welsh tales translated by Lady Charlotte Guest from the Red Book of Hergest, a manuscript from the thirteenth or fourteenth century that contains tales composed centuries earlier<; Holy Grail>the cup from which Christ is said to have drunk at the Last Supper and which was used to catch his blood at the Crucifixion<

column4: Affective Fallacy>the judging of a work of art in terms of its results, especially its emotional effect<; Intentional Fallacy>the judging of the meaning or success of a work of art by the author’s expressed or ostensible intention in producing it<; Frankfurt School>A group of Marxist social theorists associated with the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt.<; Ratiocination>a process of reasoning from data to conclusions<; Touchstone>a critical standard, in Matthew Arnold’s sense: lines and expressions of the great masters used as a test of the quality of other poetry<; Intertextuality>a term created by Julia Kristeva, who said, “Every text builds itself as a mosaic of quotations, every text is absorption and transformation of another text.<; Comparative Literature>the study of literatures of different languages, nations, and periods<; Influence>a term used in literary history for the impact that a writer, work, school, or whole foreign or early culture has on an individual writer or work<; Autotelic>a nondidactic work—that is, one whose end lies within itself and does not depend on the achievement of objectives outside the work<; Tour de force>a feat of strength and virtuosity<; Four Senses of Interpretation>the levels traditionally used in interpreting scriptural and allegorical materials: the literal, the allegorical, the moral, and the anagogical<; Explication de texte>a method, originating in the teaching of literature in France, involving the painstaking analysis of the meanings, relationships, and ambiguities of the words, images, and other small units that make up a literary work<; Textual Criticism>a scholarly activity that attempts to establish the authoritative text of a work<; Concrete Universal>A literary representation in which a particular, concrete thing embodies a general or universal truth.<; Criticism>the analysis, study, and evaluation of individual works of art as well as the formulation of general principles for the examination of such works<; Restraint>writing which holds in decent check the emotional elements of a given situation<; Analysis>a method by which a thing is separated into parts, and those parts are given rigorous, logical, detailed scrutiny<; Analytical Criticism>criticism that views the work of art as an autonomous whole and believes that its meaning, nature, and significance can be discovered by applying rigorous and logical systems of analysis to its several parts and their organization<; Displacement>in Freudian analysis of dreams and other expressions, one of the devices for coping with a challenging problem, as when a desire to kill someone becomes a desire to insult that person<; Genre Criticism>that type of criticism dedicated to defining genres and tracing their histories and interactions<; Hermeneutics>theory of interpretation; a term once limited to the interpretation of religious texts, particularly the allegorical<; Logocentrism>a key term in deconstruction; it argues that there is a persistent but morbid centering of Logos (meaning thought, truth, law, reason, logic, word, and the Word) in Western thought since Plato<; Practical Criticism>criticism in which aesthetic principles are applied to specific works; often called “applied criticism,” the term is used in opposition to theoretical criticism<; Review>a notice of a current work or performance<; Theoretical Criticism>criticism that attempts to arrive at general principles and to formulate inclusive aesthetic tenets<; Utile et Dulce>Horace’s principle that poetry should be both useful and pleasing.<; Auteur Theory>a critical method, from the French politique des auteurs, by which a film is viewed as the product of its auteur, or director, and is judged by the quality of its expression of the director’s personality or worldview<; Biographical Fallacy>the interpretation of a work of art through heavy reliance on aspects of the maker’s life as the basis for understanding<; Classic, Classical (adjectives)>of recognized excellence or belonging to established tradition; used specifically to designate the literature or culture of Greece and Rome or later literature that partakes of its qualities<; Classic (noun)>in the singular, classic is usually applied to a piece of literature that by common consent has achieved a recognized superior status in literary history; also an author of similar standing<; Commentary>scholarly remarks specifically concerning details of substance or text, usually matters of information and not of judgment<; Context>matter that surrounds a word or text in question<; Critic>one who estimates and passes judgment on the nature, value, and quality of artistic works<; Criticism, Types of>the various ways in which criticism—the description, justification, analysis, or judgment of art—may be classified, such as Aristotelian versus Platonic<; Critique>a critical examination of a work of art with a view to determining its nature and assessing its value according to some established standards<; Decorum>a term loosely describing what is proper to a character, subject, or setting<; Heresy of Paraphrase, The>the critical view that paraphrase is heretical because a work of art means what it means in the terms in which it delivers that meaning<; Formal Criticism>criticism that examines a work in terms of the type or genre to which it belongs<; Expressive Theory of Criticism>m. H. Abrams’s term for a theory that holds the object of art to be the expression of the artist’s emotions, impressions, or beliefs; an essential doctrine of romantic critics<; Dissemination>in Jacques Derrida’s application, a term exploiting its root in Latin semen (“seed”) and a fancied relation to Greek sēma (“sign”) to suggest that meaning in language is variously scattered<; Examen>a detailed study<; Higher Criticism>certain aspects of the study of biblical texts in the nineteenth century, seeking to determine the authorship, date, place of origin, and historical credibility of the books of the Bible<; Linguistics and Literary Criticism>the connection between the study of language and of literature, which reached a high point after World War II when the techniques of structural linguistics were extended to individual texts and to literature as a whole<; Mythical Method>t. S. Eliot’s phrase (1923) for the structure of Joyce’s Ulysses, which sustains a “continuous parallel” between Homer’s Odyssey and a one-day narrative of contemporaneity<; Metacriticism>a process or method whose primary subject is the critical examination of the nomenclature, premises, principles, or structure of criticism itself<; Model>an earlier work that serves as a verbal source without necessarily providing any deeper thematic resonances<; Interpretation, Fourfold Method>the levels employed in biblical interpretation in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance<; Mimetic Theory of Art>a theory emphasizing the actuality imitated in the artwork<; Misreading>a reading—or reading in general—that makes a mistake in perception or interpretation<; Judicial Criticism>see Criticism, Types of<; Pragmatic Theory of Art>a theory of art, according to M. H. Abrams, in which the major interest is in the effect that the art object produces in its audience<; Objective Theory of Art>m. H. Abrams’s term for the view that holds the literary work to be most significant as an object in itself, independent of its composition, the actuality it imitates, its author’s intention, or its effect<; Prosaics>formed by analogy with Poetics: the systematic study of the principles of prose<; Texture>the elements remaining in a literary work after a paraphrase of its argument has been made<; Tension>a term introduced by Allen Tate, meaning the integral unity that results from the successful resolution of the conflicts of abstraction and concreteness, of general and particular, of denotation and connotation<; Source>the person, manuscript, or book from which something is derived<; Zoilus>a severe, carping critic (from Zoilus of Amphipolis, fourth century B.C., known as “Homeromastix—scourge of Homer”)<

column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Paradox>a statement that although seemingly contradictory or absurd may actually be well-founded or true<; Metaphor>an analogy identifying one object with another and ascribing to the first object one or more of the qualities of the second<; Simile>a figure in which a similarity between two objects is directly expressed<; Litotes>a form of understatement in which a thing is affirmed by stating the negative of its opposite<; Consonance>the relation between words in which the final consonants in the stressed syllables agree but the vowels that precede them differ<; Metonymy>the substitution of the name of an object closely associated with a word for the word itself<; Synecdoche>a trope in which a part signifies the whole or the whole signifies the part<; Assonance>generally, patterning of vowel sounds without regard to consonants<; Apostrophe>a figure of speech in which someone (usually but not always absent), some abstract quality, or a nonexistent personage is directly addressed as though present<; Zeugma>a term used in several ways, all involving a sort of “yoking”; for example, as a synonym of syllepsis, when an object-taking word has two or more objects on different levels<; Allusion>a figure of speech that makes brief reference to a historical or literary figure, event, or object<; Dissonance>harsh and inharmonious sounds; a marked breaking of the music of poetry, which may be intentional, as it often is in Browning and Hardy<; Onomatopoeia>words that by their sound suggest their meaning: “hiss,” “buzz,” “whirr,” “sizzle.<; Sigmatism>The excessive or deliberate repetition of the s sound.<; Tautology>the use of repetitious words<; Anaphora>one of the devices of repetition, in which the same expression (word or words) is repeated at the beginning of two or more lines, clauses, or sentences<; Enjambment (Enjambement)>the continuation of the sense and grammatical construction of a line on to the next verse or couplet<; Oxymoron>a self-contradictory combination of words or smaller verbal units; usually noun-noun, adjective-adjective, adjective-noun, adverb-adverb, or adverb-verb<; Alliteration>the repetition of initial identical consonant sounds or any vowel sounds in successive or closely associated syllables<; Leonine Rhyme>the internal rhyming of the last stressed syllable before the caesura, with the last stressed syllable of the line<; Conceit>a type of poetic metaphor implying ingenuity; originally, the term—cognate and almost synonymous with “concept”—implied something conceived in the mind<; Chiasmus>a pattern in which the second part is balanced against the first but with the parts reversed<; Feminine Rhyme>a rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllables are followed by an undifferentiated identical unstressed syllable<; Iamb (or Iambus)>a foot consisting of an unaccented syllable and an accented<; Trochee>a foot consisting of an accented and an unaccented syllable<; Synesthesia>the concurrent response of two or more of the senses to the stimulation of one<; Polyptoton>the repetition in close proximity of words that have the same roots<; Ambiguity>the state of having more than one meaning, with resultant uncertainty as to the intended significance of the statement<; Compound Rhyme>rhyme between primary and secondary stressed syllables<; Resonance>The quality of a work or image to evoke associations, meanings, and feelings beyond its literal content.<; Imagery>the collection of images in a literary work; in another sense, synonymous with trope or figure of speech<; Epanalepsis>the repetition at the end of a clause of a word or phrase that occurred at its beginning<; Masculine Rhyme>rhyme that falls on the stressed concluding syllables of the rhyme words<; Euphemism>a device in which indirectness replaces directness of statement, usually in an effort to avoid offensiveness<; Irony>the recognition of a reality different from appearance<; Realistic Period in American Literature, 1865-1900>the period following the Civil War, marked by the triumphant emergence of industrialism and the rise of realism<; Spondee>a foot composed of two accented syllables<; Reification>the treatment of abstractions as concrete things<; Metathesis>the interchange of position between sounds in a word<; Jacobean Age>that portion of the Renaissance during the reign of James I (1603-1625)<; Personification>a figure that endows animals, ideas, abstractions, and inanimate objects with human form, personality, intelligence, and emotions<; Romantic Period in American Literature, 1830-1865>the period between the “second revolution” of the Jacksonian Era and the close of the Civil War, which saw the testing of a nation and its development by ordeal<; Spenserian Sonnet>a sonnet of the English type in that it has three quatrains and a couplet but features quatrains joined by the use of linking rhymes: abab bcbe cdcd ee<; Anapest>a metrical foot consisting of three syllables, with two unaccented syllables followed by an accented one<; Dactyl>a foot consisting of one accented syllable followed by two unaccented<; Muckrakers>a group of American writers who between 1902 and 1911 worked to expose the dishonest methods and unscrupulous motives in big business and in city, state, and national government<; Caroline>applied in general to the age of Charles I of England (1625-1642) and in particular to the spirit of the court<; Miltonic Sonnet>a variation made by Milton on the Italian sonnet, in which the rhyme scheme is kept but the “turn” between the octave and the sestet is eliminated<; Pleonasm>the use of superfluous syllables or words<; Harangue>a vehement speech designed to arouse strong emotions<; Pathetic Fallacy>a phrase coined by Ruskin to denote the tendency to credit nature with human emotions<; Edwardian Age>the period between the death of Victoria in 1901 and the beginning of World War I in 1914, so called after Edward VII, who ruled from 1901 to 1910<; Epiphany>literally, a manifestation or showing-forth, usually of some divine being; given currency as a critical term by James Joyce<; Asyndeton>a condensed form of expression in which elements customarily joined by conjunctions are presented in series without the conjunctions<; Boustrophedon>running alternately from left to right and from right to left; a term—literally, “ox plowing”—that describes the direction of writing in certain ancient inscriptions<; Italian Sonnet>a sonnet divided into an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet rhyming cdecde<; Satanic School>southey’s phrase (1821) for the literary group of Byron, Shelley, Hunt, and others, whose irregular lives and radical ideas suggested the term<; Soliloquy>a speech delivered while the speaker is alone (solus), calculated to inform the audience of what is passing in the character’s mind<; Kenning>a figurative phrase used in Old Germanic languages as a synonym for a simple noun<; Inversion>the placing of a sentence element out of its normal position<; Period of Confession and Postmodernism in American Literature, 1960—>the period beginning in the 1960s, a time of uncertainty, revolt, and cynicism in America and a strong turning inward of many American writers<; Rhyme>identity of terminal sound between accented syllables, usually occupying corresponding positions in two or more lines of verse<; Truncation>in metrics, the omission of a syllable or syllables at the beginning or end of a line<; Spasmodic School>a phrase applied by W. E. Aytoun in 1854 to a group of contemporary English poets<; Augustan>specifically refers to the age of the Emperor Augustus of Rome; by analogy, applied to other epochs when literary culture was high, such as the Augustan Age of English letters<; Aside>a dramatic convention by which an actor directly addresses the audience but is not supposed to be heard by the other actors on the stage<; Parnassians>a group of nineteenth-century French poets, so called from their journal Parnasse contemporain<; Agrarians>literally people living in an agricultural society or espousing its merits; in literary history, usually a group of Southern American writers who published The Fugitive (1922-1925)<; Pyrrhic>a foot of two unaccented syllables<; Terza rima>a three-line stanza, supposedly devised by Dante (for his Divine Comedy) with rhyme scheme aba bcb cdc ded and so forth<; Allonym>the name of an actual person other than the author that is signed by the author to a work<; Barbarism>a mistake in the form of a word or a word that results from such a mistake<; Lost Generation>a group of American writers, born around 1900, who served in the First World War and reacted against certain tendencies of older writers in the 1920s<; Pun>a play on words based on the similarity of sound between two words with different meanings<; Eye Rhyme>rhyme that appears correct from the spelling but is not so from the pronunciation<; Epistolary Novel>a novel in which the narrative is carried forward by letters written by one or more of the characters<; Polysyndeton>the use of more conjunctions than is normal<; Sonnet>a poem almost invariably of fourteen lines and following one of several set rhyme schemes<; Syllepsis>a grammatically correct construction in which one word is placed in the same grammatical relationship to two words but in quite different senses<; Dead Metaphor>a figure of speech used so long that it is taken in its denotative sense only, without any conscious comparison to a physical object it once conveyed<; Objective Correlative>t. S. Eliot’s term for a pattern of objects, actions, or events or a situation that can serve effectively to awaken in the reader an emotional response without being a direct statement of that subjective emotion<; Cockney School>a derogatory title applied by Blackwood’s Magazine to a group of nineteenth-century writers—including William Hazlitt, Leigh Hunt, and John Keats—because of their alleged poor taste in such matters as diction and rhyme<; Meliorism>the belief—widely held in the nineteenth century—that society has an innate tendency toward improvement and that that tendency can be furthered by conscious human effort<; In Medias Res>a term from Horace, literally “in or into the middle parts of things,” applied to the technique of opening a story in the middle of the action<; Pantoum>the pantoum may consist of any number of four-line stanzas, but in any case, the second and fourth lines of one stanza must reappear as the first and third lines of the following stanza<; Volta>the turn in thought—from question to answer; problem to solution—that occurs at the beginning of the sestet in the Italian sonnet<; Shakespearean Sonnet>the English sonnet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Eponym>A person from whose name the name of a thing, place, or term is derived.<; Aestheticism>a nineteenth-century literary movement that rested on the credo of “art for art’s sake.<; Colonial Period in American Literature, 1607-1765>the period from the founding of Jamestown to the Stamp Act in 1765, when the writing produced in America was generally utilitarian, polemical, or religious<; Hartford Wits>a group of Connecticut writers, active around the period of the American Revolution<; Haiku>a form of Japanese poetry that states—in three lines of five, seven, and five syllables—a clear picture designed to arouse a distinct emotion and suggest a specific spiritual insight<; Symploce>a figure of speech combining anaphora and epistrophe: the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses and of another at their end<; Antithesis>a figure of speech characterized by strongly contrasting words, clauses, sentences, or ideas<; Ballad>a form of verse to be sung or recited and characterized by its presentation of an exciting episode in narrative or dramatic form<; Caesura (or Cesura)>a pause or break in a line of verse<; Fugitives, The>a group associated with Vanderbilt University, which in the 1920s published the magazine The Fugitive<; Elision>the omission of part of a word<; Malapropism>an inappropriateness of speech resulting from the use of one word for another, which resembles it<; New York School>a group of American poets who flourished between 1950 and 1970, distinguished by urbanity, wit, learning, spontaneity, and exuberance<; Rondeau>a set French verse pattern; artificial but very popular with many English poets<; Spoonerism>an accidental interchange of sounds—usually the initial consonants—in two or more words<; Broken Rhyme>the breaking of a word at the end of a line for the sake of a rhyme<; Blank Verse>unrhymed but otherwise regular verse—usually iambic pentameter<; Lake Poets and Lake School>coleridge, Wordsworth, and Southey—three poets who at the beginning of the nineteenth century were living in the Lake District of northwest England (Cumbria and Lancashire)<; Knickerbocker Group>a New York group of writers during the first half of the nineteenth century, named after Washington Irving’s Knickerbocker’s History of New York<; Pastoral>a poetic treatment of shepherds and rustic life, after the Latin for “shepherd”: pastor<; Senryu>a form with the same structure as the haiku—seventeen syllables in lines of five, seven, and five—but relying on humor or satire rather than conventions related to the seasons<; Understatement>a common figure of speech in which the literal sense of what is said falls detectably short of (or “under”) the magnitude of what is being talked about<; Romantic Period in English Literature, 1798-1870>in the period between the publication of Lyrical Ballads (1798) and the death of Dickens, English literature was dominated by romanticism<; Carpe Diem>“Seize the day”; a phrase used by Horace and applied to literature, especially lyric poems, that exemplifies the spirit of “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.<; Ubi Sunt Formula>a convention much used in verse, rhetorically asking “where are those who were before us?” (ubi sunt qui ante nos fuerunt?<; Affective Fallacy>the judging of a work of art in terms of its results, especially its emotional effect<; English Sonnet>a sonnet consisting of three quatrains followed by a couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Free Verse>vers libre; verse that is relatively free, managing without rhyme, meter, or regular rhythm<; Heteromerous Rhyme>a fairly rare species of multiple rhyme (also called “mosaic”) in which typically one word is forced into a rhyme with two or more words<; Pre-Raphaelitism>the movement begun in 1848 by the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Holman-Hunt, John Everett Millais, and others as a protest against the conventional methods of painting<; Novel of Manners>a novel dominated by social customs, manners, conventions, and habits of a definite social class<; Tetrameter>a line consisting of four feet<; Transcendentalism>a reliance on the intuition and the conscience—a form of idealism; a philosophical romanticism reaching America a generation or two after it developed in Europe<; Surrealism>a movement in art emphasizing the expression of the imagination as realized in dreams and presented without conscious control<; Run-on Lines>the carrying over of grammatical structure from one line to the next<; Allegory>a form of extended metaphor in which objects, persons, places, and actions in a narrative are equated with meanings outside the narrative itself<; Elegy>a sustained formal poem setting forth meditations on death or another solemn theme<; Limerick>a form of light verse that follows a definite pattern: five anapestic lines of which the first, second, and fifth, consisting of three feet, rhyme; and the third and fourth lines, consisting of two feet, rhyme<; Hypallage>a figure of speech in which an epithet is moved from the proximate to the less proximate of a group of nouns<; Aubade>a lyric about dawn or a morning serenade—a song of lovers parting at dawn<; Caudate Sonnet>an Italian form, rarely adopted into English, in which a standard fourteen-line sonnet is augmented by the addition of other lines, including “tails.<; Martian School (or Martians)>a school of British poets born in the 1940s—so labeled by James Fenton after Craig Raine’s A Martian Sends a Postcard Home (1979)—who struggle to see the world afresh, as might a visitor from Mars<; column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Litotes>a form of understatement in which a thing is affirmed by stating the negative of its opposite<; Understatement>a common figure of speech in which the literal sense of what is said falls detectably short of (or “under”) the magnitude of what is being talked about<; Gigantism>Exaggeration of size or scale, especially for comic or grotesque effect.<; Meiosis>intentional understatement for humorous or satiric effect<; Overstatement>exaggeration; hyperbole<
