column4: Chrestomathy>a collection of choice passages to be used in the study of a language or a literature and, thus, a kind of anthology<; Blood and Thunder>a class of work specializing in bloodshed and violence<; Concordance>an alphabetical index of most or all of the words in a text or in the works of an author<; Vade Mecum>an article that one keeps constantly on hand<; Incunabulum>any book printed in the last part of the fifteenth century (before 1501)<; Omnibus (Latin dative plural, “for all”)>a volume of selected works, usually by one author but sometimes by several on one subject<; Duodecimo>a book size, designating signatures that result from sheets folded to twelve leaves or twenty-four pages<; Folio>a standard-size sheet of paper folded in half<; Anthology>literally “a gathering of flowers”; a collection of writing—either prose or poetry—usually by various authors<; Jest Books>collections of humorous, witty, or satirical anecdotes and jokes that had some vogue in Europe in the sixteenth and succeeding centuries<; Canon>a standard of judgment; a criterion. Also, the authorized or accepted list of books belonging in the Christian Bible or of the works of any author<; Emblem Books>collections of emblems, each consisting of a motto expressing a moral idea, accompanied by a symbolic picture and a short poem<; Allusion Book>a collection of allusions to a writer or a writer’s works, sometimes for a specific period<; Courtesy Books>a class of books that, flourishing in late Renaissance times, dealt with the training of the “courtly” person<; Miscellany>a group of diverse items<; Lexicography>the making of dictionaries or lexicons<; Octavo>a book size designating a book whose signature results from sheets folded to eight leaves or sixteen pages<; Compendium>a brief condensation of a longer work or of a whole field of knowledge<; Hornbook>a kind of primer common in England from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries<; Prequel>a sequel that is set at an earlier time than the work it follows<; Bibelot>A small decorative object or trinket; also, a miniature book.<; Page-Turner>A book so exciting that the reader cannot stop reading.<; Magnum Opus>A great work; the most important work of an artist or writer.<; Commonplace Book>a classified collection of quotations or arguments prepared for reference purposes<; Dictionaries>works that arrange words alphabetically and give explanations of their meanings, derivations, and pronunciations<; Lexicon>a word list or wordbook; a vocabulary; a standard term for dictionary<; Catalog>a list of people, things, or attributes<; Coffee Table Book>a large expensive handsome nonfiction volume, usually with many illustrations, too big for an ordinary shelf and suited to display; once called a “grand piano book.<; Gift Books>miscellaneous collections of literary materials published annually in book form for purchase as gifts<; Limited Edition>an edition of a book or other printed matter limited to a fixed number—often with special paper, type, and binding—and sometimes numbered and signed<; Volume>sometimes a synonym for book, occasionally with special reference to poetry<; Sequel>a literary work that continues from another<; Catalogue Raisonné>A comprehensive, annotated catalogue of all the known works of an artist.<; ABC-Book, Abcee-Book, Absey-Book>a primer or horn-book that introduces a subject, sometimes in the form of a catechism of dialogue<; Ana>miscellaneous sayings, anecdotes, gossip, and scraps of information about a particular person, place, or event; or a book that records such sayings and anecdotes<; Ancilla (literally, “maidservant”)>an ancillary aid in the study of a subject<; Annuals>books appearing in successive numbers at intervals of one year and usually reviewing the events of the year within specified fields of interest<; Binding>the outer part of a book, made of paper or something more substantial<; Board Book>a small book with few pages and many pictures, printed on sturdy boards for use by very young children<; Book Sizes>terms such as folio, quarto, and octavo used in describing book sizes, based on the number of times a printed sheet is folded<; Book>in general, any collection of sheets of paper or a similar material, customarily fastened along one edge and often protected by covers<; Block Books>books printed from engraved blocks of wood<; Breviora>a collection of brief writings or sayings<; Cahier>a French word related to quire, now generally applied to an exercise book, pamphlet, or fascicle<; Breviary>a collection of lessons, calendars, and outlines for services to aid Roman Catholic priests in reciting the Divine Offices for each day and in discharging other churchly responsibilities<; Chapbook>a small book or pamphlet—usually a single signature of sixteen or thirty-two pages, poorly printed, and crudely illustrated—sold in England and America through the eighteenth century by peddlers or “chapmen.<; Codex>a manuscript book, particularly of biblical or classical writing<; Companion>a reference work intended to help the reader of a certain text, set of texts, or field of study<; Cover>the binding, wrapper, backing, jacket, or other such outer material of a book—specifically, the illustrated front cover of a periodical<; Cyclopedia (or Cyclopedia)>same as encyclopedia<; Flap>the ends of a paper dust jacket that are folded under to keep the covering in place<; Dust Jacket (also Dust Cover)>a detachable paper cover, wrapper, or jacket on a clothbound book normally having advertising copy, illustrations, advertisements, and other such materials<; Enumerative Bibliography>a listing of works of a particular country, author, printer, or type or on a particular subject<; Encyclopedia (or Encyclopaedia)>an inclusive compendium of information<; Enchiridion>a handbook, manual, or vade mecum<; Etiquette Books (Renaissance)>books of instruction in manners, conduct, and the art of governing for young princes and noblemen<; Elizabethan Miscellanies>poetical anthologies compiled in the Elizabethan Age<; Manual>a handbook; a book offering information and guidance on any subject<; Monograph>a rather indefinite term for a piece of scholarly writing, usually on a relatively limited topic<; Manuscript, Medieval>the art of manuscript-making, highly developed in the Middle Ages, when there was no mechanical means for multiplying copies<; Posy (Posie)>an anthology (“a collection of flowers”); also a motto, usually in verse, inscribed on a ring<; Opus>a work of any sort, sometimes disparagingly<; Poetical Miscellanies>see Miscellany<; Short-Title Catalogue>a catalogue of books by short title, the best known being Pollard and Redgrave’s Short-Title Catalogue of Books Printed in England, Scotland, and Ireland... 1475-1640 (1926)<; Sequelula>a little sequel<; Subject Bibliography>a list of books, articles, manuscripts, or other forms of writing—either complete or selected—on any of various principles or some specific subject<; T.e.g.>bookseller’s abbreviation of “top edges gilt.<; the opposite of anacrusis<; Comedy>originally, works marked by a happy ending and a less exalted style than tragedy; a lighter form than tragedy that aims primarily to amuse<; Doggerel>rude verse; any poorly executed attempt at poetry<; Goliardic Verse>lilting Latin verse, usually satiric, composed by university students and wandering scholars in Germany, France, and England in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries<; Eiron>a basic comic character in Greek drama—typically a swindler, trickster, hypocrite, or picaresque rogue—who feigns ignorance in order to trick others<; Dizain>A poem or stanza of ten lines, usually with eight or ten syllables per line.<; Anonym>An anonymous person or work; also, a pseudonym used to conceal identity.<; Alazon>the braggart or impostor in Greek comedy<; Coup de Théâtre>a surprising and usually unmotivated stroke in a drama that produces a sensational effect; by extension, anything designed solely for effect<; Epitaph>an inscription used to mark burial places<; Darwinism>thought affected by the research and theories of Charles Darwin (1809-1882), especially The Origin of Species (1859)<; Doppelganger>german, “double goer”; a mysterious double, a common figure in literature<; Gothic>originally the Goths, a single Germanic tribe, but broadened to mean Teutonic or Germanic and, later, “medieval” in general<; Koine>the language spoken throughout the ancient Greek world; colloquial Attic with numerous supplements from other dialects and other languages<; Incunabulum>any book printed in the last part of the fifteenth century (before 1501)<; Inkhornists>a group in the Renaissance who favored the introduction of heavy Latin and Greek words into the standard English vocabulary<; Troubadour>a name given to the lyric poets and composers of Provence (southern France) in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries<; “Tribe of Ben”>a contemporary nickname for young poets and dramatists of the seventeenth century who acknowledged “rare Ben Jonson” as their master<; Marinism>An ornate, extravagant poetic style of conceits and wordplay, after the Italian poet Giambattista Marino.<; Amphibology (Amphibologia or Amphiboly)>statements capable of two different meanings—a kind of ambiguity<; Anagram>a word or phrase made by transposing the letters of another<; Antagonist>the character directly opposed to the protagonist<; Antibacchius>a metrical foot of three syllables, of which the first two are stressed and the third unstressed (accentual) or the first two are long and the third short (quantitative)<; Byronism>the qualities associated with Lord Byron (1788-1824), whose unique electricity provoked the coining of such terms as “Byronic,” “Byroniad,” and “Byronism.<; Figure Poem>a poem written so that its printed shape suggests its subject matter<; Hymn>a poem expressing religious emotion and generally intended to be sung by a chorus<; Hobson-Jobson>the process of transforming something foreign into a more familiar native article<; Point of View>the vantage point from which an author presents a story<; Orphism>defined by Gerald L. Bruns as “the idea of poetic speech as the ground of all signification.<; Reggae>a style of music, song, and performance that became popular in the 1970s, beginning in Jamaica and spreading through the Caribbean<; Pararhyme>an acoustic effect—systematically practiced by Wilfred Owen, W. H. Auden, Keith Douglas, and others—whereby the place of ordinary rhyme is taken by a combination of alliteration and consonance rhyme<; Omnibus (Latin dative plural, “for all”)>a volume of selected works, usually by one author but sometimes by several on one subject<; Pictorialism>pictorial style, extended from painting to the other arts insofar as they are capable of representing or depicting; usually patronizing or pejorative<; Quarto>a book size designating a book whose signatures result from sheets folded to four leaves (eight pages)<; Poulter’s Measure>a couplet—now rarely used—with a first line in iambic hexameter and a second line in iambic heptameter<; Scat>a vocal style developed during the 1920s, with a singer improvising patterns of repetitive nonsense syllables that suggest the sound of a musical instrument<; Stoicism>the philosophy of the Stoics, a group of Greek philosophers, founded by Zeno late in the fourth century B.C. Portmanteau Words>words formed by telescoping two words into one, as “smog” from “smoke” and “fog.<; Ananym>a word fabricated by spelling another word backwards<; Metaplasm>the movement of any element in a piece of language from its customary place<; Aphaeresis (also Aphairese, Apheresis)>the omission of an initial, unstressed syllable at the beginning of a word<; Folk Etymology>a common procedure—resembling false etymology—whereby an unfamiliar word is reshaped into something familiar<; Homeoptoton (also Homeoptoton)>a series of words in the same case or other grammatical form<; Mesostich>A poem in which letters in the middle of the lines spell out a word or name.<; Acronym>a word formed by combining the initial letters or syllables of a series of words to form a name<; Cacozelia>An affected and tasteless use of foreign or learned words in an effort to sound elegant.<; Epenthesis>The insertion of a sound or letter into the middle of a word.<; False Friend>a word that people may think they know the meaning of; most often, a foreign word cognate with a native word but with divergent meaning<; Hapax Legomenon>a word or grammatical form that occurs only once; literally, from the Greek, “something said only once.<; Howler>a small error that begins in innocence or ignorance and ends in folly and potential embarrassment<; Paragram>generally, a word that resembles another and is used in its place for the sake of euphemism, apotropaic deformation, insult, avoidance of libel, or some other purpose<; Anastomosis>a scientific term for the interconnection between two entities<; Anaptyxis>insertion of a vowel sound between two consonant sounds<; Catchword>a word so often repeated that it is identified with a person or object<; Synonyms>words with the same or similar meanings<; Vox Nihili>a worthless or meaningless word<; Eclipsis>The omission of a word or sound; ellipsis.<; Antonym>A word opposite in meaning to another word.<; Homonym>A word with the same spelling or sound as another but a different meaning.<; Haplology>The omission of one of two similar adjacent syllables in pronunciation.<; Perissology>Wordiness; the use of more words than necessary.<; Mondegreen>A misheard word or phrase, especially from a song or poem, that gives a new meaning.<; Cryptarithm>a sophisticated puzzle in which letters of the alphabet are assigned a numerical value such that a spelled-out formula (normally addition) is true of both the words and the numbers<; Nexility>rare word for compactness of utterance<; Metastasis>a rapid transition from one point to another, sometimes for the sake of deception<; Metanalysis>reinterpretation or misconstruction of the division between words or other units<; Paraphemism>a coinage or other makeshift designed to avoid confusion or embarrassment<; Eggcorn>The mistaken substitution of a similar-sounding word or phrase that still makes some sense.<; Etymology>The origin and historical development of a word; the study of word origins.<; Monovocalic>Written using only one vowel.<; Synaloepha>The merging of two adjacent vowels into one syllable, especially by eliding a final vowel before an initial one.<; Acrophony>calling a written symbol by the name of something that has that symbol at its beginning<; ABC, A B C, A.B.C.>(1) An alphabetical acrostic; a poem in which stanzas or lines begin with the letters of the alphabet. (2) A primer teaching the alphabet or other elementary parts of a field of study<; Affix>a verbal element added before (prefix), inside (infix), or after (suffix) a base to change the meaning<; Analytic-Prefixal>one term for the practices of altering verbal units by means of adding a separate element at the beginning<; Anaphone (or Anaphony)>the acoustic counterpart of the anagram<; Blends (or Blend Words)>another name for portmanteau words<; Coined Words>words consciously manufactured, as opposed to those entering the language as a result of some more usual process of language development<; Compensation>a means of making up for omissions in a line; a form of substitution<; Diectasis>lengthening a word by the interpolation of a syllable<; Enantiomorph>an object that is a mirror image of another<; Ghost>(1) Or “ghost word”—a word created by a misprint or a misreading<; Hypheresis (also Hyphæresis)>the omission of material in the body of a word<; Loan Word>a word that passes in its native form from one language to another without being translated<; Meta->a prefix often applied by contemporary critics to various literary terms, forming such words as metacriticism and metafiction<; Parasynthesis>derivation from a stem-word in such a way as not to affect accent<; Relique>an old spelling of “relic.<; Proparalepsis>the addition of a syllable to the end of a word<; Prefix>material placed at the beginning of a word or word group—sometimes remaining a separate word (as the “to” as an infinitive prefix) but often joined to the basic word (as in “reform”)<; Schüttelreime>“Shuttle rhyme”; the German equivalent of the spoonerism, which turns on the transposition of initial letters<

Aytoun in 1854 to a group of contemporary English poets<; Aestheticism>a nineteenth-century literary movement that rested on the credo of “art for art’s sake.<; Pre-Raphaelitism>the movement begun in 1848 by the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Holman-Hunt, John Everett Millais, and others as a protest against the conventional methods of painting<; Transcendentalism>a reliance on the intuition and the conscience—a form of idealism; a philosophical romanticism reaching America a generation or two after it developed in Europe<; Surrealism>a movement in art emphasizing the expression of the imagination as realized in dreams and presented without conscious control<; Harlem Renaissance>the first major, self-conscious literary movement of African-American writers, although there had been much black writing in America earlier<; Vorticism>a movement in modern poetry, originating in 1914 with Wyndham Lewis, related to certain abstract developments in painting and sculpture<; Naturalism>the application of principles of scientific determinism to literature; a term best reserved for a literary movement in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries<; Great Awakening, The>see Awakening, the Great<; Minimalism>a modern movement in politics, economics, and all the arts, especially noticeable in architecture (Mies van der Rohe: “Less is more”) and music (for example, the works of Anton Webern)<; Expressionism>a movement affecting painting and literature, which followed and went beyond impressionism in its efforts to “objectify inner experience.<; Movement, The>a focus of British literary activity in the mid-1950s, mostly in poetry and prose fiction, with emphases on normality, regularity, practicality, stoicism, traditionalism, and solid middle-class values<; Imagists>a group of poets active in England and America between 1909 and 1918<; Luminism>a movement in painting, especially since about 1875, in which the art concentrates on the effect of light<; Impressionism>a highly personal manner of writing in which the author presents materials as they appear to an individual temperament at a precise moment rather than as they are presumed to be in actuality<; Oxford Movement>a reform movement in the English Church begun at Oxford in 1833 and led by John Henry Newman; also known as the “Tractarian Movement” and the “Anglo-Catholic Revival.<; Symbolism>in its broad sense, the use of one object to represent or suggest another; in literature, the serious and extensive use of symbols<; Dadaism>a movement in Europe during and just after World War I that ignored logical relationships between idea and statement, argued for absolute freedom, and delivered itself of numerous provocative manifestoes<; Puritanism>a movement that developed in England about the middle of the sixteenth century and later spread its influence into the New England colonies in America<; Storm and Stress>an eighteenth-century German movement; see Sturm und Drang<; Cubism>An early twentieth-century art movement that represented subjects from multiple viewpoints in fragmented, geometric form.<; Neoclassicism>the classicism that dominated English literature in the Restoration age and in the eighteenth century<; Modernism>A broad movement in the arts (about 1890–1940) marked by a deliberate break with traditional forms and experimentation with new ones.<; Age of Reason>the Enlightenment in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, a period that emphasized self-knowledge, self-control, rationalism, discipline, and the rule of law, order, and decorum<; Enlightenment>a philosophical movement of the eighteenth century, particularly in France but effectively over much of Europe and America<; Medievalism>a spirit of sympathy for the Middle Ages, along with a desire to preserve or revive certain qualities of medieval life<; Romanticism>a movement of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that marked the reaction in literature, philosophy, art, religion, and politics from the neoclassicism and formal orthodoxy of the preceding period<; Sturm und Drang (Storm and Stress)>a movement in Germany during the last quarter of the eighteenth century, named after Klinger’s drama Sturm und Drang (1776)<; Apocalyptics>a movement in English poetry flourishing between 1935 and 1950, led by Henry Treece and J. R. Hendry; resembling surrealism, it favored extreme imagery<; Formalism (or Formalist Criticism)>criticism that emphasizes the form of the artwork, with “form” variously construed to mean generic form, type, verbal form, grammatical and syntactical form, rhetorical form, or verse form<; Magic Realism (or Magical Realism)>an international tendency in the graphic and literary arts in which contrasting elements—such as the supernatural, myth, dream, fantasy—invade a conventionally realistic surface<; Spoken Word Movement>A movement in poetry written to be performed aloud, emphasizing sound, rhythm, and audience.<; Acmeism>a movement in Russian poetry, begun around 1912 by members of the Poets’ Guild, to promote precise treatment of realistic subjects<; Avant-Garde>a military metaphor drawn from the French “vanguard” and applied to new writing that shows striking (and usually self-conscious) innovations in style, form, and subject matter<; Gaelic Movement>a movement that began late in the nineteenth century, embodied in the Gaelic League founded by Douglas Hyde in 1893, devoted to the preservation of the Gaelic language<; Irish Literary Movement, Irish Literary Revival, Irish Renaissance>variant terms for the movement that encouraged the production of Anglo-Irish literature<; Brook Farm>A utopian community founded in Massachusetts in 1841 by members of the Transcendentalist movement.<; Arts and Crafts Movement>a movement—beginning in northern Europe in the later nineteenth century but soon with worldwide influence—that emphasized utility, individual craft, handiwork, simplicity, artistic versatility, and local native materials<; Celtic Revival, The>a term sometimes used for the Gaelic Movement, the Celtic Renaissance, or the Irish Literary Movement, as well as for the eighteenth-century movement<; Postmodernism>A late twentieth-century movement marked by skepticism toward grand narratives, irony, pastiche, and self-reflexivity.<; Ancients and Moderns, Quarrel of the>the controversy that took place in France and England in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries over the relative merits of classical and contemporary cultures<; Celtic Renaissance (or Celtic Revival or Irish Renaissance)>a movement aimed at the preservation of the Gaelic language (the Gaelic Movement), the reconstruction of early Celtic history and literature, and the stimulation of a new literature authentically Celtic (especially Irish) in spirit<; Little Theater Movement>a succession of efforts to encourage the writing and production of significant plays, as opposed to productions designed primarily for box office success<; Battle of the Books, The>a quarrel between adherents of classical and of modern writing in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries<; Industrial Revolution>the social-political-economic struggle that characterized life in England for a hundred years or more, most intensely in the last quarter of the eighteenth and first quarter of the nineteenth centuries<; Postmodern>applied to much contemporary writing, particularly with reference to the use of experimental forms, following and questioning the assumptions of modernism<; War of the Theaters>a series of quarrels among certain Elizabethan dramatists (1598-1602)<; Chartism>A British working-class movement (1838–1848) demanding political reform through the People’s Charter.<; Constructivism>A Russian avant-garde movement of the 1910s–1920s that treated art as a constructed object serving social purposes.<; Spatialism>A mid-twentieth-century experimental poetry movement that treated the page as a visual space.<; Anglo-Catholic Revival>see Oxford Movement<; Awakening, The Great>a great revival of emotional religion in America, the movement being at its height about 1740-1745 under the leadership of Jonathan Edwards<; Celtic Revival, The (Eighteenth Century)>a literary movement that, in the last half of the eighteenth century, stressed the use of the historical, literary, and mythological traditions of the ancient Celts, particularly the Welsh<; Cubist Poetry>poetry that attempts to do in verse what cubist painters do on canvas—that is, take the elements of an experience, fragment them, and then rearrange them in a meaningful new synthesis<; Formalism (Russian)>a lively and important multidisciplinary school that flourished around 1920<; Movement>new development or direction in literary activity or interest, as the Oxford movement or the free verse movement<; Imagism>see Imagists<; Vers Libre>a nineteenth-century French poetic movement to free poetry from strict rules resulted in cadenced and rhythmic poetry called vers libre, which means “free verse.<; Unanimism>a movement associated with “Jules Romains” in the first quarter of the twentieth century, emphasizing the collective spirit (unanimity) in society and even in language<; Tractarianism>the religious attitudes and principles of the founders of the Oxford movement, as set forth in the ninety Tracts for the Times (1833-1841)<

column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Paradox>a statement that although seemingly contradictory or absurd may actually be well-founded or true<; Metaphor>an analogy identifying one object with another and ascribing to the first object one or more of the qualities of the second<; Simile>a figure in which a similarity between two objects is directly expressed<; Litotes>a form of understatement in which a thing is affirmed by stating the negative of its opposite<; Metonymy>the substitution of the name of an object closely associated with a word for the word itself<; Synecdoche>a trope in which a part signifies the whole or the whole signifies the part<; Apostrophe>a figure of speech in which someone (usually but not always absent), some abstract quality, or a nonexistent personage is directly addressed as though present<; Allusion>a figure of speech that makes brief reference to a historical or literary figure, event, or object<; Onomatopoeia>words that by their sound suggest their meaning: “hiss,” “buzz,” “whirr,” “sizzle.<; Oxymoron>a self-contradictory combination of words or smaller verbal units; usually noun-noun, adjective-adjective, adjective-noun, adverb-adverb, or adverb-verb<; Conceit>a type of poetic metaphor implying ingenuity; originally, the term—cognate and almost synonymous with “concept”—implied something conceived in the mind<; Synesthesia>the concurrent response of two or more of the senses to the stimulation of one<; Ambiguity>the state of having more than one meaning, with resultant uncertainty as to the intended significance of the statement<; Imagery>the collection of images in a literary work; in another sense, synonymous with trope or figure of speech<; Euphemism>a device in which indirectness replaces directness of statement, usually in an effort to avoid offensiveness<; Irony>the recognition of a reality different from appearance<; Personification>a figure that endows animals, ideas, abstractions, and inanimate objects with human form, personality, intelligence, and emotions<; Pathetic Fallacy>a phrase coined by Ruskin to denote the tendency to credit nature with human emotions<; Kenning>a figurative phrase used in Old Germanic languages as a synonym for a simple noun<; Dead Metaphor>a figure of speech used so long that it is taken in its denotative sense only, without any conscious comparison to a physical object it once conveyed<; Antithesis>a figure of speech characterized by strongly contrasting words, clauses, sentences, or ideas<; Caesura (or Cesura)>a pause or break in a line of verse<; Understatement>a common figure of speech in which the literal sense of what is said falls detectably short of (or “under”) the magnitude of what is being talked about<; Allegory>a form of extended metaphor in which objects, persons, places, and actions in a narrative are equated with meanings outside the narrative itself<; Hypallage>a figure of speech in which an epithet is moved from the proximate to the less proximate of a group of nouns<; Controlling Image>an image or metaphor that runs throughout and determines the form or nature of a literary work<; Motif (or Motive)>a simple element that serves as a basis for expanded narrative; or, less strictly, a conventional situation, device, interest, or incident<; Double Entendre>a statement that is deliberately ambiguous, one of whose possible meanings is risqué or suggestive of some impropriety<; Diminishing Metaphor>a type of metaphor that utilizes a deliberate discrepancy of connotation between tenor and vehicle<; Metalepsis>a complex figure, also called transumption, that adds one trope or figure to another with such extreme compression that the literal sense is eclipsed or reduced to anomaly or nonsense<; Analogue>something that is analogous to or like another given thing<; Anthropomorphism>the ascription of human characteristics to nonhuman objects<; Dramatic Irony>a situation in which the words or acts of a character carry a meaning unperceived by the character but understood by the audience<; Epithet>strictly, an adjective used to point out a characteristic of a person or thing<; Symbol>something that is itself and also stands for something else<; Gigantism>Exaggeration of size or scale, especially for comic or grotesque effect.<; Discordia Concors>a term used by Samuel Johnson for “a combination of dissimilar images or discovery of occult resemblances in things apparently unlike” in metaphysical poetry<; Prosopopoeia>another name for personification<; Epic Simile>an elaborated comparison, more involved and ornate than an ordinary simile, in a conscious imitation of the Homeric manner<; Analogy>a comparison of two things, alike in certain aspects; particularly, a method used in exposition and description by which something unfamiliar is explained by being compared to something more familiar<; Mixed Figures>the incongruous mingling of one figure of speech with another immediately following<; Metaphysical Conceit>an ingenious kind of conceit widely used by the Metaphysical poets, who explored all areas of knowledge to find—in the startlingly esoteric or the shockingly commonplace—telling and unusual analogies for their ideas<; Amphibology (Amphibologia or Amphiboly)>statements capable of two different meanings—a kind of ambiguity<; Pictorialism>pictorial style, extended from painting to the other arts insofar as they are capable of representing or depicting; usually patronizing or pejorative<; Symbolism>in its broad sense, the use of one object to represent or suggest another; in literature, the serious and extensive use of symbols<; Anachronism>assignment of something to a time when it was not in existence<; Antiphrasis>irony, the satirical or humorous use of a word or phrase to convey an idea exactly opposite to its real significance<; Transumption>another name for metalepsis<; Transverse Alliteration>alliteration of the patterns abab or abba; successive or chiastic cynghanedd<; Aporia>a point of doubt and indecision<; Enantiosis>an utterance that says the opposite of what is meant; irony<; Hyperbaton>a figure of speech in which normal sentence order is transposed or rearranged in a major way<; Meiosis>intentional understatement for humorous or satiric effect<; Zoomorphism>The attribution of animal form or characteristics to humans, gods, or objects.<; Ambivalence>mutually conflicting feelings or attitudes<; Heaping Figure>the heaping up of epithets, as in the quasi-Homeric description of the Citizen in James Joyce’s Ulysses<; Leitmotif (also Leitmotiv, Leitmotive)>in art, a recurrent repetition of some word, phrase, situation, or idea<; Image>a literal and concrete representation of a sensory experience or of an object that can be known by one or more of the senses; originally, a sculptured, cast, or modeled representation of a person<; Antonomasia>a figure of speech in which a proper name is substituted for a general idea that it represents<; Figurative Language>departure from the normal order, construction, or meaning of words<; Homeric Simile>see Epic Simile<; Trope>in rhetoric, a figure of speech involving a “turn” or change of sense—the use of a word in a sense other than the literal<; Tenor>In I. A. Richards’s terms, the subject of a metaphor, to which the vehicle is compared.<; Accismus>a form of irony: a pretended refusal that is insincere or hypocritical<; Antanaclasis>a figure in which two sharply different senses of a single word are exploited<; Dysphemism>the opposite of euphemism<; Reliteralization>the process of returning a metaphorical expression to a literal meaning<; Vehicle>the immediate subject, as opposed to the ultimate or ulterior intentional subject, of a metaphor<; Synathroesmus>a piling up of items<; Ekphrasis (also Ecphrasis)>the representation of a visual or graphic work inside a literary work; sometimes used for the representation of an artwork of any kind<; Petrarchan Conceit>the kind of conceit used by Petrarch in his love sonnets and widely imitated or ridiculed by Renaissance English sonneteers<; Paradiastole>(1) Distinguishing two meanings of the same word. (2) Euphemistic replacement of a negative word with something more pleasant<; Periphrasis>an indirect, abstract, roundabout method of stating ideas; the application of the old conviction that “the longest way ’round is the shortest way home.<; Tapinosis>belittlement by (1) using a humble term such as “union card” for “doctoral degree” or (2) using exaggeration in parts of a description<; Sarcasm>a caustic and bitter expression of strong disapproval<; Equivocation>The deliberate use of ambiguous language to mislead or avoid commitment.<; Epitrope>A figure in which the speaker ironically concedes or grants permission, often to make a point.<; Spin>Slanting information to create a favorable interpretation, especially in politics and public relations.<; Catachresis>strictly, any misuse or misapplication of a word; sometimes used for a mixed figure<; Figures of Speech>the various uses of language that depart from customary construction, order, or significance<; Dieresis>a pause in a line of verse that falls at the end of a foot; now usually called caesura<; Device>a term with various archaic or poetic meanings, including a heraldic or emblematic design, the motto accompanying such a design, a fanciful invention or conceit, or something devised for dramatic presentation<; Juxtaposition>The placement of two or more things side by side, often to compare or contrast them.<; Ambages>a form of circumlocution in which the truth is spoken in a way that tends to deceive or mislead<; Bull (also Irish Bull)>a composition marked by such thoroughgoing incongruity and contradiction that it is at best ridiculous (“I hear footprints”) and at worst chaotically nonsensical<; Four Master Tropes>kenneth Burke’s designation for metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, and irony<; Hypotyposis>vivid description, especially when used for rhetorical or dramatic effect<; Irish Bull>see Bull<; Overstatement>exaggeration; hyperbole<; Reference>a direct indication of a topic or work<; Synoeceiosis, Synaeciosis, Syneciosis>associating opposite things, as in oxymoron and paradox<

column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Paradox>a statement that although seemingly contradictory or absurd may actually be well-founded or true<; Metaphor>an analogy identifying one object with another and ascribing to the first object one or more of the qualities of the second<; Simile>a figure in which a similarity between two objects is directly expressed<; Litotes>a form of understatement in which a thing is affirmed by stating the negative of its opposite<; Consonance>the relation between words in which the final consonants in the stressed syllables agree but the vowels that precede them differ<; Metonymy>the substitution of the name of an object closely associated with a word for the word itself<; Synecdoche>a trope in which a part signifies the whole or the whole signifies the part<; Assonance>generally, patterning of vowel sounds without regard to consonants<; Apostrophe>a figure of speech in which someone (usually but not always absent), some abstract quality, or a nonexistent personage is directly addressed as though present<; Zeugma>a term used in several ways, all involving a sort of “yoking”; for example, as a synonym of syllepsis, when an object-taking word has two or more objects on different levels<; Allusion>a figure of speech that makes brief reference to a historical or literary figure, event, or object<; Dissonance>harsh and inharmonious sounds; a marked breaking of the music of poetry, which may be intentional, as it often is in Browning and Hardy<; Onomatopoeia>words that by their sound suggest their meaning: “hiss,” “buzz,” “whirr,” “sizzle.<; Sigmatism>The excessive or deliberate repetition of the s sound.<; Tautology>the use of repetitious words<; Anaphora>one of the devices of repetition, in which the same expression (word or words) is repeated at the beginning of two or more lines, clauses, or sentences<; Enjambment (Enjambement)>the continuation of the sense and grammatical construction of a line on to the next verse or couplet<; Oxymoron>a self-contradictory combination of words or smaller verbal units; usually noun-noun, adjective-adjective, adjective-noun, adverb-adverb, or adverb-verb<; Alliteration>the repetition of initial identical consonant sounds or any vowel sounds in successive or closely associated syllables<; Leonine Rhyme>the internal rhyming of the last stressed syllable before the caesura, with the last stressed syllable of the line<; Conceit>a type of poetic metaphor implying ingenuity; originally, the term—cognate and almost synonymous with “concept”—implied something conceived in the mind<; Chiasmus>a pattern in which the second part is balanced against the first but with the parts reversed<; Feminine Rhyme>a rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllables are followed by an undifferentiated identical unstressed syllable<; Iamb (or Iambus)>a foot consisting of an unaccented syllable and an accented<; Trochee>a foot consisting of an accented and an unaccented syllable<; Synesthesia>the concurrent response of two or more of the senses to the stimulation of one<; Polyptoton>the repetition in close proximity of words that have the same roots<; Ambiguity>the state of having more than one meaning, with resultant uncertainty as to the intended significance of the statement<; Compound Rhyme>rhyme between primary and secondary stressed syllables<; Resonance>The quality of a work or image to evoke associations, meanings, and feelings beyond its literal content.<; Imagery>the collection of images in a literary work; in another sense, synonymous with trope or figure of speech<; Epanalepsis>the repetition at the end of a clause of a word or phrase that occurred at its beginning<; Masculine Rhyme>rhyme that falls on the stressed concluding syllables of the rhyme words<; Euphemism>a device in which indirectness replaces directness of statement, usually in an effort to avoid offensiveness<; Irony>the recognition of a reality different from appearance<; Realistic Period in American Literature, 1865-1900>the period following the Civil War, marked by the triumphant emergence of industrialism and the rise of realism<; Spondee>a foot composed of two accented syllables<; Reification>the treatment of abstractions as concrete things<; Metathesis>the interchange of position between sounds in a word<; Jacobean Age>that portion of the Renaissance during the reign of James I (1603-1625)<; Personification>a figure that endows animals, ideas, abstractions, and inanimate objects with human form, personality, intelligence, and emotions<; Romantic Period in American Literature, 1830-1865>the period between the “second revolution” of the Jacksonian Era and the close of the Civil War, which saw the testing of a nation and its development by ordeal<; Spenserian Sonnet>a sonnet of the English type in that it has three quatrains and a couplet but features quatrains joined by the use of linking rhymes: abab bcbe cdcd ee<; Anapest>a metrical foot consisting of three syllables, with two unaccented syllables followed by an accented one<; Dactyl>a foot consisting of one accented syllable followed by two unaccented<; Muckrakers>a group of American writers who between 1902 and 1911 worked to expose the dishonest methods and unscrupulous motives in big business and in city, state, and national government<; Caroline>applied in general to the age of Charles I of England (1625-1642) and in particular to the spirit of the court<; Miltonic Sonnet>a variation made by Milton on the Italian sonnet, in which the rhyme scheme is kept but the “turn” between the octave and the sestet is eliminated<; Pleonasm>the use of superfluous syllables or words<; Harangue>a vehement speech designed to arouse strong emotions<; Pathetic Fallacy>a phrase coined by Ruskin to denote the tendency to credit nature with human emotions<; Edwardian Age>the period between the death of Victoria in 1901 and the beginning of World War I in 1914, so called after Edward VII, who ruled from 1901 to 1910<; Epiphany>literally, a manifestation or showing-forth, usually of some divine being; given currency as a critical term by James Joyce<; Asyndeton>a condensed form of expression in which elements customarily joined by conjunctions are presented in series without the conjunctions<; Boustrophedon>running alternately from left to right and from right to left; a term—literally, “ox plowing”—that describes the direction of writing in certain ancient inscriptions<; Italian Sonnet>a sonnet divided into an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet rhyming cdecde<; Satanic School>southey’s phrase (1821) for the literary group of Byron, Shelley, Hunt, and others, whose irregular lives and radical ideas suggested the term<; Soliloquy>a speech delivered while the speaker is alone (solus), calculated to inform the audience of what is passing in the character’s mind<; Kenning>a figurative phrase used in Old Germanic languages as a synonym for a simple noun<; Inversion>the placing of a sentence element out of its normal position<; Period of Confession and Postmodernism in American Literature, 1960—>the period beginning in the 1960s, a time of uncertainty, revolt, and cynicism in America and a strong turning inward of many American writers<; Rhyme>identity of terminal sound between accented syllables, usually occupying corresponding positions in two or more lines of verse<; Truncation>in metrics, the omission of a syllable or syllables at the beginning or end of a line<; Spasmodic School>a phrase applied by W. E. Aytoun in 1854 to a group of contemporary English poets<; Augustan>specifically refers to the age of the Emperor Augustus of Rome; by analogy, applied to other epochs when literary culture was high, such as the Augustan Age of English letters<; Aside>a dramatic convention by which an actor directly addresses the audience but is not supposed to be heard by the other actors on the stage<; Parnassians>a group of nineteenth-century French poets, so called from their journal Parnasse contemporain<; Agrarians>literally people living in an agricultural society or espousing its merits; in literary history, usually a group of Southern American writers who published The Fugitive (1922-1925)<; Pyrrhic>a foot of two unaccented syllables<; Terza rima>a three-line stanza, supposedly devised by Dante (for his Divine Comedy) with rhyme scheme aba bcb cdc ded and so forth<; Allonym>the name of an actual person other than the author that is signed by the author to a work<; Barbarism>a mistake in the form of a word or a word that results from such a mistake<; Lost Generation>a group of American writers, born around 1900, who served in the First World War and reacted against certain tendencies of older writers in the 1920s<; Pun>a play on words based on the similarity of sound between two words with different meanings<; Eye Rhyme>rhyme that appears correct from the spelling but is not so from the pronunciation<; Epistolary Novel>a novel in which the narrative is carried forward by letters written by one or more of the characters<; Polysyndeton>the use of more conjunctions than is normal<; Sonnet>a poem almost invariably of fourteen lines and following one of several set rhyme schemes<; Syllepsis>a grammatically correct construction in which one word is placed in the same grammatical relationship to two words but in quite different senses<; Dead Metaphor>a figure of speech used so long that it is taken in its denotative sense only, without any conscious comparison to a physical object it once conveyed<; Objective Correlative>t. S. Eliot’s term for a pattern of objects, actions, or events or a situation that can serve effectively to awaken in the reader an emotional response without being a direct statement of that subjective emotion<; Cockney School>a derogatory title applied by Blackwood’s Magazine to a group of nineteenth-century writers—including William Hazlitt, Leigh Hunt, and John Keats—because of their alleged poor taste in such matters as diction and rhyme<; Meliorism>the belief—widely held in the nineteenth century—that society has an innate tendency toward improvement and that that tendency can be furthered by conscious human effort<; In Medias Res>a term from Horace, literally “in or into the middle parts of things,” applied to the technique of opening a story in the middle of the action<; Pantoum>the pantoum may consist of any number of four-line stanzas, but in any case, the second and fourth lines of one stanza must reappear as the first and third lines of the following stanza<; Volta>the turn in thought—from question to answer; problem to solution—that occurs at the beginning of the sestet in the Italian sonnet<; Shakespearean Sonnet>the English sonnet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Eponym>A person from whose name the name of a thing, place, or term is derived.<; Aestheticism>a nineteenth-century literary movement that rested on the credo of “art for art’s sake.<; Colonial Period in American Literature, 1607-1765>the period from the founding of Jamestown to the Stamp Act in 1765, when the writing produced in America was generally utilitarian, polemical, or religious<; Hartford Wits>a group of Connecticut writers, active around the period of the American Revolution<; Haiku>a form of Japanese poetry that states—in three lines of five, seven, and five syllables—a clear picture designed to arouse a distinct emotion and suggest a specific spiritual insight<; Symploce>a figure of speech combining anaphora and epistrophe: the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses and of another at their end<; Antithesis>a figure of speech characterized by strongly contrasting words, clauses, sentences, or ideas<; Ballad>a form of verse to be sung or recited and characterized by its presentation of an exciting episode in narrative or dramatic form<; Caesura (or Cesura)>a pause or break in a line of verse<; Fugitives, The>a group associated with Vanderbilt University, which in the 1920s published the magazine The Fugitive<; Elision>the omission of part of a word<; Malapropism>an inappropriateness of speech resulting from the use of one word for another, which resembles it<; New York School>a group of American poets who flourished between 1950 and 1970, distinguished by urbanity, wit, learning, spontaneity, and exuberance<; Rondeau>a set French verse pattern; artificial but very popular with many English poets<; Spoonerism>an accidental interchange of sounds—usually the initial consonants—in two or more words<; Broken Rhyme>the breaking of a word at the end of a line for the sake of a rhyme<; Blank Verse>unrhymed but otherwise regular verse—usually iambic pentameter<; Lake Poets and Lake School>coleridge, Wordsworth, and Southey—three poets who at the beginning of the nineteenth century were living in the Lake District of northwest England (Cumbria and Lancashire)<; Knickerbocker Group>a New York group of writers during the first half of the nineteenth century, named after Washington Irving’s Knickerbocker’s History of New York<; Pastoral>a poetic treatment of shepherds and rustic life, after the Latin for “shepherd”: pastor<; Senryu>a form with the same structure as the haiku—seventeen syllables in lines of five, seven, and five—but relying on humor or satire rather than conventions related to the seasons<; Understatement>a common figure of speech in which the literal sense of what is said falls detectably short of (or “under”) the magnitude of what is being talked about<; Romantic Period in English Literature, 1798-1870>in the period between the publication of Lyrical Ballads (1798) and the death of Dickens, English literature was dominated by romanticism<; Carpe Diem>“Seize the day”; a phrase used by Horace and applied to literature, especially lyric poems, that exemplifies the spirit of “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.<; Ubi Sunt Formula>a convention much used in verse, rhetorically asking “where are those who were before us?” (ubi sunt qui ante nos fuerunt?<; Affective Fallacy>the judging of a work of art in terms of its results, especially its emotional effect<; English Sonnet>a sonnet consisting of three quatrains followed by a couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Free Verse>vers libre; verse that is relatively free, managing without rhyme, meter, or regular rhythm<; Heteromerous Rhyme>a fairly rare species of multiple rhyme (also called “mosaic”) in which typically one word is forced into a rhyme with two or more words<; Pre-Raphaelitism>the movement begun in 1848 by the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Holman-Hunt, John Everett Millais, and others as a protest against the conventional methods of painting<; Novel of Manners>a novel dominated by social customs, manners, conventions, and habits of a definite social class<; Tetrameter>a line consisting of four feet<; Transcendentalism>a reliance on the intuition and the conscience—a form of idealism; a philosophical romanticism reaching America a generation or two after it developed in Europe<; Surrealism>a movement in art emphasizing the expression of the imagination as realized in dreams and presented without conscious control<; Run-on Lines>the carrying over of grammatical structure from one line to the next<; Allegory>a form of extended metaphor in which objects, persons, places, and actions in a narrative are equated with meanings outside the narrative itself<; Elegy>a sustained formal poem setting forth meditations on death or another solemn theme<; Limerick>a form of light verse that follows a definite pattern: five anapestic lines of which the first, second, and fifth, consisting of three feet, rhyme; and the third and fourth lines, consisting of two feet, rhyme<; Hypallage>a figure of speech in which an epithet is moved from the proximate to the less proximate of a group of nouns<; Aubade>a lyric about dawn or a morning serenade—a song of lovers parting at dawn<; Caudate Sonnet>an Italian form, rarely adopted into English, in which a standard fourteen-line sonnet is augmented by the addition of other lines, including “tails.<; Martian School (or Martians)>a school of British poets born in the 1940s—so labeled by James Fenton after Craig Raine’s A Martian Sends a Postcard Home (1979)—who struggle to see the world afresh, as might a visitor from Mars<; Jeremiad>a work that foretells destruction because of the evil of a group<; Putative Author>the fictional author of a work, supposedly written by someone other than its actual author<; Peripety (or Peripeteia)>the reversal of fortune for a protagonist—possibly either a fall, as in a tragedy, or a success, as in a comedy<; Restoration Age>the literary period embracing the latter part of the seventeenth century, named for the restoration of the Stuarts in 1660<; Abridgment>a shortened version of a work but one that attempts to preserve essential elements<; Chrestomathy>a collection of choice passages to be used in the study of a language or a literature and, thus, a kind of anthology<; Climax>a rising order of importance in the ideas expressed<; Controlling Image>an image or metaphor that runs throughout and determines the form or nature of a literary work<; Harlem Renaissance>the first major, self-conscious literary movement of African-American writers, although there had been much black writing in America earlier<; Naturalistic and Symbolistic Period in American Literature>the period between 1900 and 1930 in America, divided by World War I into a part dominated by naturalism and a part marked by growing international awareness and symbolism<; Philistinism>the worship of material and mechanical prosperity and the disregard of culture, beauty, and spirit<; Revolutionary and Early National Period in American Literature, 1765-1830>the period of the establishment of the new nation, ending with the “second revolution” represented by the ascendancy of Jacksonian democracy<; Cacophony>the opposite of euphony; a harsh, unpleasant combination of sounds<; Catharsis>aristotle’s term, in the Poetics, for the “proper purgation” of pity and fear effected by tragedy<; Madrigal>a short lyric, usually dealing with love or a pastoral theme and designed for—or at least suitable for—a musical setting<; Mimesis>the Greek for imitation, often used specifically to indicate Aristotle’s theory of imitation<; Pentameter>a line of verse of five feet<; Renaissance>the period of transition from the medieval to the modern world in Western Europe; the word means “rebirth.<; Slant Rhyme>near rhyme; usually the substitution of assonance or consonance for true rhyme<; Burlesque>a form of comedy characterized by ridiculous exaggeration and distortion, marked by a discrepancy between subject matter and style<; Chiaroscuro>contrasting light and shade<; Gongorism>a highly affected style taking its name from the Spanish poet Luis de Góngora y Argote (1561-1627), whose writings exhibited stylistic extravagances<; Legend>a narrative or tradition handed down from the past; distinguished from a myth by having more of historical truth and perhaps less of the supernatural<; Syzygy>in classical prosody, a term for two coupled feet serving as a unit<; Aesthetic Distance>the effect produced when an emotion or an experience—whether autobiographical or not—is so objectified that it can be understood as being independent of the immediate experience of its maker<; Didacticism>instructiveness in a work, one purpose of which is to give guidance, particularly in moral, ethical, or religious matters<; Hedonism>a doctrine that pleasure is the chief good of human beings<; Heteroglossia>“Different tongues” or “different speech”; a term introduced by Mikhail Bakhtin to designate the presence of more than one voice in a given narrative or another work<; Internal Rhyme>rhyme that occurs at some place before the last syllables in a line<; Realistic Period in English Literature, 1870-1914>the period in which the reaction to romanticism reached its peak in full-fledged realism, in the latter portion of Victoria’s reign and the reign of Edward VII<; Pseudonym>a false name sometimes assumed by writers and others<; Rhopalic>a sequence that “thickens” as it moves toward its end, with each word a syllable longer than the preceding one<; Victorian>a term used (1) to designate broadly the literature written during the reign of Queen Victoria (1837-1901); and (2) to suggest a certain complacency, hypocrisy, or squeamishness assumed to characterize Victorian attitudes<; Transferred Epithet>an adjective used to limit a noun that it really does not logically modify<; Tanka>a type of Japanese poetry similar to the haiku<; Anadiplosis>a kind of repetition in which the last word or phrase of one sentence or line is repeated at the beginning of the next<; Beat Generation>a group of American poets and novelists of the 1950s and 1960s in rebellion against the prevailing culture<; Clerihew>a form of light verse invented by and named for Edmund Clerihew Bentley (1875-1956), who also wrote detective fiction<; Motif (or Motive)>a simple element that serves as a basis for expanded narrative; or, less strictly, a conventional situation, device, interest, or incident<; Metafiction>a work of fiction, a major concern of which is the nature of fiction itself<; Neoclassic Period>the period in English literature between the return of the Stuarts to the English throne in 1660 and the publication of Lyrical Ballads by Wordsworth and Coleridge in 1798<; Identical Rhyme>a phenomenon, also called redundant rhyme or rime riche, in which a syllable both begins and ends in the same way as a rhyming syllable, without being the same word<; Hiatus>a pause or break between two vowel sounds not separated by a consonant<; Vorticism>a movement in modern poetry, originating in 1914 with Wyndham Lewis, related to certain abstract developments in painting and sculpture<; Scriblerus Club>a club organized in London in 1714 by Jonathan Swift to satirize literary incompetence<; Verbum Infans Formula>a conventional paradoxical topos, meaning “the unspeaking word,” applied to the infant (infans, “not speaking”) Christ, who incarnates the Word (verbum)<; Memento Mori>A reminder of death, such as a skull, used to encourage reflection on mortality.<; Black Mountain School>certain writers—Charles Olson, Robert Creeley, and Robert Duncan among them—associated with Black Mountain College, an experimental school in North Carolina<; End-Stopped Lines>lines in which both the grammatical structure and the sense reach completion at the end<; “Graveyard School”>a group of eighteenth-century poets who wrote long poems on death and immortality<; Exposition>one of the four chief types of composition, with the others being argumentation, description, and narration; its purpose is to explain something<; Epigram>a pithy saying, often antithetical; also a short poem characterized by compression, balance, and polish<; Elizabethan Age>the segment of the Renaissance during the reign of Elizabeth I (1558-1603)<; Early Tudor Age, 1500-1557>the period in which the ideals of the Renaissance were rapidly replacing those of the Middle Ages, marked by the reformation of the English church and the revival of learning known as Humanism<; Equivoque>a kind of pun in which language is so used that it has two different but appropriate meanings<; Dramatic Monologue>a poem that reveals “a soul in action” through the speech of one character in a dramatic situation<; Humanism>broadly, any attitude that tends to exalt the human element, as opposed to the supernatural, divine elements—or as opposed to the grosser, animal elements<; Reduplication>(1) The rhetorical repetition of a word or phrase; (2) repetition of material in a syllable, common for diminutives or nicknames<; Ploce>a kind of repetition whereby different forms and senses of a word are “woven” through an utterance<; Reversal>the change in fortune for a protagonist<; Novel of Character>a novel that emphasizes character rather than exciting episode<; Early Victorian Age, 1832-1870>a time of the gradual tempering of the romantic impulse and the steady growth of realism<; Heteronym>a word spelled the same as another but pronounced and defined differently<; Villanelle>a fixed nineteen-line form, originally French, employing only two rhymes and repeating two of the lines according to a set pattern<; Satire>a work or manner that blends a censorious attitude with humor and wit for improving human institutions or humanity<; Exegesis>an explanation and interpretation of a text<; Merism>generally, a repetition of parts; specifically, the use of a pair of opposites to mean a whole<; Kabuki>a popular form of theater in Japan since the mid-seventeenth century<; Rhetorical Accent>the accent determined by the meaning or intention of the sentence; used in metrics in opposition to metrical accent, in which only the prosodic pattern of the line determines the placement of stress<; Solecism>a violation of prescriptive grammatical rules<; Acrostic>a composition, usually verse, arranged in such a way that it spells words, phrases, or sentences when certain letters are selected according to an orderly sequence<; Angry Young Men>a group of British writers in the 1950s and 1960s who demonstrated a particular bitterness in their attacks on outmoded, bourgeois values<; Digression>the insertion of material often not closely related to the subject in a work<; Euphony>pleasing sounds; the opposite of cacophony<; Double Entendre>a statement that is deliberately ambiguous, one of whose possible meanings is risqué or suggestive of some impropriety<; Late Victorian Age, 1870-1901>the period between 1870 and the death of Queen Victoria, which saw the full flowering of the movement toward realism<; Parenthesis>an explanatory remark inside a statement and frequently separated from it by parentheses ( )<; Picaresque Novel>a chronicle—usually autobiographical—presenting the life story of a rascal of low degree engaged in menial tasks and making his living more through his wits than his industry<; Petrarchan Sonnet>the Italian sonnet<; Parallelism>such an arrangement that one element of equal importance with another is similarly developed and phrased<; Typology>the study of allegorical symbols, especially with the Bible, in which much of the Old Testament is read as a type of the revelation to come in the New Testament<; Anglo-Italian Sonnet>a sonnet combining the rhyme schemes of the English sonnet (ababcdcdefefgg) and the Italian sonnet (abbaabbacdecde), most often with an octave from the former and a sestet from the latter<; Bloomsbury Group>a group of writers and thinkers, many of whom lived in Bloomsbury, a residential district near central London<; Carmen Figuratum>a figure poem, one so written that the form of the printed words suggests the subject matter<; Commonwealth (or Puritan) Interregnum>the period between the execution of Charles I in 1649 and the restoration of the monarchy in 1660, during which England was ruled by Parliament under the control of Oliver Cromwell<; Existentialism>a group of attitudes, current during and after World War II, that emphasizes existence rather than essence and sees the inadequacy of human reason to explain the enigma of the universe<; Geneva School>a group of critics, including Georges Poulet, Marcel Raymond, Albert Béguin, and the early J. Hillis Miller, who see a literary work as a series of existential expressions of the author’s individual consciousness<; Modernist Period in English Literature>the period in England beginning with World War I in 1914, marked by the flowering of talent and experiment in the twenties, and ending around 1965<; Neologism (or Neology)>a new word introduced into a language, especially for enhancing style<; Homeoteleuton>sameness or similarity of endings of consecutive words or words near each other—often considered unsettling or graceless but sometimes unavoidable<; Parataxis>an arrangement of sentences, clauses, phrases, or words in coordinate rather than subordinate constructions, often without connectives<; Tragicomedy>a play that employs a plot suitable to tragedy but ends happily, like a comedy<; Amphigory (or Amphigouri)>verse that sounds well but contains little or no sense or meaning; either nonsense verse or nonsensical parody<; Archaism>obsolete phrasing, idiom, syntax, or spelling<; Bathos>the effect resulting from the unsuccessful effort to achieve dignity or sublimity of style; an unintentional anticlimax, dropping from the sublime to the ridiculous<; Fleshly School of Poetry, The>a critical essay by Robert W. Buchanan (as “Thomas Maitland”) in the Contemporary Review, October 1871, attacking Swinburne, Morris, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti<; Hubris>overweening pride or insolence that results in the misfortune of the protagonist of a tragedy<; Naturalism>the application of principles of scientific determinism to literature; a term best reserved for a literary movement in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries<; Tagline>(1) Punchline. (2) Material placed under a document or illustration; a caption. (3) Matter printed under a headline to amplify a main point<; Triolet>one of the simpler French verse forms, consisting of eight lines with only two rhymes, the first two lines being repeated as the last two and the first line recurring also as the fourth<; Prolepsis>A flash-forward; the anticipation of a future event as if it had already happened.<; Transcendental Club>An informal group of New England Transcendentalists who met from 1836 to about 1840.<; Curtal Sonnet>gerard Manley Hopkins’s name for a sonnet that has been curtailed<; Eulogy>a dignified, formal speech or form of writing that praises a person or a thing<; Deus (or Dea) ex Machina>the employment of some unexpected and improbable incident to make things turn out right<; Great Awakening, The>see Awakening, the Great<; Encomium>in Greek literature, a composition in praise of a living person, object, or event—but not a god—delivered before a special audience<; Dialectic>in the broadest sense, simply the art of argumentation or debate; in classical literature, the tradition of continuing debate or discussion of eternally unresolved issues<; Intentional Fallacy>the judging of the meaning or success of a work of art by the author’s expressed or ostensible intention in producing it<; Minimalism>a modern movement in politics, economics, and all the arts, especially noticeable in architecture (Mies van der Rohe: “Less is more”) and music (for example, the works of Anton Webern)<; Kailyard School>a group of Scottish writers whose work dealt idealistically with village life in Scotland<; Paean>a song of praise or joy; originally, an ode sung by a Greek chorus in honor of Apollo<; Syncope>a cutting short of words through the omission of a letter or a syllable<; Xenoglossia (also Xenoglossia, Xenolalia)>the intelligible use of a foreign language that one does not know<; Perfect Rhyme (or True Rhyme)>Rhyme in which the stressed vowels and all following sounds are identical, while the preceding consonants differ.<; Bildungsroman>a novel that deals with the development of a young person, usually from adolescence to maturity; it is frequently autobiographical<; Bluestockings>women of pronounced intellectual interests<; Flat Character>e. M. Forster’s term for a character constructed around a single idea or quality<; Diminishing Metaphor>a type of metaphor that utilizes a deliberate discrepancy of connotation between tenor and vehicle<; Denotation>the basic meaning of a word, independent of its emotional coloration or associations<; Mosaic>another name for heteromerous rhyme<; Metalepsis>a complex figure, also called transumption, that adds one trope or figure to another with such extreme compression that the literal sense is eclipsed or reduced to anomaly or nonsense<; Masque>a spectacle characterized by a procession of masked figures, developed from medieval disguisings or mummings and adopted by the aristocracy<; Rime Riche>words with identical sounds but different meanings<; Persona>literally, a mask; a “second self” created by an author and through whom the narrative is told<; Novel of Incident>a novel in which episodic action dominates and plot and character are subordinate<; Ode>a single, unified strain of exalted lyrical verse, directed to a single purpose, and dealing with one theme<; Tableau>an interlude in which the actors freeze in position and then resume action as before or hold their positions until the curtain falls<; Theme>a central idea; in nonfiction, the general topic of discussion; in poetry, fiction, and drama, the abstract concept made concrete through representation<; Syncopation>a musical term used for the effect produced by a temporary displacing or shifting of the regular beat<; Round Character>a term used by E. M. Forster for a character sufficiently complex to be able to surprise the reader without losing credibility<; Analogue>something that is analogous to or like another given thing<; Anecdote>a short narrative detailing particulars of an interesting episode or event<; Anthropomorphism>the ascription of human characteristics to nonhuman objects<; Braggadocio>a noisy braggart who is actually a coward<; Cliché>any expression so often used that its freshness and clarity have worn off; from the French word for a stereotype plate<; Hagiography>writing about saints; by extension, a biography that praises the virtues of its subject<; Fireside Poets>a group of poets devoted to providing intellectual and moral education for the new generation of literates produced by free public education in the nineteenth century<; Dandyism>a literary style used by the English and French decadent writers of the last quarter of the nineteenth century, marked by excessively refined emotion and preciosity of language<; Flyting>an extended and vigorous verbal exchange<; Gasconade>bravado or boastful talk, because Gascons were considered inveterate boasters<; Federalist Age in American Literature>the period between the formation of the national government and the “Second Revolution” of Jacksonian Democracy<; Literary Club, The (also Doctor Johnson’s Circle)>a club formed in London in 1764 at the suggestion of Sir Joshua Reynolds, the painter, and with the cooperation of Samuel Johnson<; Liminality>the state of being on a threshold in space or time<; Mythopoeia>myth-making, construed as either an individual function of a single artist or a collective spirit<; Manga>a style of comic book or graphic novel, originally Japanese, typically presenting a story of fantasy, science fiction, or romance, with drawings in panels or strips<; Idiom>a use of words peculiar to a given language; an expression that cannot be translated literally<; Rebus>a text in which ordinary verbal symbols are supplemented by pictures and other devices to suggest a total meaning<; Parody>a composition imitating another—usually serious—piece<; Postmodernist Period in English Literature, 1965—>the period of English literature beginning around 1965, in which the characteristics of the 1950s continued and were accentuated<; Static Character>a character who changes little if at all<; Roman à Clef>a novel in which actual persons are presented under the guise of fiction<; Shaped Verse>a poem so constructed that its printed form suggests its subject matter<; Stichomythia>a form of repartee developed in classical drama and often employed by Elizabethan writers, especially those imitating the Senecan tragedies<; Animism>The attribution of a living soul or spirit to inanimate objects, plants, and natural forces.<; Assonance Rhyme>assonance is a common substitution for end rhyme in the popular ballad<; Connotation>the emotional implications and associations that words may carry, as distinguished from their denotative meanings<; Dirge>a wailing song sung at a funeral or in commemoration of death; a short lyric of lamentation<; Freytag’s Pyramid>a diagram of the structure of a five-act tragedy, given by Gustav Freytag in Technik des Dramas (1863)<; Foreshadowing>the presentation of material in a work in such a way that later events are prepared for<; Great Chain of Being>the belief that everything partakes of a hierarchical system, extending upward from inanimate matter to living things, to the rational human being, to angels, and finally to God<; Echo Verse>poetry in which the closing syllables of one line are repeated, as by an echo, in the following line with a different meaning, forming a reply or a comment<; Invocation>an address to a deity for aid<; Lollards>the followers of John Wycliffe, who inspired a popular religious reform movement in England late in the fourteenth century<; Hexameter>a line of six feet; in Latin or Greek, the conventional medium for epic and didactic poetry<; Macaronic>(1) Pejoratively, “a blockhead” or “a dandy.” (2) Writing that combines two or more languages<; Parable>an illustrative story teaching a lesson<; Rhetorical Question>a question propounded for its rhetorical effect and not requiring a reply or intended to induce a reply<; Redende Name>german, “speaking name”; a name that is significant<; Wellerism>a type of expression, named for Dickens’s Sam and Tony Weller, with three parts: an utterance, a speaker, and a situation<

column4: Synesthesia>the concurrent response of two or more of the senses to the stimulation of one<; Reification>the treatment of abstractions as concrete things<; Gongorism>a highly affected style taking its name from the Spanish poet Luis de Góngora y Argote (1561-1627), whose writings exhibited stylistic extravagances<; Aesthetic Distance>the effect produced when an emotion or an experience—whether autobiographical or not—is so objectified that it can be understood as being independent of the immediate experience of its maker<; Bathos>the effect resulting from the unsuccessful effort to achieve dignity or sublimity of style; an unintentional anticlimax, dropping from the sublime to the ridiculous<; Dandyism>a literary style used by the English and French decadent writers of the last quarter of the nineteenth century, marked by excessively refined emotion and preciosity of language<; Gothic>originally the Goths, a single Germanic tribe, but broadened to mean Teutonic or Germanic and, later, “medieval” in general<; Marinism>An ornate, extravagant poetic style of conceits and wordplay, after the Italian poet Giambattista Marino.<; Pictorialism>pictorial style, extended from painting to the other arts insofar as they are capable of representing or depicting; usually patronizing or pejorative<; Euphuism>an affected style that flourished late in the sixteenth century in England, especially in court circles<; Grotesque>any decorative art characterized by fantastic representations of human and animal forms often combined into formal distortions of the natural to the point of absurdity, ugliness, or caricature<; Macabre>a gruesome combination of farce and tragedy, as in the danse macabre or Dance of Death<; Purple Patch>a piece of notably fine writing<; Plain Style>the simplest of the three classical types of style; the others are the high and the middle<; Subjectivity>the quality of originating and existing in the mind of a perceiving subject and not necessarily corresponding to any object outside that mind<; Tone (or Tone Color)>the attitudes toward the subject and toward the audience implied in a literary work; also a musical quality in language<; Objectivity>a quality in an artwork of impersonality and freedom from the expression of personal sentiments, attitudes, or emotions by the author<; Doric>simple; applied to a rustic of “broad” dialect or to simple idyllic pieces of literature, after the Doric dialect of ancient Greece, thought of as lacking in refinement<; Baroque>a term applied first to the architectural style that flourished in Europe from the late sixteenth century until well into the eighteenth century<; Restraint>writing which holds in decent check the emotional elements of a given situation<; Pindarism>generally, following the practice of Pindar; specifically, lapsing into exaggerated enthusiasm—in a manner associated with Pindar<; Flosculation>Florid or flowery language; ornate style.<; Polyphonic Prose>Prose that uses the devices of poetry, such as rhyme, meter, and alliteration.<; Artificiality>a term used to characterize a work that is consciously and deliberately mannered, affected, elaborate, conventional, studied, or self-conscious<; Attic Salt>writing distinguished by its classic refinement, its intellectual sharpness, and its elegant but stinging wit; salt in this sense means “wit.<; Asterism>urbane humor, marked by subtle irony and polite mockery<; Demotic Style>a term applied by Northrop Frye to a style shaped by the diction, rhythms, syntax, and associations of ordinary speech<; Mood>in a literary work, the mood is the emotional-intellectual attitude of the author toward the subject<; Sesquipedalian>used for a style unduly and pretentiously polysyllabic; literally, “a foot and a half.<; Sentimentality>the effort to induce an emotional response disproportionate to the situation and thus to substitute heightened and generally unthinking feeling for normal ethical and intellectual judgment<; Wardour-Street English>a style strongly marked by archaisms; an insincere, artificial expression<; Sublime>characterized by nobility and grandeur, impressive, exalted, raised above ordinary human qualities—these were asserted to be the essential qualities of great art in the treatise On the Sublime by Longinus (A.D. 50)<; Style>the manner of expression, combining two elements: the idea to be expressed and the individuality of the author<; Alliterative Prose>a medieval tradition of giving dignity to prose by adding prosodic devices from alliterative verse<; Attic>writing characterized by a clear, simple, polished, and witty style<; Fustian>a derogatory term for overblown diction; originally, a coarse, cotton cloth dyed to resemble velveteen<; Grand Style, The>a concept, traceable back to Longinus, involving a host of lofty elements: nobility of character, sublimity of conception, dignified simplicity or severity of utterance, and grandeur of scope<; Mannerism>a highly affected style that was fashionable in the graphic arts around the turn of the sixteenth century, roughly contemporary with gongorism and marinism in literature<; Hieratic Style>a self-consciously formal and elaborate style, in contrast to the demotic (Northrop Frye); literally “priestly,” originally applied to a conventionalized style of ancient Egyptian writing<; Prose>in its broadest sense, the term is applied to all forms of written or spoken expression not having a regular rhythmic pattern<; Poetic Diction>language chosen for a supposedly inherent poetic quality<; Period Style>literary manners, especially in poetry, that distinguish a given period<; Prose Rhythm>the recurrence of stress and emphasis at irregular intervals, affording a pleasurable rise and fall<; Picturesque>a word applied to certain kinds of writing by analogy to a type of painting that sought a middle ground between the sublime and the beautiful<; Treatment>(1) General manner or style in handling a subject. (2) In film, a preliminary sketch of a screenplay or adaptation<; Subjective>something expressive in a personal manner of inward convictions, beliefs, dreams, or ideals<; Stylistics>the formal and objective study of style<; Slice of Life>the unselective and non-evaluative presentation of a segment of life<; Sensual and Sensuous>sensuous characterizes writing that plays fully on the various senses of the reader; sensual implies writing that is fleshly or carnal<; Whimsical>a general term characterizing writing that is fanciful, odd, eccentric<
