column4: Surrealism>a movement in art emphasizing the expression of the imagination as realized in dreams and presented without conscious control<; Philistinism>the worship of material and mechanical prosperity and the disregard of culture, beauty, and spirit<; Didacticism>instructiveness in a work, one purpose of which is to give guidance, particularly in moral, ethical, or religious matters<; Existentialism>a group of attitudes, current during and after World War II, that emphasizes existence rather than essence and sees the inadequacy of human reason to explain the enigma of the universe<; Naturalism>the application of principles of scientific determinism to literature; a term best reserved for a literary movement in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries<; Minimalism>a modern movement in politics, economics, and all the arts, especially noticeable in architecture (Mies van der Rohe: “Less is more”) and music (for example, the works of Anton Webern)<; Sentimentalism>(1) An overindulgence in emotion, especially the conscious effort to induce emotion in order to enjoy it; (2) an optimistic overemphasis of the goodness of humanity<; Expressionism>a movement affecting painting and literature, which followed and went beyond impressionism in its efforts to “objectify inner experience.<; Regionalism>fidelity to a particular geographical area; the representation of its habits, speech, manners, history, folklore, or beliefs<; Local Color Writing>writing that exploits the speech, dress, mannerisms, habits of thought, and topography peculiar to a certain region, primarily for the portrayal of the life of a geographical setting<; Impressionism>a highly personal manner of writing in which the author presents materials as they appear to an individual temperament at a precise moment rather than as they are presumed to be in actuality<; Provincialism>a word, phrase, or manner of expression peculiar to a special region and not commonly used outside that region—therefore, not fashionable or sophisticated<; Byronism>the qualities associated with Lord Byron (1788-1824), whose unique electricity provoked the coining of such terms as “Byronic,” “Byroniad,” and “Byronism.<; Symbolism>in its broad sense, the use of one object to represent or suggest another; in literature, the serious and extensive use of symbols<; Structuralism>an intellectual movement utilizing the methods of structural linguistics and structural anthropology<; Historicism>a set of concepts about works of literature and their relationships to the social and cultural contexts in which they were produced<; Realism>in the broadest literary sense, fidelity to actuality in its representation; more precisely, the nineteenth-century movement centered in the novel<; Classicism>a body of doctrine thought to be derived from or to reflect the qualities of ancient Greek and Roman culture, including restraint, restricted scope, and dominance of reason<; Cynicism>doubt of the generally accepted standards or of the innate goodness of human action<; Neoclassicism>the classicism that dominated English literature in the Restoration age and in the eighteenth century<; Modernism>A broad movement in the arts (about 1890–1940) marked by a deliberate break with traditional forms and experimentation with new ones.<; Rationalism>The view that reason, not experience or revelation, is the chief source of knowledge.<; Romanticism>a movement of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that marked the reaction in literature, philosophy, art, religion, and politics from the neoclassicism and formal orthodoxy of the preceding period<; Magic Realism (or Magical Realism)>an international tendency in the graphic and literary arts in which contrasting elements—such as the supernatural, myth, dream, fantasy—invade a conventionally realistic surface<; Feudalism>the system of social and political organization that prevailed in Western Europe during much of the medieval period<; Orientalism>a quality of thought or expression associated with the Orient, the East, or Asia and sometimes even including Israel and Greece<; Postmodernism>A late twentieth-century movement marked by skepticism toward grand narratives, irony, pastiche, and self-reflexivity.<; Pooterism>Self-important, petty, and pompous behavior, after Charles Pooter in The Diary of a Nobody.<; Absurd>in contemporary literature and criticism, a term applied to the sense that human beings—cut off from their roots—live in meaningless isolation in an alien universe<; New Formalism (or Neoformalism)>a movement in verse writing, so named around 1980, concerned with the production of verse with recognizable rhythms, meters, rhymes, stanza patterns, and structures<; Postmodern>applied to much contemporary writing, particularly with reference to the use of experimental forms, following and questioning the assumptions of modernism<; Sentimentality>the effort to induce an emotional response disproportionate to the situation and thus to substitute heightened and generally unthinking feeling for normal ethical and intellectual judgment<; Antitheism>Active opposition to theism or to belief in a god.<; Atheism>Disbelief in or lack of belief in the existence of a god or gods.<; Altruism>Selfless concern for the welfare of others.<; Egoism>The view that self-interest is the proper motive or basis of conduct; excessive concern with oneself.<; Empiricism>The view that knowledge comes chiefly from sense experience.<; Individualism>The view that emphasizes the moral worth, independence, and self-reliance of the individual.<; Critical Realism>realistic fiction in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, particularly in America<; Genteel Tradition>a tradition of conventional correctness in American writing in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries<; Modern>having to do with recent times and the present day; in a narrow sense, more or less synonymous with “modernist.<; Sensibility>a reliance on feelings as guides to truth and not on reason and law<

column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Paradox>a statement that although seemingly contradictory or absurd may actually be well-founded or true<; Metaphor>an analogy identifying one object with another and ascribing to the first object one or more of the qualities of the second<; Simile>a figure in which a similarity between two objects is directly expressed<; Litotes>a form of understatement in which a thing is affirmed by stating the negative of its opposite<; Consonance>the relation between words in which the final consonants in the stressed syllables agree but the vowels that precede them differ<; Metonymy>the substitution of the name of an object closely associated with a word for the word itself<; Synecdoche>a trope in which a part signifies the whole or the whole signifies the part<; Assonance>generally, patterning of vowel sounds without regard to consonants<; Apostrophe>a figure of speech in which someone (usually but not always absent), some abstract quality, or a nonexistent personage is directly addressed as though present<; Zeugma>a term used in several ways, all involving a sort of “yoking”; for example, as a synonym of syllepsis, when an object-taking word has two or more objects on different levels<; Allusion>a figure of speech that makes brief reference to a historical or literary figure, event, or object<; Dissonance>harsh and inharmonious sounds; a marked breaking of the music of poetry, which may be intentional, as it often is in Browning and Hardy<; Onomatopoeia>words that by their sound suggest their meaning: “hiss,” “buzz,” “whirr,” “sizzle.<; Sigmatism>The excessive or deliberate repetition of the s sound.<; Tautology>the use of repetitious words<; Anaphora>one of the devices of repetition, in which the same expression (word or words) is repeated at the beginning of two or more lines, clauses, or sentences<; Enjambment (Enjambement)>the continuation of the sense and grammatical construction of a line on to the next verse or couplet<; Oxymoron>a self-contradictory combination of words or smaller verbal units; usually noun-noun, adjective-adjective, adjective-noun, adverb-adverb, or adverb-verb<; Alliteration>the repetition of initial identical consonant sounds or any vowel sounds in successive or closely associated syllables<; Leonine Rhyme>the internal rhyming of the last stressed syllable before the caesura, with the last stressed syllable of the line<; Conceit>a type of poetic metaphor implying ingenuity; originally, the term—cognate and almost synonymous with “concept”—implied something conceived in the mind<; Chiasmus>a pattern in which the second part is balanced against the first but with the parts reversed<; Feminine Rhyme>a rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllables are followed by an undifferentiated identical unstressed syllable<; Iamb (or Iambus)>a foot consisting of an unaccented syllable and an accented<; Trochee>a foot consisting of an accented and an unaccented syllable<; Synesthesia>the concurrent response of two or more of the senses to the stimulation of one<; Polyptoton>the repetition in close proximity of words that have the same roots<; Ambiguity>the state of having more than one meaning, with resultant uncertainty as to the intended significance of the statement<; Compound Rhyme>rhyme between primary and secondary stressed syllables<; Resonance>The quality of a work or image to evoke associations, meanings, and feelings beyond its literal content.<; Imagery>the collection of images in a literary work; in another sense, synonymous with trope or figure of speech<; Epanalepsis>the repetition at the end of a clause of a word or phrase that occurred at its beginning<; Masculine Rhyme>rhyme that falls on the stressed concluding syllables of the rhyme words<; Euphemism>a device in which indirectness replaces directness of statement, usually in an effort to avoid offensiveness<; Irony>the recognition of a reality different from appearance<; Realistic Period in American Literature, 1865-1900>the period following the Civil War, marked by the triumphant emergence of industrialism and the rise of realism<; Spondee>a foot composed of two accented syllables<; Reification>the treatment of abstractions as concrete things<; Metathesis>the interchange of position between sounds in a word<; Jacobean Age>that portion of the Renaissance during the reign of James I (1603-1625)<; Personification>a figure that endows animals, ideas, abstractions, and inanimate objects with human form, personality, intelligence, and emotions<; Romantic Period in American Literature, 1830-1865>the period between the “second revolution” of the Jacksonian Era and the close of the Civil War, which saw the testing of a nation and its development by ordeal<; Spenserian Sonnet>a sonnet of the English type in that it has three quatrains and a couplet but features quatrains joined by the use of linking rhymes: abab bcbe cdcd ee<; Anapest>a metrical foot consisting of three syllables, with two unaccented syllables followed by an accented one<; Dactyl>a foot consisting of one accented syllable followed by two unaccented<; Muckrakers>a group of American writers who between 1902 and 1911 worked to expose the dishonest methods and unscrupulous motives in big business and in city, state, and national government<; Caroline>applied in general to the age of Charles I of England (1625-1642) and in particular to the spirit of the court<; Miltonic Sonnet>a variation made by Milton on the Italian sonnet, in which the rhyme scheme is kept but the “turn” between the octave and the sestet is eliminated<; Pleonasm>the use of superfluous syllables or words<; Harangue>a vehement speech designed to arouse strong emotions<; Pathetic Fallacy>a phrase coined by Ruskin to denote the tendency to credit nature with human emotions<; Edwardian Age>the period between the death of Victoria in 1901 and the beginning of World War I in 1914, so called after Edward VII, who ruled from 1901 to 1910<; Epiphany>literally, a manifestation or showing-forth, usually of some divine being; given currency as a critical term by James Joyce<; Asyndeton>a condensed form of expression in which elements customarily joined by conjunctions are presented in series without the conjunctions<; Boustrophedon>running alternately from left to right and from right to left; a term—literally, “ox plowing”—that describes the direction of writing in certain ancient inscriptions<; Italian Sonnet>a sonnet divided into an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet rhyming cdecde<; Satanic School>southey’s phrase (1821) for the literary group of Byron, Shelley, Hunt, and others, whose irregular lives and radical ideas suggested the term<; Soliloquy>a speech delivered while the speaker is alone (solus), calculated to inform the audience of what is passing in the character’s mind<; Kenning>a figurative phrase used in Old Germanic languages as a synonym for a simple noun<; Inversion>the placing of a sentence element out of its normal position<; Period of Confession and Postmodernism in American Literature, 1960—>the period beginning in the 1960s, a time of uncertainty, revolt, and cynicism in America and a strong turning inward of many American writers<; Rhyme>identity of terminal sound between accented syllables, usually occupying corresponding positions in two or more lines of verse<; Truncation>in metrics, the omission of a syllable or syllables at the beginning or end of a line<; Spasmodic School>a phrase applied by W. E. Aytoun in 1854 to a group of contemporary English poets<; Augustan>specifically refers to the age of the Emperor Augustus of Rome; by analogy, applied to other epochs when literary culture was high, such as the Augustan Age of English letters<; Aside>a dramatic convention by which an actor directly addresses the audience but is not supposed to be heard by the other actors on the stage<; Parnassians>a group of nineteenth-century French poets, so called from their journal Parnasse contemporain<; Agrarians>literally people living in an agricultural society or espousing its merits; in literary history, usually a group of Southern American writers who published The Fugitive (1922-1925)<; Pyrrhic>a foot of two unaccented syllables<; Terza rima>a three-line stanza, supposedly devised by Dante (for his Divine Comedy) with rhyme scheme aba bcb cdc ded and so forth<; Allonym>the name of an actual person other than the author that is signed by the author to a work<; Barbarism>a mistake in the form of a word or a word that results from such a mistake<; Lost Generation>a group of American writers, born around 1900, who served in the First World War and reacted against certain tendencies of older writers in the 1920s<; Pun>a play on words based on the similarity of sound between two words with different meanings<; Eye Rhyme>rhyme that appears correct from the spelling but is not so from the pronunciation<; Epistolary Novel>a novel in which the narrative is carried forward by letters written by one or more of the characters<; Polysyndeton>the use of more conjunctions than is normal<; Sonnet>a poem almost invariably of fourteen lines and following one of several set rhyme schemes<; Syllepsis>a grammatically correct construction in which one word is placed in the same grammatical relationship to two words but in quite different senses<; Dead Metaphor>a figure of speech used so long that it is taken in its denotative sense only, without any conscious comparison to a physical object it once conveyed<; Objective Correlative>t. S. Eliot’s term for a pattern of objects, actions, or events or a situation that can serve effectively to awaken in the reader an emotional response without being a direct statement of that subjective emotion<; Cockney School>a derogatory title applied by Blackwood’s Magazine to a group of nineteenth-century writers—including William Hazlitt, Leigh Hunt, and John Keats—because of their alleged poor taste in such matters as diction and rhyme<; Meliorism>the belief—widely held in the nineteenth century—that society has an innate tendency toward improvement and that that tendency can be furthered by conscious human effort<; In Medias Res>a term from Horace, literally “in or into the middle parts of things,” applied to the technique of opening a story in the middle of the action<; Pantoum>the pantoum may consist of any number of four-line stanzas, but in any case, the second and fourth lines of one stanza must reappear as the first and third lines of the following stanza<; Volta>the turn in thought—from question to answer; problem to solution—that occurs at the beginning of the sestet in the Italian sonnet<; Shakespearean Sonnet>the English sonnet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Eponym>A person from whose name the name of a thing, place, or term is derived.<; Aestheticism>a nineteenth-century literary movement that rested on the credo of “art for art’s sake.<; Colonial Period in American Literature, 1607-1765>the period from the founding of Jamestown to the Stamp Act in 1765, when the writing produced in America was generally utilitarian, polemical, or religious<; Hartford Wits>a group of Connecticut writers, active around the period of the American Revolution<; Haiku>a form of Japanese poetry that states—in three lines of five, seven, and five syllables—a clear picture designed to arouse a distinct emotion and suggest a specific spiritual insight<; Symploce>a figure of speech combining anaphora and epistrophe: the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses and of another at their end<; Ballad>a form of verse to be sung or recited and characterized by its presentation of an exciting episode in narrative or dramatic form<; Caesura (or Cesura)>a pause or break in a line of verse<; Elision>the omission of part of a word<; Malapropism>an inappropriateness of speech resulting from the use of one word for another, which resembles it<; Rondeau>a set French verse pattern; artificial but very popular with many English poets<; Spoonerism>an accidental interchange of sounds—usually the initial consonants—in two or more words<

column4: Manga>a style of comic book or graphic novel, originally Japanese, typically presenting a story of fantasy, science fiction, or romance, with drawings in panels or strips<; Nekuia>a work having to do with the land of the dead, especially a visit by a living person<; Epistolary Literature>literature—usually prose fiction—entirely or partly written as letters<; Myth>an anonymous story that presents supernatural episodes as a means of interpreting natural events<; Dystopia>literally, “bad place”; an account of an imaginary world, usually in the future, in which present tendencies are carried out to their intensely unpleasant culminations<; Saga>in a strict sense, Icelandic and Norse stories of the medieval period that give accounts of heroic adventure<; Utopia>a fiction describing an imaginary ideal world<; Local Color Writing>writing that exploits the speech, dress, mannerisms, habits of thought, and topography peculiar to a certain region, primarily for the portrayal of the life of a geographical setting<; Popular Literature>writing in one of the commercially viable modes, especially prose fiction<; Anime>japanese adaptation of the French for “animated cartoon,” applied to styles of film and television productions drawn with extreme stylization and asymmetrical design<; Potboiler>something written solely for money<; Belles-Lettres>literature—drama, poetry, fiction, criticism, and essays—that lives because of inherent imaginative and artistic rather than scientific, philosophical, or intellectual qualities<; Chronicle>a form of historical writing that differs from annals in its concern with larger aspects of history<; Panegyric>a formal composition lauding a person for an achievement; a eulogy<; Riddle>a puzzling question or description to be solved, with a dignified ancestor in the riddles of ancient and medieval literature<; Robinsonade (also Robinsonnade)>a term coined by J. G. Schnabel in 1731 for a work similar to Robinson Crusoe, with a shipwreck on a desert island followed by adventures of survival<; Apocalyptics>a movement in English poetry flourishing between 1935 and 1950, led by Henry Treece and J. R. Hendry; resembling surrealism, it favored extreme imagery<; Cloak and Sword>the term comes from the Spanish comedia de capa y espada, a type of drama in which the ingredients were gallant cavaliers, lovely ladies, elegance, adventure, and intrigue<; Wisdom Literature>literature in which literary elements—plot, character, and so forth—are subordinate to the direct formulaic expression of moral wisdom and truth<; Cloak and Dagger>a type of novel or a play that deals with espionage or intrigue<; Cycle>a term—originally meaning “circle”—applied to a collection of poems or romances centering on some outstanding event or character<; Uchronia>A work of fiction set in an alternate history.<; Bestiary>a type of literature popular during the medieval period in which the habits of beasts, birds, and reptiles were made the text for allegory<; Cyberpunk>science fiction in the mode popular after 1975, with elements from cybernetics, robotics, and advanced computing on the one hand and punk rock culture on the other<; Erotic Literature (or Erotica)>a type of writing characterized by treatment of sexual love in more or less explicit detail<; Recantation>a palinode; a formal repudiation of something written earlier<; Palinode>a piece of writing recanting or retracting a previous writing—particularly such a recanting in verse of an earlier ode<; Pornography>writing designed to arouse sexual lust<; Treatise>formerly used of any writing or story; now restricted to a formal treatment of a serious subject<; Set Piece>a work of any conventional kind, designed to impress<; Techno-Thriller>a work of fiction characteristically involving military or paramilitary characters in far-fetched adventures centering on technical equipment: weaponry, computers, space technology, and vehicles<; Agitprop>“Agitational propaganda,” originally in behalf of the Soviet Union and communist ideology (the word is a Russian combination dating from the 1930s); later applied to any propagandistic effort<; Escape Literature>writing whose clear intention is to amuse and beguile by offering readers a strong world, exciting adventures, or puzzling mysteries<; Fiction>narrative writing drawn from the imagination rather than from history or fact<; Diary>a day-by-day chronicle of events; a journal<; Maggot>a fanciful piece of whimsy—sometimes perverse or morbid<; Hommage>a tribute or act of homage by one artist to another<; Propaganda>material propagated for the purpose of advocating a political or ideological position; also the mechanism for such propaganda<; Pseudomorph>a mineralogical term adapted for a literary work with a title that belongs to a form different from that of the work itself<; Westerns>literature set in the western United States and dealing with the lives of frontier men and women<; Science Fiction>a form of fantasy in which scientific facts, assumptions, or hypotheses form the basis—by logical extrapolation—of adventures in the future, on other planets, or in other dimensions in time or space<; Chronography>The writing of history in chronological order; chronology.<; Alternative History>a species of fiction in which much depends on some major reversal of known geography or history<; Anabasis>an account of a military advance or other movement—a general title bestowed in specific homage to Xenophon’s account of Cyrus the Younger’s expedition into Asia<; Annals>narratives of historical events recorded year by year<; Anatomy>logical dissection or analysis; a term that came into common use in England late in the sixteenth century in the sense of Robert Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy (1621)<; Apocalyptic>literature that predicts the ultimate destiny—usually destruction—of the world, often through complex symbolism<; Children’s Literature>a loosely defined body of work consisting of books written for children, usually understood as applying to children up to about age twelve<; Eutopia>an ideally good place; the word was devised as a play on Utopia, which means “no-place.<; Elizabethan Literature>literature produced in England during the Elizabethan Age—that is, 1558-1603, although the meaning is often extended to include the Jacobean age that ended in 1625<; Historical Fiction>fiction whose setting is in some time other than that in which it is written<; Prose>in its broadest sense, the term is applied to all forms of written or spoken expression not having a regular rhythmic pattern<; Novel>any extended fictional narrative almost always in prose, customarily restricted to narratives in which the representation of character is central<; Young Adult>a classification of literature, especially fiction, designed for readers between ages eighteen and twenty-five<

column4: Madrigal>a short lyric, usually dealing with love or a pastoral theme and designed for—or at least suitable for—a musical setting<; Paean>a song of praise or joy; originally, an ode sung by a Greek chorus in honor of Apollo<; Dirge>a wailing song sung at a funeral or in commemoration of death; a short lyric of lamentation<; Threnody>a song of death; a dirge<; Lai>a song or short narrative poem<; Hymn>a poem expressing religious emotion and generally intended to be sung by a chorus<; Reggae>a style of music, song, and performance that became popular in the 1970s, beginning in Jamaica and spreading through the Caribbean<; Scat>a vocal style developed during the 1920s, with a singer improvising patterns of repetitive nonsense syllables that suggest the sound of a musical instrument<; Antiphon>the verse or verses of a psalm, traditional passage, or portion of the liturgy changed or sung by alternating choirs during Divine Office in the Roman Catholic church<; Rap>earlier, informal conversation; later, a style of performance that usually involves improvised rhymed verse sung or chanted to recorded instrumental music<; Serenade>a composition written as though intended to be sung out-of-doors at night under a window and in praise of a loved one<; Requiem>a chant embodying a prayer for the repose of the dead; a dirge; a solemn mass beginning with Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine (“Give eternal rest to them, O Lord”)<; Round>a song for at least three voices, in which each singer begins a line or a phrase behind the preceding one but repeats what the preceding one is singing<; Calypso>a type of music that originated in the West Indies, particularly Trinidad<; Blues>an African-American folk song developed in the southern United States<; Canticle>originally, a prose chant or hymn taken verbatim from a Biblical text; later applied to any chant and to any poem with its genesis in the rhythms and symbols of religion<; Chantey (also Shanty)>a sailors’ song marked by strong rhythm and, in the days of sail, used to accompany certain forms of repetitious hard labor (such as weighing anchor) performed by seamen working in a group<; Folk Song>a song of unknown authorship preserved and transmitted orally<; Slam>a mode of informal public performance and competition by poets<; Spoken Word Movement>A movement in poetry written to be performed aloud, emphasizing sound, rhythm, and audience.<; Keen>an Irish funeral song<; Glee>a poem written as though to be sung by a group<; Patter Song>most often, a comic solo of rapidly spoken words with only sketchy musical accompaniment<; Coronach>a song of lamentation; a funeral dirge<; Chanson>a song; originally composed of two-line stanzas each ending in a refrain, now almost any simple poem intended to be sung<; Libretto>the text or book, containing the story, tale, or plot of an opera or of any long musical composition—a cantata, for instance<; Mad Song>a verse supposedly spoken or sung by an insane person<; Report Song, Reporting Poem>a verse including a degree of repetition or echo<; Talking Blues>a type of blues song with a strong narrative dimension (although sometimes employing a refrain and some of the features of the ballad)<; Anthem>an arrangement of words from the Bible, usually from the Psalms, for church worship with responsive singing; in popular use, any song of praise, rejoicing, or reverence<; Ballad-Opera>a sort of burlesque opera that flourished on the English stage for several years following the appearance of John Gay’s The Beggar's Opera (1728), still the best-known example<; Burletta>term used in the late eighteenth century for a variety of musical dramatic forms, somewhat like the ballad-opera, the extravaganza, and the pantomime<; Carol (or Carole)>in medieval France, a carole was a dance and later its accompanying song; carol later came to mean any joyous song, then a hymn of religious joy, and finally a Christmas hymn<; Catch>in music, a round for at least three voices, in which each singer begins a line or a phrase behind the preceding one<; Canzonet (also Canzonetta)>a little song; specifically, a solo with more than one movement<; Chant>loosely used to mean a song, but more particularly, the term signifies the intoning of words to a monotonous musical measure of few notes<; Comic Opera>an operetta—or comedy opera—stressing spectacle and music but employing spoken dialogue<; Come-All-Ye>a type of song, usually anonymous, with “come all ye” at the beginning or in a refrain or moralizing conclusion<; Counting-Out Rhyme or Song>a formulaic chant used to determine who is to be excluded from or included in an activity; largely but not exclusively a children’s concern<; Country Song>a poem related to country life, customarily having to do with young love<; Ditty>a song; a refrain. Any short, simple, popular melody<; Dub>a type of poetry originating in Jamaica around 1975 with words improvised to a background of recorded music<; Drinking Song>a song sung while drinking or otherwise having to do with drinking<; Light Opera>a form of opera that lacks the passion, dignity, and seriousness of grand opera<; Lay (or Lai)>a song or short narrative poem<; Hymnody (or Hymnology)>the formal study of hymns, including the words and the music as well as details of performance, conventions, traditions, and aesthetic interactions<; Jingle>a versicle, or short verse or sentence, set to catchy music and used to sell something<; Melic Poetry>poetry written to be accompanied by the lyre or flute<; Matin>a morning song, as of birds<; Hornpipe>an obsolete wind instrument, a dance to its music (usually by one person), or the music for such a dance<; Musical Comedy>a combination of music with comic drama<; Plainsong>the singing or chanting of nonmetrical materials with the free rhythm of ordinary speech; from the Latin cantus planus, even or level singing<; Operetta>a comic opera, with music, songs, and spectacular effects but with the dialogue spoken<; Opera>musical drama in which the dialogue instead of being spoken is sung to the accompaniment of instrumental music<; Psalm>a lyrical composition of praise<; Opéra bouffe>a French term for a very light form of comic opera developed from vaudeville music and said to be the ancestor of the comic operas of Gilbert and Sullivan<; Shanty>a sailor’s working song<; Tenson (also Tenzon)>a verse contest between troubadours; also a lyric piece composed for such a contest<; Song>a lyric poem adapted to musical expression<

column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Paradox>a statement that although seemingly contradictory or absurd may actually be well-founded or true<; Metaphor>an analogy identifying one object with another and ascribing to the first object one or more of the qualities of the second<; Simile>a figure in which a similarity between two objects is directly expressed<; Litotes>a form of understatement in which a thing is affirmed by stating the negative of its opposite<; Consonance>the relation between words in which the final consonants in the stressed syllables agree but the vowels that precede them differ<; Metonymy>the substitution of the name of an object closely associated with a word for the word itself<; Synecdoche>a trope in which a part signifies the whole or the whole signifies the part<; Assonance>generally, patterning of vowel sounds without regard to consonants<; Apostrophe>a figure of speech in which someone (usually but not always absent), some abstract quality, or a nonexistent personage is directly addressed as though present<; Zeugma>a term used in several ways, all involving a sort of “yoking”; for example, as a synonym of syllepsis, when an object-taking word has two or more objects on different levels<; Allusion>a figure of speech that makes brief reference to a historical or literary figure, event, or object<; Dissonance>harsh and inharmonious sounds; a marked breaking of the music of poetry, which may be intentional, as it often is in Browning and Hardy<; Onomatopoeia>words that by their sound suggest their meaning: “hiss,” “buzz,” “whirr,” “sizzle.<; Sigmatism>The excessive or deliberate repetition of the s sound.<; Tautology>the use of repetitious words<; Anaphora>one of the devices of repetition, in which the same expression (word or words) is repeated at the beginning of two or more lines, clauses, or sentences<; Enjambment (Enjambement)>the continuation of the sense and grammatical construction of a line on to the next verse or couplet<; Oxymoron>a self-contradictory combination of words or smaller verbal units; usually noun-noun, adjective-adjective, adjective-noun, adverb-adverb, or adverb-verb<; Alliteration>the repetition of initial identical consonant sounds or any vowel sounds in successive or closely associated syllables<; Leonine Rhyme>the internal rhyming of the last stressed syllable before the caesura, with the last stressed syllable of the line<; Conceit>a type of poetic metaphor implying ingenuity; originally, the term—cognate and almost synonymous with “concept”—implied something conceived in the mind<; Chiasmus>a pattern in which the second part is balanced against the first but with the parts reversed<; Feminine Rhyme>a rhyme in which the rhyming stressed syllables are followed by an undifferentiated identical unstressed syllable<; Iamb (or Iambus)>a foot consisting of an unaccented syllable and an accented<; Trochee>a foot consisting of an accented and an unaccented syllable<; Synesthesia>the concurrent response of two or more of the senses to the stimulation of one<; Polyptoton>the repetition in close proximity of words that have the same roots<; Ambiguity>the state of having more than one meaning, with resultant uncertainty as to the intended significance of the statement<; Compound Rhyme>rhyme between primary and secondary stressed syllables<; Resonance>The quality of a work or image to evoke associations, meanings, and feelings beyond its literal content.<; Imagery>the collection of images in a literary work; in another sense, synonymous with trope or figure of speech<; Epanalepsis>the repetition at the end of a clause of a word or phrase that occurred at its beginning<; Masculine Rhyme>rhyme that falls on the stressed concluding syllables of the rhyme words<; Euphemism>a device in which indirectness replaces directness of statement, usually in an effort to avoid offensiveness<; Irony>the recognition of a reality different from appearance<; Realistic Period in American Literature, 1865-1900>the period following the Civil War, marked by the triumphant emergence of industrialism and the rise of realism<; Spondee>a foot composed of two accented syllables<; Reification>the treatment of abstractions as concrete things<; Metathesis>the interchange of position between sounds in a word<; Jacobean Age>that portion of the Renaissance during the reign of James I (1603-1625)<; Personification>a figure that endows animals, ideas, abstractions, and inanimate objects with human form, personality, intelligence, and emotions<; Romantic Period in American Literature, 1830-1865>the period between the “second revolution” of the Jacksonian Era and the close of the Civil War, which saw the testing of a nation and its development by ordeal<; Spenserian Sonnet>a sonnet of the English type in that it has three quatrains and a couplet but features quatrains joined by the use of linking rhymes: abab bcbe cdcd ee<; Anapest>a metrical foot consisting of three syllables, with two unaccented syllables followed by an accented one<; Dactyl>a foot consisting of one accented syllable followed by two unaccented<; Muckrakers>a group of American writers who between 1902 and 1911 worked to expose the dishonest methods and unscrupulous motives in big business and in city, state, and national government<; Caroline>applied in general to the age of Charles I of England (1625-1642) and in particular to the spirit of the court<; Miltonic Sonnet>a variation made by Milton on the Italian sonnet, in which the rhyme scheme is kept but the “turn” between the octave and the sestet is eliminated<; Pleonasm>the use of superfluous syllables or words<; Harangue>a vehement speech designed to arouse strong emotions<; Pathetic Fallacy>a phrase coined by Ruskin to denote the tendency to credit nature with human emotions<; Edwardian Age>the period between the death of Victoria in 1901 and the beginning of World War I in 1914, so called after Edward VII, who ruled from 1901 to 1910<; Epiphany>literally, a manifestation or showing-forth, usually of some divine being; given currency as a critical term by James Joyce<; Asyndeton>a condensed form of expression in which elements customarily joined by conjunctions are presented in series without the conjunctions<; Boustrophedon>running alternately from left to right and from right to left; a term—literally, “ox plowing”—that describes the direction of writing in certain ancient inscriptions<; Italian Sonnet>a sonnet divided into an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet rhyming cdecde<; Satanic School>southey’s phrase (1821) for the literary group of Byron, Shelley, Hunt, and others, whose irregular lives and radical ideas suggested the term<; Soliloquy>a speech delivered while the speaker is alone (solus), calculated to inform the audience of what is passing in the character’s mind<; Kenning>a figurative phrase used in Old Germanic languages as a synonym for a simple noun<; Inversion>the placing of a sentence element out of its normal position<; Period of Confession and Postmodernism in American Literature, 1960—>the period beginning in the 1960s, a time of uncertainty, revolt, and cynicism in America and a strong turning inward of many American writers<; Rhyme>identity of terminal sound between accented syllables, usually occupying corresponding positions in two or more lines of verse<; Truncation>in metrics, the omission of a syllable or syllables at the beginning or end of a line<; Spasmodic School>a phrase applied by W. E. Aytoun in 1854 to a group of contemporary English poets<; Augustan>specifically refers to the age of the Emperor Augustus of Rome; by analogy, applied to other epochs when literary culture was high, such as the Augustan Age of English letters<; Aside>a dramatic convention by which an actor directly addresses the audience but is not supposed to be heard by the other actors on the stage<; Parnassians>a group of nineteenth-century French poets, so called from their journal Parnasse contemporain<; Agrarians>literally people living in an agricultural society or espousing its merits; in literary history, usually a group of Southern American writers who published The Fugitive (1922-1925)<; Pyrrhic>a foot of two unaccented syllables<; Terza rima>a three-line stanza, supposedly devised by Dante (for his Divine Comedy) with rhyme scheme aba bcb cdc ded and so forth<; Allonym>the name of an actual person other than the author that is signed by the author to a work<; Barbarism>a mistake in the form of a word or a word that results from such a mistake<; Lost Generation>a group of American writers, born around 1900, who served in the First World War and reacted against certain tendencies of older writers in the 1920s<; Pun>a play on words based on the similarity of sound between two words with different meanings<; Eye Rhyme>rhyme that appears correct from the spelling but is not so from the pronunciation<; Epistolary Novel>a novel in which the narrative is carried forward by letters written by one or more of the characters<; Polysyndeton>the use of more conjunctions than is normal<; Sonnet>a poem almost invariably of fourteen lines and following one of several set rhyme schemes<; Syllepsis>a grammatically correct construction in which one word is placed in the same grammatical relationship to two words but in quite different senses<; Dead Metaphor>a figure of speech used so long that it is taken in its denotative sense only, without any conscious comparison to a physical object it once conveyed<; Objective Correlative>t. S. Eliot’s term for a pattern of objects, actions, or events or a situation that can serve effectively to awaken in the reader an emotional response without being a direct statement of that subjective emotion<; Cockney School>a derogatory title applied by Blackwood’s Magazine to a group of nineteenth-century writers—including William Hazlitt, Leigh Hunt, and John Keats—because of their alleged poor taste in such matters as diction and rhyme<; Meliorism>the belief—widely held in the nineteenth century—that society has an innate tendency toward improvement and that that tendency can be furthered by conscious human effort<; In Medias Res>a term from Horace, literally “in or into the middle parts of things,” applied to the technique of opening a story in the middle of the action<; Pantoum>the pantoum may consist of any number of four-line stanzas, but in any case, the second and fourth lines of one stanza must reappear as the first and third lines of the following stanza<; Volta>the turn in thought—from question to answer; problem to solution—that occurs at the beginning of the sestet in the Italian sonnet<; Shakespearean Sonnet>the English sonnet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg<; Eponym>A person from whose name the name of a thing, place, or term is derived.<; Aestheticism>a nineteenth-century literary movement that rested on the credo of “art for art’s sake.<; Colonial Period in American Literature, 1607-1765>the period from the founding of Jamestown to the Stamp Act in 1765, when the writing produced in America was generally utilitarian, polemical, or religious<; Hartford Wits>a group of Connecticut writers, active around the period of the American Revolution<; Haiku>a form of Japanese poetry that states—in three lines of five, seven, and five syllables—a clear picture designed to arouse a distinct emotion and suggest a specific spiritual insight<; Symploce>a figure of speech combining anaphora and epistrophe: the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses and of another at their end<; Ballad>a form of verse to be sung or recited and characterized by its presentation of an exciting episode in narrative or dramatic form<; Caesura (or Cesura)>a pause or break in a line of verse<; Elision>the omission of part of a word<; Malapropism>an inappropriateness of speech resulting from the use of one word for another, which resembles it<; Rondeau>a set French verse pattern; artificial but very popular with many English poets<; Spoonerism>an accidental interchange of sounds—usually the initial consonants—in two or more words<

column4: Invocation>an address to a deity for aid<; Annotation>the addition of explanatory notes to a text by the author or an editor to explain, translate, cite sources, give bibliographical data, comment, gloss, or paraphrase<; Definition>a brief explanation of the meaning of a term<; Epigraph>an inscription on stone or on a statue or a coin<; Acknowledgements>a conventional component of the front matter of some printed documents—particularly nonfiction articles and books—wherein authors acknowledge help received from individuals and institutions<; Addenda (plural of Addendum)>matter to be added to a piece of writing<; Footnote>material added to a text to provide additional information or documentation<; Prolegomenon>a preface; an introductory section of a book or a set of studies preliminary to further work<; Bibliography>a list of printed (or manuscript) materials on any chosen topic, or of works of a particular country, author, or printer; the term is used in several senses<; Apology>the word often appears in literature, especially in titles, in its older sense of defense<; Blurb>a term applied in the book trade to the hyperbolically encomiastic matter printed on the jackets of books or elsewhere<; Gloss>an explanation of a difficult word in a text by a marginal or interlinear word or phrase, usually in a more familiar language<; Introduction>the opening of a piece of writing<; Index>a systematic list of items in a book, volume, or series, along with some indication of location; at one time, index meant table of contents<; Lemniscus>a symbol used in antiquity for glosses and annotations<; Marginalia>marginal material, literal or figurative<; Induction>an old word for introduction<; Paraphrase>a restatement of an idea in such a way as to retain the meaning while changing the diction and form<; Rubric>A heading, title, or instruction in a manuscript or book, traditionally written in red.<; Argument>a statement summarizing the plot or stating the meaning of a long poem or occasionally of a play<; Colophon>a publisher’s symbol or device formerly placed at the end of a book but now more generally used on the title page or elsewhere near the beginning<; Commentary>scholarly remarks specifically concerning details of substance or text, usually matters of information and not of judgment<; Glossary>a list, usually alphabetical, of terms needing explanation<; Foreword>a short preliminary statement that explains some aspect of the work to follow<; Enumerative Bibliography>a listing of works of a particular country, author, printer, or type or on a particular subject<; Headnote>material in the form of a note placed at the head of a page; the physical opposite of a footnote and usually without numbers, asterisks, or other symbols<; Entry>an individual item listed or entered in a record, diary, or catalog; in an old usage, a preface; also a theatrical entrance<; Lemma>variously used to mean a theme or argument, especially when employed as a title, motto, or caption<; Hypolemniscus>a mark like the division symbol minus the upper dot formerly used for annotations and glosses, especially in biblical commentary<; Part Title>a title given to a subsidiary part of a work<; Prolusion>one of many words meaning a prefatory piece of writing; also a preliminary exercise<; Prelude>a short poem, introductory in character, prefixed to a long poem or to a section of a long poem<; Preface>a statement at the beginning of a book or article—and separate from it—which states the purpose of the work, makes necessary acknowledgments, and informs the reader of pertinent facts<; Preamble>an introduction<; Paralipomena (plural of paralipomenon)>something omitted from a text but later included in an appendix or elsewhere<; Proem>a brief introduction; a preface or preamble<; Prologue>an introduction most frequently associated with drama and especially common in England in the plays of the Restoration and the eighteenth century<; Superscription>a heading, address, or epigraph written before or above a text<; Subject Bibliography>a list of books, articles, manuscripts, or other forms of writing—either complete or selected—on any of various principles or some specific subject<; Tail-Piece>a device placed at the end of a text or major part of a text; see colophon<

column4: Mythopoeia>myth-making, construed as either an individual function of a single artist or a collective spirit<; Muses, The>nine goddesses represented as presiding over the various departments of art and science<; Nekuia>a work having to do with the land of the dead, especially a visit by a living person<; Myth>an anonymous story that presents supernatural episodes as a means of interpreting natural events<; Mythos>The plot or story of a work; also, a body of myths belonging to a culture.<; Nemesis>the Greek goddess of retributive justice or vengeance<; Graces, The>in Greek myth, the three sister goddesses who confer grace, beauty, charm, and joy on human beings and nature<; Euhemerism>a Sicilian Greek named Euhemerus of around the fourth century B.C. has given his name to a practice of explaining myths as the exaggeration of human stories, so that gods are understood to be deified heroes and kings<; Four Ages>a scheme of great antiquity—dividing history into a line or cycle of ages—conventionally associated with gold, silver, brass, and iron<; Furies, The>In Greek and Roman mythology, the goddesses of vengeance who pursue wrongdoers.<; Calliope>In Greek mythology, the Muse of epic poetry.<; Erato>In Greek mythology, the Muse of lyric and love poetry.<; Urania>In Greek mythology, the Muse of astronomy.<; Divine Afflatus>Divine inspiration; the creative impulse believed to come from a god.<; Parnassus>a Greek mountain famed as the haunt of Apollo and the Muses<; Pegasus>the winged horse of Grecian fable said to have sprung from Medusa’s body at her death<; Clio>In Greek mythology, the Muse of history.<; Mnemosyne>In Greek mythology, the goddess of memory and mother of the Muses.<; Polyhymnia>In Greek mythology, the Muse of sacred song and hymns.<; Terpsichore>In Greek mythology, the Muse of dance and choral song.<; Fates, The>the three sisters—Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos—who, the Greeks and Romans believed, controlled the birth, life, and death of all human beings<; Melpomene>In Greek mythology, the Muse of tragedy.<; Thalia>In Greek mythology, the Muse of comedy and pastoral poetry.<; Apollonian (or, earlier, Apollinian)>a term used, along with Dionysian, in Friedrich Nietzsche’s The Birth of Tragedy for contrasting elements in Greek tragedy<; Götterdämmerung>a German word meaning “the twilight of the gods.<; Dionysian>a term used by Friedrich Nietzsche for the spirit in Greek tragedy associated with Dionysus, the god of wine<

column4: Objective Correlative>t. S. Eliot’s term for a pattern of objects, actions, or events or a situation that can serve effectively to awaken in the reader an emotional response without being a direct statement of that subjective emotion<; Heteroglossia>“Different tongues” or “different speech”; a term introduced by Mikhail Bakhtin to designate the presence of more than one voice in a given narrative or another work<; Vorticism>a movement in modern poetry, originating in 1914 with Wyndham Lewis, related to certain abstract developments in painting and sculpture<; Alienation Effect>bertolt Brecht’s term (translating the German Verfremdungseffekt) for a quality of theater by which the audience is kept at such a distance that unthinking emotional and personal involvement is inhibited<; Freytag’s Pyramid>a diagram of the structure of a five-act tragedy, given by Gustav Freytag in Technik des Dramas (1863)<; Wellerism>a type of expression, named for Dickens’s Sam and Tony Weller, with three parts: an utterance, a speaker, and a situation<; Discordia Concors>a term used by Samuel Johnson for “a combination of dissimilar images or discovery of occult resemblances in things apparently unlike” in metaphysical poetry<; Melopoeia>a Greek term renovated by Ezra Pound, who used it for the whole articulatory-acoustic-auditory range of poetry<; Euhemerism>a Sicilian Greek named Euhemerus of around the fourth century B.C. has given his name to a practice of explaining myths as the exaggeration of human stories, so that gods are understood to be deified heroes and kings<; Carnivalesque>a term introduced by Mikhail Bakhtin to describe a spirit of carnival in literature, marked by fun, attention to the body, defiance of authority, variety, heteroglossia, and play<; Grimm’s Law>a principle formulated by Jakob Grimm in 1822 that describes a complex of relations among consonants in Indo-European languages<; Hebraism>Matthew Arnold’s term for the moral, strict-conscience element of culture, contrasted with Hellenism.<; Ockham’s (or Occam’s) Razor>the principle of parsimony, attributed to William of Ockham: “Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity.<; Touchstone>a critical standard, in Matthew Arnold’s sense: lines and expressions of the great masters used as a test of the quality of other poetry<; Grammatology>Derrida’s term for the study of writing as a system, prior to and distinct from speech.<; Sprung Rhythm>a term coined by Gerard Manley Hopkins for rhythm based on the number of stressed syllables in a line without regard to the number of unstressed syllables<; Rubáiyát>the plural of the Arabic word for quatrain; hence, a collection of four-lined stanzas<; Hellenism>The culture and ideals of ancient Greece; Matthew Arnold’s term for the free play of intellect, contrasted with Hebraism.<; Inscape>gerard Manley Hopkins’s term for the “individually distinctive” inner structure or nature of a thing; hence, the essence of a natural object<; Negative Capability>john Keats’s phrase (1817) for the quality of a person who “is capable of being in uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact & reason.<; Outride>a term Gerard Manley Hopkins applied to a slack syllable—that is, an unstressed syllable—added to a foot<; “Sweetness and Light”>a phrase given great popularity by Matthew Arnold, who used it as the title of the first chapter of Culture and Anarchy (1869)<; Bad Quartos>a. W. Pollard’s term for certain notably corrupt, garbled, and nearly incoherent early editions of Shakespeare’s plays<; Comstockery>the overzealous and prudish censorship of literature and the other arts because of their supposed immorality<; Esemplastic>a term applied by Coleridge to the quality in the imagination that enables it to shape disparate things into a unified whole<; Instress>gerard Manley Hopkins’s term for the force—ultimately divine—that creates the inscape of an object or event and impresses it on the mind of the beholder<; Petrarchan Conceit>the kind of conceit used by Petrarch in his love sonnets and widely imitated or ridiculed by Renaissance English sonneteers<; Phanopoeia>ezra Pound’s term for the power of language to cast visual images onto the mind or imagination<; Chronotope>Bakhtin’s term for the connectedness of time and space as represented in a literary work.<; Counterpoint Rhythm>a term used by Gerard Manley Hopkins to describe the superimposing of a different rhythm on one already established<; Dissociation of Sensibility>a term given wide currency by T. S. Eliot (in “The Metaphysical Poets,” 1921) to describe a disjunction of thought and feeling in the writers of the seventeenth and later centuries<; Dialogism>according to Mikhail Bakhtin, a feature of certain literature that permits the polyphonic interplay of many different voices rather than allowing a single monologic voice to dominate<; Logopoeia>a term coined by Ezra Pound to identify one way in which poetry charges language with meaning<; Mythical Method>t. S. Eliot’s phrase (1923) for the structure of Joyce’s Ulysses, which sustains a “continuous parallel” between Homer’s Odyssey and a one-day narrative of contemporaneity<; Homosocial>a word coined by Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick for the range of same-sex bonds among men, whether heterosexual or homosexual<; Spatial Form>joseph Frank’s term for forms of modern writing that suspend or abolish the customary temporal structure of literature and substitute virtual space for time<

column4: Acrostic>a composition, usually verse, arranged in such a way that it spells words, phrases, or sentences when certain letters are selected according to an orderly sequence<; Angry Young Men>a group of British writers in the 1950s and 1960s who demonstrated a particular bitterness in their attacks on outmoded, bourgeois values<; Digression>the insertion of material often not closely related to the subject in a work<; Euphony>pleasing sounds; the opposite of cacophony<; Double Entendre>a statement that is deliberately ambiguous, one of whose possible meanings is risqué or suggestive of some impropriety<; Late Victorian Age, 1870-1901>the period between 1870 and the death of Queen Victoria, which saw the full flowering of the movement toward realism<; Parenthesis>an explanatory remark inside a statement and frequently separated from it by parentheses ( )<; Picaresque Novel>a chronicle—usually autobiographical—presenting the life story of a rascal of low degree engaged in menial tasks and making his living more through his wits than his industry<; Petrarchan Sonnet>the Italian sonnet<; Parallelism>such an arrangement that one element of equal importance with another is similarly developed and phrased<; Typology>the study of allegorical symbols, especially with the Bible, in which much of the Old Testament is read as a type of the revelation to come in the New Testament<; Anglo-Italian Sonnet>a sonnet combining the rhyme schemes of the English sonnet (ababcdcdefefgg) and the Italian sonnet (abbaabbacdecde), most often with an octave from the former and a sestet from the latter<; Bloomsbury Group>a group of writers and thinkers, many of whom lived in Bloomsbury, a residential district near central London<; Carmen Figuratum>a figure poem, one so written that the form of the printed words suggests the subject matter<; Commonwealth (or Puritan) Interregnum>the period between the execution of Charles I in 1649 and the restoration of the monarchy in 1660, during which England was ruled by Parliament under the control of Oliver Cromwell<; Existentialism>a group of attitudes, current during and after World War II, that emphasizes existence rather than essence and sees the inadequacy of human reason to explain the enigma of the universe<; Geneva School>a group of critics, including Georges Poulet, Marcel Raymond, Albert Béguin, and the early J. Hillis Miller, who see a literary work as a series of existential expressions of the author’s individual consciousness<; Modernist Period in English Literature>the period in England beginning with World War I in 1914, marked by the flowering of talent and experiment in the twenties, and ending around 1965<; Neologism (or Neology)>a new word introduced into a language, especially for enhancing style<; Homeoteleuton>sameness or similarity of endings of consecutive words or words near each other—often considered unsettling or graceless but sometimes unavoidable<; Parataxis>an arrangement of sentences, clauses, phrases, or words in coordinate rather than subordinate constructions, often without connectives<; Tragicomedy>a play that employs a plot suitable to tragedy but ends happily, like a comedy<; Amphigory (or Amphigouri)>verse that sounds well but contains little or no sense or meaning; either nonsense verse or nonsensical parody<; Archaism>obsolete phrasing, idiom, syntax, or spelling<; Bathos>the effect resulting from the unsuccessful effort to achieve dignity or sublimity of style; an unintentional anticlimax, dropping from the sublime to the ridiculous<; Fleshly School of Poetry, The>a critical essay by Robert W. Buchanan (as “Thomas Maitland”) in the Contemporary Review, October 1871, attacking Swinburne, Morris, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti<; Hubris>overweening pride or insolence that results in the misfortune of the protagonist of a tragedy<; Naturalism>the application of principles of scientific determinism to literature; a term best reserved for a literary movement in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries<; Tagline>(1) Punchline. (2) Material placed under a document or illustration; a caption. (3) Matter printed under a headline to amplify a main point<; Triolet>one of the simpler French verse forms, consisting of eight lines with only two rhymes, the first two lines being repeated as the last two and the first line recurring also as the fourth<; Prolepsis>A flash-forward; the anticipation of a future event as if it had already happened.<; Transcendental Club>An informal group of New England Transcendentalists who met from 1836 to about 1840.<; Curtal Sonnet>gerard Manley Hopkins’s name for a sonnet that has been curtailed<; Eulogy>a dignified, formal speech or form of writing that praises a person or a thing<; Deus (or Dea) ex Machina>the employment of some unexpected and improbable incident to make things turn out right<; Great Awakening, The>see Awakening, the Great<; Encomium>in Greek literature, a composition in praise of a living person, object, or event—but not a god—delivered before a special audience<; Dialectic>in the broadest sense, simply the art of argumentation or debate; in classical literature, the tradition of continuing debate or discussion of eternally unresolved issues<; Intentional Fallacy>the judging of the meaning or success of a work of art by the author’s expressed or ostensible intention in producing it<; Minimalism>a modern movement in politics, economics, and all the arts, especially noticeable in architecture (Mies van der Rohe: “Less is more”) and music (for example, the works of Anton Webern)<; Kailyard School>a group of Scottish writers whose work dealt idealistically with village life in Scotland<; Paean>a song of praise or joy; originally, an ode sung by a Greek chorus in honor of Apollo<; Syncope>a cutting short of words through the omission of a letter or a syllable<; Xenoglossia (also Xenoglossia, Xenolalia)>the intelligible use of a foreign language that one does not know<; Perfect Rhyme (or True Rhyme)>Rhyme in which the stressed vowels and all following sounds are identical, while the preceding consonants differ.<; Bildungsroman>a novel that deals with the development of a young person, usually from adolescence to maturity; it is frequently autobiographical<; Bluestockings>women of pronounced intellectual interests<; Flat Character>e. M. Forster’s term for a character constructed around a single idea or quality<; Diminishing Metaphor>a type of metaphor that utilizes a deliberate discrepancy of connotation between tenor and vehicle<; Denotation>the basic meaning of a word, independent of its emotional coloration or associations<; Mosaic>another name for heteromerous rhyme<; Metalepsis>a complex figure, also called transumption, that adds one trope or figure to another with such extreme compression that the literal sense is eclipsed or reduced to anomaly or nonsense<; Masque>a spectacle characterized by a procession of masked figures, developed from medieval disguisings or mummings and adopted by the aristocracy<; Rime Riche>words with identical sounds but different meanings<; Persona>literally, a mask; a “second self” created by an author and through whom the narrative is told<; Novel of Incident>a novel in which episodic action dominates and plot and character are subordinate<; Ode>a single, unified strain of exalted lyrical verse, directed to a single purpose, and dealing with one theme<; Tableau>an interlude in which the actors freeze in position and then resume action as before or hold their positions until the curtain falls<; Theme>a central idea; in nonfiction, the general topic of discussion; in poetry, fiction, and drama, the abstract concept made concrete through representation<; Syncopation>a musical term used for the effect produced by a temporary displacing or shifting of the regular beat<; Round Character>a term used by E. Virelay>a French verse form (related to lai) of which the number of stanzas and the number of lines to the stanza are unlimited<; Dénouement>literally, “unknotting”; the final unraveling of a plot; the solution of a mystery; an explanation or outcome<; Kitsch>shallow, flashy art designed to have popular appeal and commercial success; from the German for “gaudy trash.<; Fabliau (plural, Fabliaux)>a humorous tale popular in medieval France<; Locus Classicus>that place or passage invariably cited as the “classic example” of a principle or type<; Roman à Thèse>french: a thesis novel—one intended to establish and illustrate a social doctrine<; Mythos>The plot or story of a work; also, a body of myths belonging to a culture.<; Doppelganger>german, “double goer”; a mysterious double, a common figure in literature<; Epithalamium (or Epithalamion)>a poem written to celebrate a wedding<; Koine>the language spoken throughout the ancient Greek world; colloquial Attic with numerous supplements from other dialects and other languages<; Montage>french for “mounting” or “editing”; in film, the juxtaposing of contrasting shots to create a meaning different from that recorded in any of the shots<; Omnibus (Latin dative plural, “for all”)>a volume of selected works, usually by one author but sometimes by several on one subject<; Scène à faire>a scene in a play so thoroughly prepared for that the author is obliged to provide it<; Débat>a type of composition usually in verse—highly popular in the Middle Ages—in which two contestants—frequently allegorical—debate a topic and refer it to a judge<; Märchen>german fairy tales, either simple folktales or short allegories laid in a fantastic realm<; Künstlerroman>a form of the apprenticeship novel in which the protagonist is an artist struggling from childhood to maturity toward an understanding of his or her creative mission<; Roman de Geste>same as chanson de geste<; Chanson de geste>a “song of great deeds”; a term applied to the early French epic<; Fin de Siècle>“End of the century,” a phrase often applied to the last ten years of the nineteenth century<; La Femme Inspiratrice>a type of real person or literary character: the woman who inspires an artist<; Jongleur>a French term for a professional musical entertainer of medieval times, analogous to the Anglo-Saxon gleeman and the later minstrel<; Pastiche>a French word for a parody or literary imitation<; Milieu>The social and cultural environment or setting in which something occurs.<; Entwicklungsroman>a German term for a type of Bildungsroman that emphasizes the development of the principal character<; Reductio ad absurdum>a “reducing to absurdity” to show the falsity of an argument or position<; Vulgate>from Latin vulgus, “crowd,” meaning “common”; chiefly, the Latin version of the Bible made by Saint Jerome in the fourth century<; Ultima Thule>the farthest possible place<; Sturm und Drang (Storm and Stress)>a movement in Germany during the last quarter of the eighteenth century, named after Klinger’s drama Sturm und Drang (1776)<; De Casibus>latin, concerning the falls (from greatness)<; Roman-Fleuve>“River novel”; a substantial, slow-moving novel that typically chronicles the lives of several generations; sometimes, a set or sequence of novels<; Bunraku>A traditional form of Japanese puppet theater.<; Jeu d’esprit>a witty playing with words; a clever sally<; Tour de force>a feat of strength and virtuosity<; Divine Afflatus>Divine inspiration; the creative impulse believed to come from a god.<; Gallicism>diction characteristic of the French language or a custom or turn of thought suggestive of the French people<; Hapax Legomenon>a word or grammatical form that occurs only once; literally, from the Greek, “something said only once.<; Explication de texte>a method, originating in the teaching of literature in France, involving the painstaking analysis of the meanings, relationships, and ambiguities of the words, images, and other small units that make up a literary work<; Theatrum Mundi>The idea that the world is a stage and people are actors on it.<; Bagatelle>in general, a trifle; in art, a work explicitly identified or labeled as a trifle<; Chanson d’aventure>a poem recounting a romantic adventure, often involving a journey on horseback or a sea voyage<; Mot juste>french for “apt or proper word”; associated with Gustave Flaubert’s principle of prose employing lucid, correct words rather than some platitude or approximation<; Parnassus>a Greek mountain famed as the haunt of Apollo and the Muses<; Novella>a tale or short story, particularly the early tales of Italian and French writers such as those of the Decameron<; Nihil obstat>latin for “nothing obstructs,” used in the Roman Catholic church to grant permission to publish a book<; Locus Desperatus>A passage in a manuscript or text so corrupt that it cannot be restored.<; Buskin>a thick-soled boot reaching halfway to the knee worn by Greek tragedians to increase their stature, even as comedians wore socks for the opposite purpose<; Chanson>a song; originally composed of two-line stanzas each ending in a refrain, now almost any simple poem intended to be sung<; Erziehungsroman>the novel of upbringing or education<; Festschrift (plural, Festschriften)>a volume of miscellaneous learned essays by the students, colleagues, or admirers of a scholar, presented on some special occasion; from the German for celebration and writing<; Mise en Scène>the stage setting of a play, including scenery, properties, and the general arrangement of the piece<; Imprimatur>an official license to print a work; usually the sign of approval of the Roman Catholic church<; Rime retournée>the relation between such syllables as “pal” and “lap”; also called amphisbaenic or boustrophedon rhyme<; Terribilita>a quality of awe-inspiring artworks in which a figure who appears to be at ease also shows great tension, strength, and the potential for terrific action; first applied to Michelangelo and his sculptures<; Sock>the low-heeled slipper conventionally worn by the comic actor on the ancient stage—hence (figuratively), comedy itself<; Rex ex Machina>A plot resolution brought about by the sudden intervention of a king.<; Utile et Dulce>Horace’s principle that poetry should be both useful and pleasing.<; Roman>The French word for a novel or long prose fiction.<; Régisseur>A stage director, especially in European theater or ballet.<; Addubitatio>latin counterpart of diaporesis, in which a speaker expresses doubt (genuine or feigned)<; Aet., Aetat.>abbreviations for the Latin aetatis suae, “of his or her age.<; Alba>a Provençal lament over the parting of lovers at the break of day—the name coming from the Provençal for “dawn.<; Ambo>a stage direction meaning “both.<; Anabasis>an account of a military advance or other movement—a general title bestowed in specific homage to Xenophon’s account of Cyrus the Younger’s expedition into Asia<; Ancilla (literally, “maidservant”)>an ancillary aid in the study of a subject<; Apotropaic>“Warding off evil.<; A Priori>a Latin phrase (“from what comes before”) for deductive reasoning, which proceeds from the general to the specific<; A Posteriori>a Latin phrase (“from what comes later”) for inductive reasoning, which proceeds from the specific to the general<; Apophrades>in the ancient Greek calendar, unlucky or unclean days when the dead visited their old houses; in Harold Bloom’s criticism, a “revisionary ratio” in which a dead precursor returns<; Apollonian (or, earlier, Apollinian)>a term used, along with Dionysian, in Friedrich Nietzsche’s The Birth of Tragedy for contrasting elements in Greek tragedy<; Apo koinou>(Greek, “in common”) Describing a peculiar construction in which two distinct clauses share an unrepeated element in common, so that the element serves two grammatical functions<; Aube>the French word for either alba or aubade<; Bon Mot>a witty repartee or statement<; Catena>latin, “chain”; a series of quotations used decoratively<; Causerie>an informal essay, usually on a literary topic, and frequently in a series<; Chronique scandaleuse>a body of scandalous gossip, usually informal and unofficial but sometimes achieving written form<; Cinéma Vérité>a method of filmmaking that relies on portable equipment and small camera crews<; Contaminatio>a practice—followed by some Roman comic writers—which involved using material from one play to rewrite another<; Conte>french for tale; originally a short tale of adventure, later used for short stories of tightly constructed plot and great concision<; Cothurnus>the buskin—a thick-soled, laced boot worn by actors in Greek tragedy<; Cratylism>the belief that there is a necessary, essential, mimetic connection between signifier and signified; from Plato’s Cratylus, which considers whether names are arbitrary or necessary<; Götterdämmerung>a German word meaning “the twilight of the gods.<; Différance>a virtually untranslatable French neologism introduced by Jacques Derrida to combine various denotations and connotations of difference, differing, deferring, and deferral<; Galgenhumor>german counterpart of gallows humor<; Eisteddfod>a Welsh festival of poetry and song, dating back many centuries<; Drame>a form of play between tragedy and comedy developed by the French in the eighteenth century and later introduced into England, where it is often called a “drama.<; Donnée>literally, “a given”; Henry James’s term for the data given, out of which one works out the meaning or solution of a work<; Film Noir>nino Frank’s name for a type of American crime film that flourished between 1940 and 1960<; Entr’acte>an entertainment—often musical—in the interlude between the acts of a play<; Ficelle>henry James’s term for a confidante, a means by which a self-effacing author conveys necessary information; literally, one of the strings by which marionettes are controlled<; Dionysian>a term used by Friedrich Nietzsche for the spirit in Greek tragedy associated with Dionysus, the god of wine<; New Novel>a term—literally from the French nouveau roman—often applied to the antinovel<; Ipse Dixit>any dogmatic statement; an edict or brief statement emphatically uttered but unsupported by proof<; Litterateur>a literary person; one who is engaged in literary work, often with a connotation of the dilettante<; Lehrstück>a didactic or teaching piece, designed to advance a political idea; originated in the theater by Bertolt Brecht<; Mirlitonade>a kazoo tune; a trifle<; Mot>french for “word”; sometimes bon mot, “good word.” A brief, apt saying<; Mise en Abyme>any occasion when a small text is imprinted on or contained in a bigger text that it replicates; from the heraldic term for a small shield on a big shield<; Loan Word>a word that passes in its native form from one language to another without being translated<; Lord of Misrule (also Abbot, King, Monk, or Master of Misrule)>around the beginning of the sixteenth century, an official appointed to preside over Christmas revels at court and in some academic communities<; Pièce bien faite>see Well-Made Play, the English equivalent of the French term<; Noir>an adjective taken over from the phrase film noir to apply to any work, especially one involving crime, that is notably dark, brooding, cynical, complex, and pessimistic<; Parergon>something done in addition to one’s ordinary business; used sometimes (as in texts of Schopenhauer and Derrida) for supplementary parts of a text<; Planh>provençal equivalent of “plaint,” used by Pound in the title of a translation<; Opsis>aristotle’s term for the spectacle as an element in drama—the least important, coming sixth in order after mythos, ethos, dianoia, lexis, and melos<; Prothalamion>from the Greek, “before the bridal chamber”; a term coined by Edmund Spenser for a poem celebrating a wedding, by analogy with epithalamion<; Redondilla>a Spanish measure, usually in octosyllabic couplets or quatrains with various rhyme schemes; used in Ezra Pound’s early “Redondillas.<; Nostos (plural Nostoi)>a work describing a return, especially a homecoming<; Opuscule (Often in Latin form opusculum, plural opuscula)>a small work<; Priapic>in classical prosody, a measure consisting of a catalectic glyconic and a pherecratean; associated with poems to Priapus<; Notabilium (plural Notabilia)>something worth noticing<; Opus>a work of any sort, sometimes disparagingly<; Notandum (plural Notanda)>something to be noted<; Récit>common French term for narrative<; Prosa, Prose>in the late Middle Ages and early Renaissance, a disdainful classification for writing not in the classical quantitative style, even that using qualitative scansion and rhyme<; Parodos>in ancient Greek drama, the odes sung by the chorus when they first enter<; Opéra bouffe>a French term for a very light form of comic opera developed from vaudeville music and said to be the ancestor of the comic operas of Gilbert and Sullivan<; Policier>a police film or one based on a roman policier; sometimes construed as a variety of film noir<; Obiter Dicta>things said “by the way”; incidental remarks<; Protasis>a classical term for the introductory act or the exposition of a drama<; Vers Libre>a nineteenth-century French poetic movement to free poetry from strict rules resulted in cadenced and rhythmic poetry called vers libre, which means “free verse.<; Schüttelreime>“Shuttle rhyme”; the German equivalent of the spoonerism, which turns on the transposition of initial letters<; Verfremdungseffekt>german for alienation effect<; Vers d’Occasion>French for occasional verse<; Symposium>a discussion by different persons of a single topic, or a collection of speeches or essays on a subject; a Greek word meaning “a drinking together” or banquet<; Slice of Life>the unselective and non-evaluative presentation of a segment of life<; Vers de circonstance>one French name for occasional verse<; Samizdat>an underground system of publication and distribution used in the former Soviet Union to print, copy, and circulate literature that was out of favor<; Tombeau>a memorial work by one artist for another; from the French for “tomb” or “tombstone.<
