column4: Montage>french for “mounting” or “editing”; in film, the juxtaposing of contrasting shots to create a meaning different from that recorded in any of the shots<; Anime>japanese adaptation of the French for “animated cartoon,” applied to styles of film and television productions drawn with extreme stylization and asymmetrical design<; Voice-Over>in film, the use of a narrator’s or commentator’s words when the speaker is not seen by the viewer<; Adventure Story (or Film)>a story in which action—often exterior, usually physical, and frequently violent—is the predominant material, stressed above characterization, motivation, or theme<; Cross-Cutting>a term used in film criticism to describe repeated movements within a connected sequence from one subject to another<; Establishing Shot>the opening shot of a film sequence—usually with a substantial distance between the camera and the scene—so that characters and actions are visibly placed in context<; Deep Focus>in film, a method by which objects both near and far away are simultaneously in focus<; Sound-Over>In film, sound whose source is not seen on screen.<; Rough Cut>In film, an early, unpolished assembly of the shots of a film.<; Hollywood Novel>a novel set in Hollywood itself or else about the film industry at large<; Action-Adventure>a style of entertainment popular in film and television productions after about 1950<; Dogme 95>a filmmaking collective established in Denmark in 1995 led by Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg and devoted to radical principles that subvert the dominance of fiction, illusion, and gimmickry<; Mise en Scène>the stage setting of a play, including scenery, properties, and the general arrangement of the piece<; Mockumentary>a mock documentary in which a work of fiction borrows the techniques of documentary<; Analytic Editing>a process in filmmaking by which a director and an editor of a film so select the details in a scene that an emphatic meaning is imposed on the viewer<; Auteur Theory>a critical method, from the French politique des auteurs, by which a film is viewed as the product of its auteur, or director, and is judged by the quality of its expression of the director’s personality or worldview<; Camera Eye Narration>a kind of storytelling, resembling the “Camera Eye” sections of John Dos Passos’s U.S.A. (1936), in which the writing gives the appearance or impression of being thoroughly objective, realistic, and anatomical<; Cinéma Vérité>a method of filmmaking that relies on portable equipment and small camera crews<; Credits>a list of names of persons and institutions that contributed to the making of a film or other such production<; Cut>in film, a switch from one image to another<; Film>a motion picture; literally, a sheet or roll of transparent material coated with a light-sensitive emulsion for making photographs or moving pictures<; Documentary Film (also Documentary)>a film that avoids actors, studios, stories, special effects, and other aspects of filmed fiction; documentaries began during the 1920s under the leadership of John Grierson<; Direct Camera>a style of objective, essentially nonnarrative, nonstaged filmmaking used in producing documentary films since the early 1960s<; Film Noir>nino Frank’s name for a type of American crime film that flourished between 1940 and 1960<; Mondo>a type of documentary film, after the Italian Mondo Cane (1961), that shows a world of bizarre and exotic customs, often emphasizing the bizarre or taboo<; Noir>an adjective taken over from the phrase film noir to apply to any work, especially one involving crime, that is notably dark, brooding, cynical, complex, and pessimistic<; Novelization>the conversion of a screenplay or a television play into novel form, usually to capitalize on its popularity<; Rack Focus>in filmmaking, a change of focus in the middle of shooting, with the effect of shifting attention from one object to another<; Phi Phenomenon (or Effect)>the psychological perception of motion resulting from persistence of vision, called the phi phenomenon by the Gestalt psychologists<; P.O.V. Shot>same as point of view shot<; Point of View Shot (also P.O.V. Shot)>a film shot that shows a scene as viewed by a character; also called subjective camera<; Policier>a police film or one based on a roman policier; sometimes construed as a variety of film noir<; Subjective Camera>in a film, camera work from the point of view of a character; also called point of view shot<; Treatment>(1) General manner or style in handling a subject. (2) In film, a preliminary sketch of a screenplay or adaptation<; Zoom Shot>in filmmaking, the shot resulting from the use of a camera lens with an adjustable focal length, so the viewer appears to move rapidly closer to or farther from an object<; Telenovela>a novel for television, very popular in Latin America and elsewhere around the world, appealing to viewers of many sorts<; Tracking Shot>a shot for which the camera, mounted on a dolly, is moved while filming, tracking an action or activity<; Fu>a technical term used in the Briggsian school of alfresco film criticism; appropriated from the Chinese “kung fu,” the Briggsian application of fu means mindless violence<

column4: Chiaroscuro>contrasting light and shade<; Sfumato>an Italian word meaning “smoked” that refers to a quality of smokily obscuring details in a painting; later applied to film and television productions with a similar quality: vapory, foggy, soft-focus, dark, or dim<; Emblem>a graphic device of some sort that stands for a special meaning<; Kitsch>shallow, flashy art designed to have popular appeal and commercial success; from the German for “gaudy trash.<; Luminism>a movement in painting, especially since about 1875, in which the art concentrates on the effect of light<; Pictorialism>pictorial style, extended from painting to the other arts insofar as they are capable of representing or depicting; usually patronizing or pejorative<; Grotesque>any decorative art characterized by fantastic representations of human and animal forms often combined into formal distortions of the natural to the point of absurdity, ugliness, or caricature<; Calligraphy>the art of beautiful writing<; Cubism>An early twentieth-century art movement that represented subjects from multiple viewpoints in fragmented, geometric form.<; Arabesque>a style of decorative design favored by the Moors as a means of giving play to their aesthetic creativity without violating the Islamic prohibition against reproducing natural forms<; Arts and Crafts Movement>a movement—beginning in northern Europe in the later nineteenth century but soon with worldwide influence—that emphasized utility, individual craft, handiwork, simplicity, artistic versatility, and local native materials<; Collage>in the pictorial arts, the assembling and pasting together of materials not usually associated with one another; in literature, works incorporating quotations, allusions, foreign expressions, and nonverbal elements<; Baroque>a term applied first to the architectural style that flourished in Europe from the late sixteenth century until well into the eighteenth century<; Ekphrasis (also Ecphrasis)>the representation of a visual or graphic work inside a literary work; sometimes used for the representation of an artwork of any kind<; Terribilita>a quality of awe-inspiring artworks in which a figure who appears to be at ease also shows great tension, strength, and the potential for terrific action; first applied to Michelangelo and his sculptures<; Constructivism>A Russian avant-garde movement of the 1910s–1920s that treated art as a constructed object serving social purposes.<; Catalogue Raisonné>A comprehensive, annotated catalogue of all the known works of an artist.<; Abstract (adjective)>opposed to concrete, the term abstract means removed from any real world; with graphic art, abstract usually connotes the nonrepresentational or nonobjective<; Mannerism>a highly affected style that was fashionable in the graphic arts around the turn of the sixteenth century, roughly contemporary with gongorism and marinism in literature<; Outsider Art>art produced by persons on the outside of every official or unofficial arena of production<; Picturesque>a word applied to certain kinds of writing by analogy to a type of painting that sought a middle ground between the sublime and the beautiful<

column4: Rondeau>a set French verse pattern; artificial but very popular with many English poets<; Blank Verse>unrhymed but otherwise regular verse—usually iambic pentameter<; Free Verse>vers libre; verse that is relatively free, managing without rhyme, meter, or regular rhythm<; Limerick>a form of light verse that follows a definite pattern: five anapestic lines of which the first, second, and fifth, consisting of three feet, rhyme; and the third and fourth lines, consisting of two feet, rhyme<; Clerihew>a form of light verse invented by and named for Edmund Clerihew Bentley (1875-1956), who also wrote detective fiction<; Villanelle>a fixed nineteen-line form, originally French, employing only two rhymes and repeating two of the lines according to a set pattern<; Amphigory (or Amphigouri)>verse that sounds well but contains little or no sense or meaning; either nonsense verse or nonsensical parody<; Triolet>one of the simpler French verse forms, consisting of eight lines with only two rhymes, the first two lines being repeated as the last two and the first line recurring also as the fourth<; Echo Verse>poetry in which the closing syllables of one line are repeated, as by an echo, in the following line with a different meaning, forming a reply or a comment<; Macaronic>(1) Pejoratively, “a blockhead” or “a dandy.” (2) Writing that combines two or more languages<; Nonsense Verse>a variety of light verse entertaining because of its strong rhythmic quality and lack of logic, often with coined nonsense words<; Projective Verse>a kind of free verse that regards meter and form as artificial and in which the poet “projects” a voice primarily through the content and the propulsive quality of breathing, which alone determines the line<; Sestina>one of the most difficult and complex of verse forms, consisting of six six-lined stanzas and a three-lined envoy<; Virelay>a French verse form (related to lai) of which the number of stanzas and the number of lines to the stanza are unlimited<; Bob and Wheel>a stanza in the revived alliterative verse of the later Middle English period in which unrhymed alliterative lines are followed by a very short line, the bob, and a short-lined rhymed quatrain, the wheel<; Fourteeners>a verse form consisting of fourteen syllables arranged in iambs<; Doggerel>rude verse; any poorly executed attempt at poetry<; Goliardic Verse>lilting Latin verse, usually satiric, composed by university students and wandering scholars in Germany, France, and England in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries<; Heroic Verse>poetry composed in heroic couplets<; Chant Royal>one of the most complex French verse forms, consisting of sixty lines arranged in five stanzas of eleven lines each and an envoy of five lines<; Quantitative Versification>a system based on rhythm determined by quantity—that is, relative length or duration of sound<; Rap>earlier, informal conversation; later, a style of performance that usually involves improvised rhymed verse sung or chanted to recorded instrumental music<; Versification>the art and practice of writing verse<; Syllabic Verse>verse in which the measure is determined by the number of syllables in the line<; Ballade>one of the most popular of the artificial French verse forms, usually three stanzas and an envoy, with a refrain recurring at the end of each stanza and of the envoy<; Prosody>the principles of versification, particularly as they refer to rhyme, meter, rhythm, and stanza<; Cento>a literary patchwork—usually in verse—made up of scraps from one or many authors<; Accentual-Syllabic Verse>verse that depends for its rhythm both on the number of syllables per line and on the pattern of accented and unaccented syllables<; Alliterative Verse>verse forms, usually Germanic or Celtic in origin, in which the metrical structure is based on patterned repetition of initial sounds within the lines<; Twiner>a sort of double limerick devised by Walter de la Mare and displayed in his Stuff and Nonsense (1927)<; Englyn>a venerable Welsh pattern of verse, usually a quatrain with complex rules governing alliteration and rhyme<; Skeltonic Verse (“Skeltonics” or “Skeltoniads”)>a rollicking form of verse employed by the English poet John Skelton (ca. 1460-1529) consisting of short lines rhymed in groups of varying length, designed to suggest unconventionality and lack of dignity<; Verset>a verse or versicle, especially one of the short verses of a religious scripture<; Versicle (also versicule, versiculus [plural versiculi])>a short verse, verset; in liturgical use, a short sentence from the Psalms recited in responsive readings<; Chain Verse>poetry in which the stanzas are linked through some pattern of repetition<; Macaronic Verse>a type of verse that mingles two or more languages<; Roundelay>a modification of the rondel<; Vers de société>brief lyrical verse in a genial, sportive mood and sophisticated in both subject and treatment<; Rondel>a French verse form—a variant of the rondeau, to which it is related historically<; Alexandrine>a verse with six iambic feet (iambic hexameter)<; Amoebean Verses>pastoral verses in matched strophes or stanzas spoken by two speakers alternately<; Correlative Verses>verses that take the form of abbreviated sentences having a linear correlative relationship<; Nursery Rhyme>brief verses—often anonymous and traditional—with percussive rhythm and frequent, heavy rhyme, written for young children<; Verse Paragraph>a nonstanzaic, continuous verse form, in which the lines are grouped in unequal blocks according to content<; Douzain>a verse of twelve lines<; Poikilomorphism>“Variable form”; applied to rare cases of verse form that preserves rhythm, meter, and stanza length but varies rhyme scheme from stanza to stanza<; Roundel>a variation of the rondeau, generally attributed to Swinburne, who wrote “A Century of Roundels.<; Adonic Verse>in Greek and Latin prosody, the measure that consists of a dactyl and a spondee or a dactyl and a trochee—probably so called after the Adonia, the festival of Adonis<; Album Verse>casual verse designed to be included in a keepsake album, especially popular in the early nineteenth century<; Anglo-Saxon Versification>see Old English Versification<; Asynartete>“Not connected”; said of a verse measure in which rhythmic members consist of two unrelated patterns<; French Forms>certain prescribed patterns, sometimes referred to as the fixed forms, that originated in France largely during the time of the troubadours<; Dub>a type of poetry originating in Jamaica around 1975 with words improvised to a background of recorded music<; Hendecasyllabic Verse>a line of eleven syllables, frequent in Greek and Latin poetry and a standard line in Italian<; Double Dactyls>a form of light verse consisting of two stanzas, each having four lines of two dactyls<; Light Verse>humorous, comic, witty poems<; Kyrielle>a rare French form, usually composed of short rhymed couplets with a word or larger verbal group repeated as a refrain<; Hudibrastic Verse>the octosyllabic couplet as adapted by Samuel Butler in his mock heroic poem Hudibras, which was published in three parts between 1663 and 1678<; Numbers>a term, now just about obsolete, meaning “measured language” or regular verse in general<; Redondilla>a Spanish measure, usually in octosyllabic couplets or quatrains with various rhyme schemes; used in Ezra Pound’s early “Redondillas.<; Qualitative Versification>versification based on patterns of accented and unaccented syllables<; Prosa, Prose>in the late Middle Ages and early Renaissance, a disdainful classification for writing not in the classical quantitative style, even that using qualitative scansion and rhyme<; Old English Versification>the metrical system employed by poets before 1100<; Vers Libre>a nineteenth-century French poetic movement to free poetry from strict rules resulted in cadenced and rhythmic poetry called vers libre, which means “free verse.<; Tumbling Verse>see Skeltonic Verse<; Society Verse>light, sophisticated verse<; Verse>used in two senses: (1) as a unit of poetry, in which case it has the same significance as stanza or line; and (2) as a name given generally to metrical composition<

column4: Terza rima>a three-line stanza, supposedly devised by Dante (for his Divine Comedy) with rhyme scheme aba bcb cdc ded and so forth<; Pantoum>the pantoum may consist of any number of four-line stanzas, but in any case, the second and fourth lines of one stanza must reappear as the first and third lines of the following stanza<; Sestina>one of the most difficult and complex of verse forms, consisting of six six-lined stanzas and a three-lined envoy<; Cinquain>any five-line stanza; more precisely, the five-line stanza used by Adelaide Crapsey, of unrhymed lines of two, four, six, eight, and two syllables<; Tercet>a stanza of three lines—a triplet—in which each line ends with the same rhyme<; Sapphic>a stanzaic pattern named for the Greek poet Sappho, with three lines of eleven or twelve syllables each and a fourth of five syllables<; Dizain>A poem or stanza of ten lines, usually with eight or ten syllables per line.<; Envoy (also envoi)>a conventionalized stanza appearing at the close of certain kinds of poems; particularly associated with the French ballade<; Ballad Stanza>the stanza of the popular or folk ballad—usually consisting of four lines rhyming abcb, with the first and third lines carrying four accents and the second and fourth carrying three<; Hymnal Stanza>see Common Measure<; Quatrain>a stanza of four lines<; Quintain (or Quintet)>a stanza of five lines<; Common Measure>see Common Meter<; Long Measure>a stanza of four lines of iambic tetrameter rhyming either abab or abcb<; Quatorzain>a stanza of fourteen lines<; Short Measure (or Meter)>a stanza widely used for hymns, consisting of four lines rhyming either abab or abcb<; Stanza>a recurrent grouping of two or more verse lines in terms of length, metrical form, and, often, rhyme scheme<; Octave>an eight-lined stanza; chiefly, the first eight-lined division of the Italian sonnet, as distinct from the sestet<; Ottava Rima>a stanza consisting of eight iambic pentameter (or hendecasyllabic) lines rhyming abababec<; Pentastich>a poem or a stanza of five lines; a quintet; a cinquain<; Alcaics>verses written according to the manner of the odes of Alcaeus—usually a four-stanza poem, with each stanza composed of four lines<; Common Meter>a stanza of four lines, with the first and third being iambic tetrameter (eight syllables) and the second and fourth iambic trimeter (six syllables), rhymed abab or abcb<; Heroic Quatrain>four lines of iambic pentameter rhyming abab, brought to perfection in Gray’s “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.<; Englyn>a venerable Welsh pattern of verse, usually a quatrain with complex rules governing alliteration and rhyme<; Heroic Stanza>another name for the heroic quatrain<; Rhyme Royal (or Rime Royal)>a seven-lined iambic pentameter stanza rhyming ababbcc, sometimes with an alexandrine (hexameter) seventh line<; Pushkin Stanza>the stanza used by Alexander Pushkin in his verse-novel Eugene Onegin: fourteen tetrameter lines rhyming abab ccdd effe gg<; Rime Couée>a tail-rhyme stanza, in which two lines—usually in tetrameter—are followed by a short line—usually in trimeter—as in aabccb<; Sextain>a stanza or strophe of six lines<; Homostrophic>consisting of structurally identical strophes; hence, made up of stanzas of the same pattern<; Tristich>a stanza of three lines<; Triad>in classical prosody, a set of three lyric stanzas—the first two (strophe and antistrophe) metrically alike and the third (epode) different<; Septet>a stanza of seven lines<; Douzain>a verse of twelve lines<; Fixed Forms>a name sometimes given to definite patterns of line and stanza<; In Memoriam Stanza>a quatrain of iambic tetrameter rhyming abba<; Strophe>a stanza; in the Pindaric ode, the first stanza and every subsequent third stanza<; Spenserian Stanza>a stanza of nine iambic lines—the first eight in pentameter and the ninth in hexameter<; Rubáiyát Stanza>the stanza that FitzGerald used for his translation of The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyam: a quatrain of iambic pentameter rhyming aaba<; Envelope Stanza>A stanza in which the opening line or rhyme is repeated at the end, enclosing the lines between.<; Burns Stanza>a variant form of the tail-rhyme stanza, named for Robert Burns, who used it frequently<; Chaucerian Stanza>see Rhyme Royal<; Contrerime>a quatrain, so named by Paul-Jean Toulet, in which an alternating syllabic scheme of 8-6-8-6 is opposed by a chiastic rhyme scheme of abba<; Heptastich>a seven-lined stanza<; French Forms>certain prescribed patterns, sometimes referred to as the fixed forms, that originated in France largely during the time of the troubadours<; Hardy Stanza>an eight-line stanza adapted and perfected by Thomas Hardy, with a ballad-like mixture of four-stress and three-stress lines<; Elegiac Stanza>the iambic pentameter quatrain, rhyming abab<; Habbie>a component of the names of stanzas used in Scottish poetry, such as the six-lined “standard Habbie” rhyming aaabab<; Hexastich>a stanza of six lines<; Keats Ode Stanza>a stanza developed by John Keats (1795-1821) for some of the odes that he wrote toward the end of his life<; Rann>in Irish literature, a piece of verse—usually a stanza or, specifically, a quatrain<; Omar Khayyam Stanza>see Rubaiyat Stanza<; Sixain>a stanza or strophe of six lines<; Tail-Rhyme Stanza>a stanza containing, among longer lines, two or more short lines that rhyme with each other and serve as “tails” to the divisions of the stanza<; Stave>a stanza, particularly of a song<; Yeats Stanza>an eight-lined stanza that W. B. Yeats employed in a few poems, including “A Prayer for My Daughter” and “Byzantium.<; Venus and Adonis Stanza>six lines of iambic pentameter rhyming ababcc, named from its use in Shakespeare’s poem<

column4: Carmen Figuratum>a figure poem, one so written that the form of the printed words suggests the subject matter<; Shaped Verse>a poem so constructed that its printed form suggests its subject matter<; Altar Poem>another term for a carmen figuratum, a poem in which the lines are so arranged that they form a design on the page, taking the shape of the subject—frequently, an altar or a cross<; Figure Poem>a poem written so that its printed shape suggests its subject matter<; Square Poem>a poem with a certain number of syllables per line and the same number of lines in a stanza<; Concrete Poetry>poetry that exploits the graphic, visual aspect of writing; a specialized application of what Aristotle called opsis (“spectacle”) and Pound “phanopoeia.<; Map Poem>a poem that gives the impression of having been written while the poet was studying a map<; Pruning Poem>a poem in which succeeding rhyme words have initial sounds or letters pared away<; Spatialism>A mid-twentieth-century experimental poetry movement that treated the page as a visual space.<; Pattern Poem>another name for carmen figuratum or figure poem<

column4: Consonance>the relation between words in which the final consonants in the stressed syllables agree but the vowels that precede them differ<; Assonance>generally, patterning of vowel sounds without regard to consonants<; Dissonance>harsh and inharmonious sounds; a marked breaking of the music of poetry, which may be intentional, as it often is in Browning and Hardy<; Sigmatism>The excessive or deliberate repetition of the s sound.<; Alliteration>the repetition of initial identical consonant sounds or any vowel sounds in successive or closely associated syllables<; Metathesis>the interchange of position between sounds in a word<; Cacophony>the opposite of euphony; a harsh, unpleasant combination of sounds<; Euphony>pleasing sounds; the opposite of cacophony<; Modulation>A change in tone, pitch, or rhythm in verse or speech.<; Diction>strictly, the use of words in oral or written discourse, including vocabulary and syntax<; Melopoeia>a Greek term renovated by Ezra Pound, who used it for the whole articulatory-acoustic-auditory range of poetry<; Transverse Alliteration>alliteration of the patterns abab or abba; successive or chiastic cynghanedd<; Cadence>in one sense, the sound pattern that precedes a marked pause or the end of a sentence, making it interrogatory, hortatory, pleading, and so forth<; Syntax>the rule-governed arrangement of words in sentences; with vocabulary, one of the two components of diction<; Paragoge>the addition of an extra letter, syllable, or sound at the end of a word<; Transvocalization>a rare species of language-to-language writing that attempts to preserve the sound of the original while using real words in the new language—not necessarily words that translate the sense of the original<; Colliteration (or Coliteration)>a name suggested for the effect—similar to alliteration—of beginning accented syllables with similar consonants<; Cynghanedd>originally a medieval Welsh term covering a wide range of verse devices, revived by Gerard Manley Hopkins to refer to harmonious patterns of interlaced multiple alliteration<; Cross-Alliteration>alliteration of two separate consonants or clusters arranged as xyxy or xyyx<; Sibilance>The repetition of hissing s, sh, and z sounds.<; Pitch>a potentially significant quality of articulated sound, determined by relative frequency, intensity, and volume; its importance varies from language to language and, in some, is an element of prosody<; Polyphonic Prose>Prose that uses the devices of poetry, such as rhyme, meter, and alliteration.<; Head Rhyme>see Alliteration<; Hyperthesis>transposition or metathesis of a sound or a syllable<; Alliterative Prose>a medieval tradition of giving dignity to prose by adding prosodic devices from alliterative verse<; Anaphone (or Anaphony)>the acoustic counterpart of the anagram<; Letter>used in some derogatory phrases to mean the sounds repeated in alliteration: “affect the letter,” “hunt the letter,” “lick the letter,” and so forth<; Lenis>a consonant with relatively gentle articulation, opposed to fortis<; Phonestheme, Phonaestheme>unit or units of sound with a specific semantic meaning, either inherently or sentimentally<; Poetic Diction>language chosen for a supposedly inherent poetic quality<; Stave-Rime (from German Stabreim)>alliteration in general or an instance of it<; Voiceless (also Unvoiced)>applied to consonant sounds uttered without voice<; Voiced>applied to consonant sounds uttered with vibration of the vocal chords<; Voiced Nasal>applied to voiced consonant sounds with a nasal component<; column4: Palimpsest>a writing surface, whether of vellum, papyrus, or other material, that has been used more than once for manuscript purposes<; Interpolation>in editing, the supplying of an item in a series or a damaged text by some process of deduction or induction<; Redaction>a revision or editing of a manuscript<; Silent Correction>an editor’s correction of an indisputably obvious error with no indication that a change has been made<; Scribal Error>an error made by a scribe in the copying of a manuscript, most commonly problems in spelling, translation, omission, repetition, and misreading<; Octapla (also Octaples)>“Eightfolds”: eight versions of a text in parallel columns; usually applied to ancient Scriptural texts<; Uncial>descriptive of large, rounded letters such as those used in some Latin and Greek manuscripts from the Middle Ages through the eighteenth century<; Sigla (plural of Siglum)>a letter or other written character used as a shorthand designation for versions of a text<; Bad Quartos>a. W. Pollard’s term for certain notably corrupt, garbled, and nearly incoherent early editions of Shakespeare’s plays<; Errata>plural of erratum; a mistake<; Paleography>the study of old forms of handwriting, important in textual studies for establishing texts and deciding authorship<; Textual Criticism>a scholarly activity that attempts to establish the authoritative text of a work<; Haplography>A copying error in which a repeated letter or word is written only once.<; Recension>a text that incorporates the best readings taken by critical editing from several sources<; Scholium (plural Scholia)>(1) A note or comment, usually a matter of interpretation or explanation. (2) A trite saying<; Center for Scholarly Editions>A committee of the Modern Language Association that reviews and approves scholarly editions of texts.<; Locus Desperatus>A passage in a manuscript or text so corrupt that it cannot be restored.<; Tetrapla>An edition of a text in four parallel versions, especially Origen’s four-column Old Testament.<; Copy Text>that text of a work used by a textual scholar as the basis with which to compare various editions, impressions, and issues in an effort to arrive at the closest possible approximation of the author’s original intent<; Emendation>a change made in a literary text by an editor for removing error or supplying a supposed correct reading that has been obscured or lost through textual inaccuracy or tampering<; Foul Copy>manuscript that—having already been used for typesetting—bears printer’s marks, editor’s queries, and frequently spike holes, ink stains, and fingerprints<; Scholiast>one who prepared the Scholia on medieval manuscripts, particularly copies of Greek and Latin texts<; Allograph>A document written by one person on behalf of another, as opposed to an autograph.<; Accidental (noun)>in textual criticism, an accidental is any element of a text not essential to the meaning of the words; most commonly, accidentals include capitalization, spelling, and punctuation<; Apparatus (also apparatus criticus, critical apparatus)>the means by which a document is presented for textual study<; Codex>a manuscript book, particularly of biblical or classical writing<; Collate>to compare in detail two or more texts, versions, editions, or printings to determine and record the points of agreement and disagreement<; Corrigenda>plural of corrigendum, an item to be corrected<; Crux>a point of decision in textual editing<; Definitive Edition>an edition claiming to have final or permanent authority<; Editing>the preparation of manuscript for the compositor and printer<; Dubia>items of uncertain or disputed authorship<; Forgeries, Literary>writings that forgers offer as the genuine writing of another, though they have themselves composed them<; Foul Proof>marked printer’s proof from which corrections have been made<; Higher Criticism>certain aspects of the study of biblical texts in the nineteenth century, seeking to determine the authorship, date, place of origin, and historical credibility of the books of the Bible<; Hexapla (also Hexaple)>a sixfold text arranged in parallel columns to permit detailed comparison of versions<; Holograph>something completely handwritten by the author<; Masorah>the body of critical commentary on the texts of Hebrew Scriptures, compiled at least a thousand years ago by Jewish scholars known as Masoretes<; Manuscript, Medieval>the art of manuscript-making, highly developed in the Middle Ages, when there was no mechanical means for multiplying copies<; Pseudo-Shakespearean Plays>plays attributed to Shakespeare at one time but now not accepted as his by the best authorities<; Ossianic Controversy>see Forgeries, Literary<; Pirated Edition>an unauthorized edition of a work, usually stolen from one country and produced for sale in another<; Paralipomena (plural of paralipomenon)>something omitted from a text but later included in an appendix or elsewhere<; Variorum Edition>an edition of an author’s work presenting complete variant readings of the possible texts and full notes of critical comments and interpretation<; Version>a particular form or variant<; Substantive>distinguished from accidental; applied to actual words and meanings of a text<; Scribe>any writer, specifically one who copies manuscripts of classical or medieval texts<

column4: Epistolary Novel>a novel in which the narrative is carried forward by letters written by one or more of the characters<; Novel of Manners>a novel dominated by social customs, manners, conventions, and habits of a definite social class<; Metafiction>a work of fiction, a major concern of which is the nature of fiction itself<; Novel of Character>a novel that emphasizes character rather than exciting episode<; Picaresque Novel>a chronicle—usually autobiographical—presenting the life story of a rascal of low degree engaged in menial tasks and making his living more through his wits than his industry<; Bildungsroman>a novel that deals with the development of a young person, usually from adolescence to maturity; it is frequently autobiographical<; Novel of Incident>a novel in which episodic action dominates and plot and character are subordinate<; Roman à Clef>a novel in which actual persons are presented under the guise of fiction<; Novel of the Soil>a special kind of regionalism in the novel, in which the lives of people struggling for existence in remote rural sections are starkly portrayed<; Psychological Novel>prose fiction that places unusual emphasis on interior characterization and on the motives, circumstances, and internal action that spring from and develop external action<; Roman à Thèse>french: a thesis novel—one intended to establish and illustrate a social doctrine<; Novel of Sensibility>a novel in which the characters have a heightened emotional response to events, producing in the reader a similar response<; Künstlerroman>a form of the apprenticeship novel in which the protagonist is an artist struggling from childhood to maturity toward an understanding of his or her creative mission<; Dime Novel>a cheaply printed, paperbound tale of adventure or detection, originally selling for about ten cents; an American equivalent of the British penny dreadful<; Gothic Novel>a novel in which magic, mystery, and chivalry are the chief characteristics<; Penny Dreadful>a cheaply produced paperbound novel or novelette of mystery, adventure, or violence popular in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries in England; equivalent of the American dime novel<; Campus Novel>a work, usually comic, set at a university<; Entwicklungsroman>a German term for a type of Bildungsroman that emphasizes the development of the principal character<; Roman Noir>a thriller; a novel in the dark mode of film noir that involves crime, detection, punishment, and corruption in high places<; Young Man from the Provinces>a phrase used by Lionel Trilling for a kind of novel that deals with the experiences of a young provincial in a great city<; Roman-Fleuve>“River novel”; a substantial, slow-moving novel that typically chronicles the lives of several generations; sometimes, a set or sequence of novels<; Sociological Novel>A novel that portrays social conditions, often in order to bring about reform.<; Apprenticeship Novel>a novel that recounts the youth and young adulthood of a protagonist who is attempting to learn the nature of the world<; Avant-Garde>a military metaphor drawn from the French “vanguard” and applied to new writing that shows striking (and usually self-conscious) innovations in style, form, and subject matter<; Documentary Novel>a form of fiction in which there is an elaborate piling up of factual data, frequently including such materials as newspaper articles, popular songs, legal reports, and trial transcripts<; Romantic Novel>a type of novel marked by strong interest in action, with episodes often based on love, adventure, and combat<; Education Novel>a form of novel developed in the late eighteenth century, presenting in fictional form a plan for the education of a young person into a desirable citizen and a morally and intellectually self-reliant individual<; Historical Novel>a novel that reconstructs a past age<; Lyrical Novel>a species of novel in which conventional narration is subordinated to the presentation of inner thoughts, feelings, and moods<; Hollywood Novel>a novel set in Hollywood itself or else about the film industry at large<; Interior Monologue>one of the techniques for presenting the stream of consciousness of a character, recording the character’s internal emotional experience<; Verse-Novel (or Novel in Verse)>a novel written in verse, using either rhymed stanzas or blank verse<; Erziehungsroman>the novel of upbringing or education<; Propaganda>material propagated for the purpose of advocating a political or ideological position; also the mechanism for such propaganda<; Political Novel>a novel in which aspects of political life are essential ingredients<; Realistic Novel>a type of novel that emphasizes truthful representation of the actual<; Well-Made Novel>a novel with a tightly constructed plot, freedom from extraneous incidents or subplots, clear motivation for the actions of its characters, and a sense of economy and inevitability<; Novel of Ideas>A novel in which the discussion of ideas is more important than plot or character.<; Roman>The French word for a novel or long prose fiction.<; Antirealistic Novel>the contemporary novel of fantasy, illogicality, and absurdity<; Detective Story>a story in which a crime—usually a murder, with the identity of the perpetrator unknown—is solved by a detective through a logical assembling and interpretation of palpable evidence, known as clues<; Didactic Novel>any novel plainly designed to teach a lesson; chiefly a synonym for the education novel, an eighteenth-century form presenting an ideal education for some young person<; Mystery Story (or Novel)>a work in which mystery or terror plays a controlling part<; New Novel>a term—literally from the French nouveau roman—often applied to the antinovel<; International Novel>a novel in which one important spring of conflict is national difference, especially among characters who must travel<; Medical Thriller>popular melodramatic fiction concentrating on plots and characters drawn from the world of illness, research, medicine, and threats such as epidemics and criminal malpractice<; Noir>an adjective taken over from the phrase film noir to apply to any work, especially one involving crime, that is notably dark, brooding, cynical, complex, and pessimistic<; Novelization>the conversion of a screenplay or a television play into novel form, usually to capitalize on its popularity<; Problem Novel>a narrative that derives its chief interest from working out some central problem<; Propaganda Novel>a novel dealing with a special social, political, economic, or moral issue or problem and possibly advocating a doctrinaire solution<; Play-Poem>the genre into which Virginia Woolf placed her novel The Waves (1931)<; Nonfiction Novel>truman Capote’s classification for In Cold Blood, in which a historical event is described in a way that exploits some of the devices of fiction<; Sentimental Novel>a novel reflecting the sentimentalism of the eighteenth century, beginning with Richardson’s Pamela (1740); also called the novel of sensibility<; Thesis Novel>a novel that deals with some problems so as to suggest a thesis, usually in the form of a solution to the problem<; Thriller>a fast-paced work involving crime, pursuit, suspense, and surprise<; Stream-of-Consciousness Novel>the type of novel taking as its subject matter the flow of the stream of consciousness of one or more of its characters<; School Story>loosely, any fiction set in a school; limited sometimes to fictions set in a school away from the student’s home during adolescence, with important influences on intellectual and moral development<; Sporting Novel>a piece of prose fiction—usually comic—having to do with sporting activities, especially fox-hunting<

Graces, The>in Greek myth, the three sister goddesses who confer grace, beauty, charm, and joy on human beings and nature<; Four Ages>a scheme of great antiquity—dividing history into a line or cycle of ages—conventionally associated with gold, silver, brass, and iron<; Trivium>the three studies leading to the bachelor’s degree in the medieval universities: grammar, logic, and rhetoric<; Calliope>In Greek mythology, the Muse of epic poetry.<; Erato>In Greek mythology, the Muse of lyric and love poetry.<; Quaternion>a work with four as a basic part of its structure<; Quadrivium>in the medieval university curriculum, the four subjects leading to the Master of Arts (Magister Artium) degree: arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy<; Four Elements>see Elements<; Trilogy>a composition in three substantial parts, each of which is in itself a complete unit<; Clio>In Greek mythology, the Muse of history.<; Polyhymnia>In Greek mythology, the Muse of sacred song and hymns.<; Septenary>A line of seven metrical feet; a group of seven.<; Terpsichore>In Greek mythology, the Muse of dance and choral song.<; Fates, The>the three sisters—Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos—who, the Greeks and Romans believed, controlled the birth, life, and death of all human beings<; Melpomene>In Greek mythology, the Muse of tragedy.<; Thalia>In Greek mythology, the Muse of comedy and pastoral poetry.<; Canonical Hours>the seven periods of the day set aside for prayers of a specified sort: matins (with lauds), prime, terce, sext, none, vespers, and complin<; Ennead>any set of nine<; Interpretation, Fourfold Method>the levels employed in biblical interpretation in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance<; Liberal Arts>studies devoted to general cultivation and education, not technical or professional<; column4: Peripety (or Peripeteia)>the reversal of fortune for a protagonist—possibly either a fall, as in a tragedy, or a success, as in a comedy<; Climax>a rising order of importance in the ideas expressed<; Exposition>one of the four chief types of composition, with the others being argumentation, description, and narration; its purpose is to explain something<; Reversal>the change in fortune for a protagonist<; Deus (or Dea) ex Machina>the employment of some unexpected and improbable incident to make things turn out right<; Freytag’s Pyramid>a diagram of the structure of a five-act tragedy, given by Gustav Freytag in Technik des Dramas (1863)<; Dénouement>literally, “unknotting”; the final unraveling of a plot; the solution of a mystery; an explanation or outcome<; Unities>the principles of dramatic structure involving the unities of action, time, and place<; Catastrophe>the conclusion of a play, particularly of a tragedy; the last of the four parts into which the ancients divided a play<; Complication>that part of a plot in which the entanglement caused by the conflict of opposing forces is developed<; Final Suspense, Moment of>the ray of hope sometimes appearing just before the catastrophe of a tragedy<; Falling Action>the second half or resolution of a dramatic plot<; Rising Action>the part of a dramatic plot that has to do with the complication of the action<; Crisis>the point at which the opposing forces that create the conflict interlock in the decisive action on which a plot will turn<; Epilogue>a concluding statement; generally, the final remarks of an actor addressed to the audience<; Point of Attack>the moment in the work at which the main action of the plot begins<; Relief Scene>that part of a tragedy—usually as a part of the falling action—whose purpose is to provide temporary emotional relaxation for the audience<; Anagnorisis>in drama, the discovery or recognition that leads to the peripety or reversal<; Introduction>the opening of a piece of writing<; Agon>literally a contest of any kind; in Greek tragedy, a prolonged dispute—often a formal debate. Agon has subsequently come to mean any conflict<; Anticlimax>an arrangement of details such that the lesser appears at the point where something greater is expected<; Conflict>the struggle that grows out of the interplay of two opposing forces<; Exciting Force>the force that starts the conflict of opposing interests and sets in motion the rising action of a play<; Dramatic Structure>the technical structure of a play, determined by the necessities of developing the dramatic conflict; the ancients compared the plot of a drama to the tying and untying of a knot<; Discovery>the revelation of a fact previously unknown, knowledge of which now results in the turning of action<; Inciting Moment>the name used by Freytag for the event or force that sets in motion the rising action of a play<; Recognition>the acquisition of knowledge previously withheld that works a decisive change; in a recognition plot, it brings about the principal reversal or peripety<; Resolution>the events following the climax<; Protasis>a classical term for the introductory act or the exposition of a drama<

column4: Proscenium>that part of the stage in a modern theater that lies between the orchestra and the curtain<; Upstaging>a stage movement in which one performer moves upstage of another (that is, to the rear of the stage), forcing the latter to turn away from the audience<; Theater in the Round>the presentation of plays on a stage surrounded by the audience<; Apron Stage>the portion of a stage that extends in front of the proscenium arch<; Backstage>an area behind and around the outer stage of a theater, with spaces for storage of props and costumes, dressing rooms, offices, and so forth<; Fourth Wall>the invisible wall of a room through which the audience conventionally witnesses what occurs on a stage imagined as a room with four walls and a ceiling, with the fourth wall being presented as just behind the curtain<; Mise en Scène>the stage setting of a play, including scenery, properties, and the general arrangement of the piece<; Pit>the part of a theater on the main floor, normally behind the stalls<; Upstage>The part of the stage farthest from the audience; also, to draw attention away from another actor.<; Arena Stage>a stage on which the actors, surrounded by the audience, make exits and entrances through the aisles<; Box Set>a stage set that realistically represents a room with three walls, with the fourth wall being imagined on the side toward the audience<; Curtain>a piece of heavy material that screens the stage from the audience and by being raised or opened and lowered or closed marks the beginning and end of an act or scene<; Green Room>an area in a theater where performers and other functionaries may gather when not carrying out their duties<; Entrance>the act of coming on stage<; P.S.>stage direction for “prompt side” (or “prompter side”)—stage left in Britain; stage right in the United States<; On Stage, Onstage>literally or figuratively on a stage<; Off Stage, Offstage>literally, not on a stage; usually applied to a voice or other sound that an audience hears without seeing the source<; O.P., o.p.>a theatrical abbreviation for “opposite the prompter” side: stage right in Britain; column4: Hyperbole>exaggeration, used to heighten effect or for humor<; Paradox>a statement that although seemingly contradictory or absurd may actually be well-founded or true<; Metaphor>an analogy identifying one object with another and ascribing to the first object one or more of the qualities of the second<; a term—literally, “ox plowing”—that describes the direction of writing in certain ancient inscriptions<; Inversion>the placing of a sentence element out of its normal position<; Symploce>a figure of speech combining anaphora and epistrophe: the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses and of another at their end<; Motif (or Motive)>a simple element that serves as a basis for expanded narrative; or, less strictly, a conventional situation, device, interest, or incident<; Parallelism>such an arrangement that one element of equal importance with another is similarly developed and phrased<; Paraleipsis, Paralepsis, or Paralipsis>pretending to say nothing about something one goes on to say quite a bit about<; Epistrophe>The repetition of the same word or phrase at the end of successive clauses or lines.<; Trope>in rhetoric, a figure of speech involving a “turn” or change of sense—the use of a word in a sense other than the literal<; Analepsis>A flashback; a narrative return to events that occurred before the present moment of the story.<; Repetition>reiteration of a word, sound, phrase, or idea<; Epitrope>A figure in which the speaker ironically concedes or grants permission, often to make a point.<; Catachresis>strictly, any misuse or misapplication of a word; sometimes used for a mixed figure<; Figures of Speech>the various uses of language that depart from customary construction, order, or significance<; Juxtaposition>The placement of two or more things side by side, often to compare or contrast them.<; Procatalepsis>A figure in which a speaker anticipates and answers an objection before it is raised.<; Agnomination (also adnomination, annomination)>a term used between 1600 and 1800 to mean, variously, any play on words, especially such as involved names of persons<; Anacoenesis (also Anachinosis)>asking a question as though to seek the opinion of one’s hearer, reader, opponent, or judge<; Aposiopesis>the intentional failure to complete a sentence<; Apophasis>a rhetorical figure in which one makes an assertion while seeming or pretending to suppress or deny it<; Epanaphora>repetition of words at the beginnings of lines or sentences; commonly called anaphora<; Hypotyposis>vivid description, especially when used for rhetorical or dramatic effect<; Hysteron Proteron>“Latter before”; a figure of speech in which what should logically come last comes first<; Metanoia>a rhetorical figure whereby a speaker retracts or corrects something said<; Occupatio>device somewhat like occultatio, especially when one says “Not to mention...” or “To say nothing of...” and then goes ahead and mentions the topic<; Occultatio>emphasizing something by appearing to pass over it or by insinuation<; Paregmenon>the same as polyptoton; the use of two different words derived from the same root<; Systrophe>a listing of several properties of something in an elaborate metaphorical catalogue<

column4: Tritagonist>the actor taking the part third in importance in a Greek drama<; Foil>any person who through contrast underscores the distinctive characteristics of another; literally, a “leaf” of bright metal placed under a jewel to increase its brilliance<; Upstaging>a stage movement in which one performer moves upstage of another (that is, to the rear of the stage), forcing the latter to turn away from the audience<; Actor>a person who performs in a drama in any form; the term has replaced the earlier player<; Method (also Stanislavski Method)>a style of acting advanced by Constantin Stanislavski by which a performer prepares for a role by thoroughly identifying with a character in order to understand background, motivation, and conflicts<; Sock>the low-heeled slipper conventionally worn by the comic actor on the ancient stage—hence (figuratively), comedy itself<; Actor-Manager>a theater manager who also acts; a familiar type during the century after 1825<; Actress>a female actor<; Audition>a test in which a performer seeking employment appears before judges who may become employers or colleagues<; Business>action as distinct from dialogue, sometimes in the form “piece of business” or “bit of business.<; Cothurnus>the buskin—a thick-soled, laced boot worn by actors in Greek tragedy<; Curtain Call>an act of homage by an audience who—by sustained applause—call for performers to reappear on stage one or more times after the curtain has fallen<; Cue>in performance, a signal—such as a word or sound effect—that it is time for something else to happen<; Double Act>an act that routinely involves two performers seldom or never appearing separately<; Double Part>in the theater, the “doubling” of roles that permits one performer to play two or more roles<; Name Part, Name Role>the role that gives a theatrical or musical work its name<; Improvisation>a work or performance that is done on the spur of the moment—and without conscious preparation or preliminary drafts or rehearsals<; Line of Business>a performer’s typical range of roles, such as Old Man, Old Woman, or ingenue<; Player>a performer in a play; a somewhat commoner term than actor in Shakespeare’s time, the word is now seldom used<; Standby>a performer ready to take the place of a regular performer in case of emergencies; such people may be used less often than ordinary understudies<; Star>a performer of superlative talent, charisma, interest, or appeal; also, a featured performer or role<; Women as Actors>the appearance of women on the stage; in Renaissance England, women were not countenanced on the professional stage, and boys were trained to act women’s parts<; Understudy>a member of a theatrical company designated to prepare to take the place of a major performer or other person (such as the stage manager)<; Supernumerary (Super)>a member of a troupe or stock company with a subordinate job in a production<; Stanislavsky Method>see Method<
